Surah Al 'Imran

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

It is Madani, two hundred verses or, except one verse. It was named thus because the chosen status of the family of 'Imran, namely 'Isa, Yahya, Maryam and her mother, was mentioned in it, with what was not mentioned in any other surah, for it contains eighty-some verses. This election has been made a proof of the election of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and of his being made the one followed by every lover of Allah and beloved of Him.

It is also called: al-Zahra' (the Radiant), because it uncovered what had become confused for the People of the Two Books concerning the affair of 'Isa (peace be upon him). Al-Aman (the Security), because whoever holds fast to what is in it is safe from error concerning his affair. Al-Kanz (the Treasure), because it contains the secrets concerning 'Isa. Al-Mujadalah (the Disputation), because some eighty-odd verses of it were revealed concerning the disputation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with the Christians of Najran. Surat al-Istighfar (the Surah of Seeking Forgiveness), because of the words in it: "and those who seek forgiveness in the hours before dawn." Taybah (the Good), because it gathers the categories of the good people in the words: "the patient, the truthful..." to its end, as stated by al-Mahayimi.

By 'Imran is meant the father of Maryam, mother of 'Isa, peace be upon them both, as will be pointed out in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam and Noah and the family of Abraham and the family of 'Imran over the worlds﴾ [Al 'Imran: 33].

The discussion on the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words:

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ ﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence﴾ [Al 'Imran: 2] ﴿He has sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it, and He revealed the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3] [1–3]

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾: the discussion of this has preceded at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence﴾ [Al 'Imran: 2]: its interpretation has already preceded in the Verse of the Throne.

﴿He has sent down to you the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3]: that is, the Qur'an. He referred to it by the generic noun, indicating its complete superiority over the rest of the individuals in possessing the perfections of the genus, as though it alone deserves to be named "the Book" to the exclusion of all others, as the explicit naming of the Torah and the Gospel hints. ﴿In truth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3]: that is, with the truth in which there is no doubt. ﴿Confirming what was before it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3]: that is, of the books revealed before it.

Al-Mahayimi said: that is, making known the truthfulness of the earlier books. Abu Muslim said: what is meant by it is that Allah, the Exalted, never sent a prophet except with the call to His Oneness and belief in Him, to His transcendence above what is unfitting for Him, and the command to justice and goodness, and with the laws which are the welfare of every age. So the Qur'an confirms those books in all of that. ﴿And He revealed the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3]: a specification of what is before it and a clarification of the elevation of their station, confirming what came before it and paving the way for what comes after it. For by this the standing of what it confirms rises in eminence and distinction, and it increases in acceptance and reverence in hearts, and the state of whoever disbelieved in them both becomes more heinous in its vileness, and it entails the severe punishment and retribution that will be mentioned. Said by Abu al-Su'ud.

"Al-Tawrah" (the Torah) is a Hebrew name meaning (the Law). "Al-Injil" (the Gospel) is a Greek word meaning (the Good News), (p-750) that is, the good report. This is the correct view, as the scholars of the two Books have stated in their works. Some men of letters attempted to apply the two words to the patterns of the Arabic language and to derive them from it, but that is a confusion without a sound basis.

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[4] ﴿Before, as guidance for mankind. And He sent down the Criterion. Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah will have a severe punishment, and Allah is Exalted in Might, Owner of Retribution.﴾

﴿Before﴾ is connected to (anzala, "He sent down"), meaning: He sent down both of them before the revelation of the Book. The explicit mention of it, despite the matter being clear, is for emphasis in clarification. ﴿As guidance for mankind﴾, i.e., for the people of Musa (Moses) and Isa (Jesus). Or it may be more general, because this Ummah (community) is bound to worship by those laws that have not been abrogated. ﴿And He sent down the Criterion﴾, which is the heavenly Books that he mentioned, because all of them are a criterion that distinguishes between truth and falsehood. Or it is the Qur'an. He repeated its mention, describing it with what is its attribute and praise, in that it separates truth from falsehood, after mentioning it by the generic name, to magnify its status and display its excellence. Al-Razi said: It may also be said that He, Exalted is He, repeated its mention to show that He sent it down after the Torah and the Gospel, so as to make it a distinction between what the Jews and the Christians differed about of truth and falsehood. On this interpretation there is no repetition. He then favored taking al-Furqan (the Criterion) to mean the miracles that Allah, Exalted is He, paired with the sending down of these distinguishing Books between their claim and the claim of the liars. He said: So al-Furqan is the overpowering miracle that indicates its truthfulness and conveys the distinction between it and the rest of the differing Books. End of quote.

It is permissible that the intended meaning of al-Furqan is (al-Mizan, "the Balance"), referred to in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear evidences and sent down with them the Book and the Balance that mankind may maintain justice﴾ [al-Hadid: 25]. Al-Mizan is justice in all matters; and the word includes all of that, due to their convergence in meaning.

(p-751) ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾, i.e., deny them: ﴿for them﴾, because of their disbelief in them: ﴿is a severe punishment.﴾ This warning was brought after what preceded it, to urge submission and to deter from disobedience. ﴿And Allah is Exalted in Might﴾, who cannot be overcome, does what He wills: ﴿Owner of Retribution﴾, i.e., of punishment. It is said: Allah took retribution from him, meaning He punished him. And an-niqmah (retribution) is requital with punishment.

The discussion concerning His saying, exalted is He:

[5] ﴿Indeed, nothing is hidden from Allah, on the earth or in the heaven.﴾

﴿Indeed, nothing is hidden from Allah, on the earth or in the heaven.﴾ That is: He is aware of the disbelief of those who disbelieve and the faith of those who believe, and He will recompense them for it.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 6:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[6] ﴿He it is Who forms you in the wombs as He wills. There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

﴿He it is Who forms you in the wombs as He wills﴾ That is: He creates you in the wombs as He wills, male and female, beautiful and ugly, wretched and happy. ﴿There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[7] ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are clear (muhkamat), they are the foundation of the Book, and others that are ambiguous (mutashabihat). As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous in it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation. But none knows its interpretation except Allah. And those firmly grounded in knowledge say, "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord." And none will be reminded except those of understanding.﴾

﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are clear﴾, clear in their indication. ﴿They are the foundation of the Book﴾, meaning its basis on which rulings are relied upon. ﴿And others that are ambiguous﴾, which are those whose true reality Allah has kept to Himself knowledge of, because their reality, about which He informed, is not made clear, or those that admit of several meanings. He described all of it as muhkam in His words, ﴿whose verses have been made firm﴾ [Hud: 1], meaning that there is no defect in it, that it is true speech, eloquent in its wording and sound in its meanings. He described it as mutashabih in His words, ﴿a Book consistent, [its parts] resembling one another﴾ [al-Zumar: 23], meaning that some of it resembles the rest in excellence and confirms the rest. ﴿As for those in whose hearts is zaigh﴾, that is, inclination away from uprightness toward disbelief, desires and innovation. ﴿They follow what is ambiguous in it﴾, ﴿seeking discord﴾, that is, seeking to cast people into doubts and confusion. ﴿And seeking its interpretation﴾, ﴿but none knows its interpretation except Allah﴾ alone. ﴿And those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾, that is, those who are steadfast and well established, is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is ﴿they say, "We believe in it"﴾, that is, in the ambiguous, according to what Allah the Exalted intended. ﴿All of it﴾, of the muhkam and the mutashabih, ﴿is from our Lord﴾, ﴿and none will be reminded except those of understanding﴾, that is, the pure intellects free from leaning toward deviant desires. This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) which Allah the Exalted introduced as praise for those firmly grounded, for the keenness of their minds and the soundness of their reflection.

Note:
The scholars have many opinions regarding the muhkam and the mutashabih, and extensive discussions. The finest treatment of this subject that I have seen is an expansive piece by Shaykh al-Islam Taqi al-Din Ahmad ibn Taymiyya, may Allah have mercy on him and be pleased with him. In it he says:

The muhkam in the Qur'an is sometimes contrasted with the mutashabih, and both are from the signs of Allah. Sometimes it is contrasted with what Allah abrogated of what Satan had cast.

Some people make it the opposite of what Allah abrogated, absolutely, so that they say, "This verse is muhkam, not abrogated," and they regard the abrogated as not muhkam, even though Allah had sent it down first, following the apparent sense of His words: ﴿Then Allah abolishes what Satan casts, then Allah makes His verses firm﴾ [al-Hajj: 52].

These are three meanings contrasted with the muhkam, which one should take care to notice.

The sum of the matter is that ihkam (making firm) sometimes occurs in the revelation itself, and so it is contrasted with what Satan casts. The muhkam revealed from Allah is what Allah has made firm, that is, He distinguished it from being confused with other things, and distinguished from it what is not part of it. Ihkam is separation, distinction, differentiation and delimitation, by which a thing is established and its perfection achieved. For this reason the meaning of prevention entered into it, just as part of the meaning of a limit (hadd) is prevention, though not all of its meaning. Sometimes ihkam occurs in preserving the revelation in the view of one who contrasts it with naskh, which is the lifting of a ruling that had been legislated; this is a technical usage (istilahi). Or it is said (and this is more fitting): the early scholars (salaf) used to call every lifting "naskh", whether it was the lifting of a ruling or the lifting of an apparent indication. So every apparent sense whose apparent meaning is abandoned due to a stronger counter-indication, such as the specification of a general term (takhsis al-'amm) or the restriction of an absolute term (taqyid al-mutlaq), is called "abrogated" in the terminology of the salaf. The casting of Satan into his recitation (umniyyah) may occur in the very wording of the one who conveys, may occur in what the hearer hears, and may occur in the understanding, as He said: ﴿He sends down water from the sky, and valleys flow according to their measure﴾ [al-Ra'd: 17]. It is well known that whoever hears, hears the text whose ruling has been lifted, or an indication of it, and Satan casts into that recitation the following of that abrogated ruling. Then Allah makes His verses firm by means of the abrogating text through which the ruling was lifted, and the intended meaning became clear. In light of this, it is valid to say that the mutashabih and the abrogated are, in this sense, the same. And Allah knows best.

Sometimes ihkam is in the interpretation and meaning, which is distinguishing the intended reality from other things, so that it is not confused with them. Opposite the muhkam are the mutashabihat, which resemble this and resemble that, so they admit of both meanings. He did not say regarding the mutashabih, "None knows its tafsir and its meaning except Allah," but He said, ﴿and none knows its interpretation except Allah﴾. This is the decisive resolution (fasl al-khitab) among those who dispute on this point. For Allah informed that none knows its interpretation except Him. The pause (waqf) here, according to what many proofs indicate, is also the position of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the majority of the Successors (tabi'un), and the great body of the Ummah. However, He did not deny their knowledge of its meaning and tafsir. Rather He said, ﴿A blessed Book which We have sent down to you, that they may ponder its verses﴾ [Sad: 29], and this includes both the muhkam verses and the mutashabih verses. What has no meaning that can be understood is not pondered over. He also said, ﴿Do they not ponder the Qur'an?﴾ [al-Nisa': 82], and He did not exempt any part of it from His command to ponder it. Allah and His Messenger only blamed those who follow the mutashabih seeking discord and seeking its interpretation. As for one who ponders both the muhkam and the mutashabih as Allah commanded, and seeks to understand it and know its meaning, Allah does not blame him; rather He commanded that and praised it.

This is shown by the fact that the interpretation (ta'wil) has been reported: the Jews who were in Madinah in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), such as Huyayy ibn Akhtab and others, sought from the disjointed letters (huruf al-hijaʾ) at the beginnings of surahs the duration of this Ummah, as a group of later scholars also followed this, in agreement with the Sabians (al-Sabi'ah) who were astrologers. They claimed that it is six hundred and ninety-three years, because that is the sum of the letters according to the abjad reckoning (hisab al-jummal), after dropping the repeated ones. This is of the kind of interpreting the events which the Qur'an reported regarding the Last Day. And it is reported that among the Christians who came as a delegation to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the delegation of Najran was one who interpreted (inna wa nahnu) as meaning that the gods are three, because this is a plural pronoun. This is an interpretation concerning belief in Allah. Those interpreted regarding the Last Day, and these interpreted regarding Allah. It is well known that (anā wa naḥnu) belongs to the mutashabih, for it may be intended to mean one who has others of his kind with him, or it may be intended to mean one who has helpers with him even if they are not of his kind, or it may be intended to mean one who glorifies himself, whom someone else with him stands in place of, because of the variety of His names, each of which stands in place of a named one.

Thus this became mutashabih, because the wording is one and the meaning varied. Homonyms (al-asma' al-mushtarakah) in wording are of the mutashabih, and some univocal terms (al-mutawati'ah) are also of the mutashabih. The people of tafsir call these "al-wujuh wa'l-nazair" (the aspects and the parallels), and they wrote books titled Kutub al-Wujuh wa'l-Nazair. So "wujuh" is for homonyms, and "nazair" is for univocal terms. Some of our authors who wrote on this thought that both wujuh and nazair are in the sense of homonyms, so that they are "nazair" from the point of view of the wording and "wujuh" from the point of view of the meaning. But the matter is not as he said. (p-755) Rather their words are explicit in what we have said, for whoever considers them. As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they abandon the muhkam, which has no ambiguity, such as: ﴿And your God is one God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163]; ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾ [Taha: 14]; ﴿Allah has not taken any son, nor was there with Him any god﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91]; ﴿He has not taken a son, and has no partner in dominion﴾ [al-Furqan: 2]; ﴿He neither begets nor is He begotten﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 3]; ﴿Nor is there to Him any equivalent﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 4]. And they follow the mutashabih, seeking discord, so that they may cause people to fall into it when they place it other than its proper place, and they distort words from their places; and seeking its interpretation, which is the reality it reports. That is because speech is of two kinds: one is inshā' (performative), in which there is a command, and the other is khabar (informative).

The ta'wil of a command is the very act that is commanded, as those among the early generations (al-salaf) who said that the Sunnah is the ta'wil of the command. 'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to frequently say in his bowing and his prostration: 'Subhanaka Allahumma wa bihamdika, Allahumma ighfir li' (Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You, O Allah, forgive me). He was interpreting the Qur'an, meaning His saying: ﴿So glorify your Lord with His praise and seek His forgiveness. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance﴾ [al-Nasr: 3]."

As for information (al-ikhbar), its ta'wil is the very thing reported when it occurs (p-756), and its ta'wil is not understanding its meaning. The term ta'wil has appeared in the Qur'an in more than one place, and this is its meaning. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We had certainly brought them a Book which We detailed with knowledge, as guidance and mercy for a people who believe﴾ [al-A'raf: 52]. ﴿Do they await except its ta'wil? The day its ta'wil comes, those who had forgotten it before will say: "The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth"﴾ [al-A'raf: 53].

So He has informed that He detailed the Book, and its detailing is its clarification and its distinguishing in such a way that it is not confused. Then He said: ﴿Do they await...﴾ [al-A'raf: 53], meaning: they wait ﴿except its ta'wil, the day its ta'wil comes﴾ [al-A'raf: 53], to the end of the verse. That is only the coming of what the Qur'an reported would occur, from the Resurrection and its portents, such as the beast, Ya'juj and Ma'juj, the rising of the sun from its west, the coming of your Lord and the angels in rows, and what is in the Hereafter of the scrolls, the scales, Paradise, the Fire, the various kinds of bliss and punishment, and other things. Then they will say: ﴿The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth. So do we have any intercessors who will intercede for us, or could we be returned so that we might do other than what we used to do?﴾ [al-A'raf: 53].

This extent of what the Qur'an has reported of these matters, its time, its measure and its description, is known only to Allah. For Allah says: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for eyes﴾ [al-Sajdah: 17]. And He says: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." Ibn 'Abbas said: "There is nothing in this world of what is in Paradise except the names." For Allah has reported that in Paradise there is wine, milk, water, silk, gold, silver, and other things. We know with certainty that those realities are not identical to these, rather there is a great difference between them, along with resemblance (p-757). As in His saying: ﴿And they will be given [fruit] in resemblance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25], according to one of the two opinions, meaning: it resembles what is in this world but is not like it. Thus the names of those realities resemble the names of these realities, just as the realities resemble the realities in some respects. So we know them when we are addressed by those names through the common measure between them, but those realities have a distinctive quality that we do not perceive in this world, and there is no way for us to perceive them because we do not perceive their essence or their like in every respect. And those realities, as they are, are the ta'wil of what Allah reported.

This contains a refutation of the Jews, the Christians, the Sabians, and other philosophers. For they deny that there is eating, drinking, clothing and marriage in Paradise, and they prohibit the existence of what the Qur'an has reported. Whoever entered Islam and was a hypocrite toward the believers interpreted that as meaning that these are parables coined to convey spiritual bliss, if he was one of the Sabian philosophers who deny the gathering of bodies. And if he was one of the hypocrites of the two religions who affirm the gathering of bodies, he interpreted that as conveying the spiritual bliss in Paradise, the pleasant hearing and the fragrant scents. Every misguided person distorts the words from their places to what he believes to be established. In this he was also following the ambiguous (al-mutashabih), since names resemble names and named things resemble named things, but they differ more than they resemble. These people follow this ambiguity, ﴿seeking discord by what they bring forth of doubts﴾, to deny that these realities exist in Paradise, and seeking its ta'wil in order to reduce it to the familiar that they know in this world. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And none knows its ta'wil except Allah﴾. For those realities, Allah said about them: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for eyes﴾ [al-Sajdah: 17], not a near-angel nor a sent prophet.

His saying: ﴿And none knows its ta'wil﴾ either has its pronoun referring to the Book or to the ambiguous. If it refers to the Book, given His saying: "from it" and "from it": ﴿They follow what is ambiguous of it, seeking discord and seeking its ta'wil﴾, then this is valid. For all the verses of the Book, both the clear and the ambiguous, in which there is a report of the unseen that we were commanded to believe in, none knows the reality of that unseen or when it will occur except Allah. This may be supported by the fact that Allah made the ta'wil for the entire Book, along with His report that it is detailed, in His saying: ﴿And We had certainly brought them a Book which We detailed with knowledge...﴾ [al-A'raf: 52], ﴿Do they await except its ta'wil...﴾ [al-A'raf: 53]. So He made the ta'wil to be what comes of the detailed Book. We have explained that this ta'wil is not known by anyone except Allah, in its time, measure, type and reality. We know only some of its attributes to the extent of our knowledge, because there is no equivalent for it among us. Likewise His saying: ﴿Rather, they denied what they did not encompass in knowledge, and its ta'wil had not yet come to them﴾ [Yunus: 39]. If the ta'wil is the whole Book and that is what is meant by it, the doubt is removed, and this is in the same position as His saying: ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its arrival? Say: "Its knowledge is only with my Lord. None will reveal its time except Him. It has become heavy upon the heavens and the earth"﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], up to His saying: ﴿Its knowledge is only with Allah﴾ [al-A'raf: 187]. Likewise His saying: ﴿The people ask you about the Hour. Say: "Its knowledge is only with Allah. And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 63]. So He informed that its knowledge is only with Allah, and that it is the knowledge of its specific time and its reality. Otherwise, we know from its attributes what we have been informed of. Thus the knowledge of its ta'wil is like the knowledge of the Hour, and the Hour is part of its ta'wil. This is clear and evident, and it does not contradict the fact that the knowledge of the Hour is with Allah, that we know from its attributes and conditions what we have known, and that we explain the texts that clarify its conditions. So this is that.

(p-759) If the pronoun refers to what is ambiguous, as many people say, then that is because what is reported of promise and threat is ambiguous, unlike command and prohibition. For this reason the narrations say: "Act upon its clear (muhkam) parts and believe in its ambiguous parts," because the intended aim in a report is belief. This is because what is reported of promise and threat contains the ambiguity that we have mentioned. Unlike command and prohibition, which are distinct and not confused with anything else, for they are matters we do, which we know by occurrence, and matters we refrain from, which we must picture.

Among what came of the word ta'wil in the Qur'an is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Rather, they denied what they did not encompass in knowledge, and its ta'wil had not yet come to them﴾ [Yunus: 39]. The pronoun in "its" refers to the Qur'an, or to "what they did not encompass in knowledge," which returns to the Qur'an. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And it was not [possible] for this Qur'an to be fabricated other than by Allah, but it is a confirmation of what was before it and a detailing of the Book, about which there is no doubt, from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [Yunus: 37]. ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say: "Then bring a surah like it, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful."﴾ [Yunus: 38]. ﴿Rather, they denied what they did not encompass in knowledge, and its ta'wil had not yet come to them. Likewise denied those before them. So see how was the end of the wrongdoers.﴾ [Yunus: 39]. ﴿And among them is one who believes in it, and among them is one who does not believe in it. And your Lord is most knowing of the corrupters.﴾ [Yunus: 40].

So Allah, glorified is He, informed that this Qur'an was not to be fabricated other than by Allah. This form indicates the impossibility of what is negated, as in His saying: ﴿And it was not for your Lord to destroy the towns unjustly while their people were reformers﴾ [Hud: 117]. Because creation is incapable of bringing the like of it, just as He challenged them and demanded of them when He said: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say: "Then bring a surah like it..."﴾ [Yunus: 38]. So this is an incapacitation (ta'jiz) of all created beings (p-760). Allah said: ﴿But [it is] a confirmation of what was before it﴾ [Yunus: 37], meaning: a confirmer of what was before it, and ﴿a detailing of the Book﴾, meaning: a detailer of the Book. So He informed that it is a confirmer of what was before it and a detailer of the Book. "The Book" is a generic noun. When He challenged those who said "he invented it," and indicated that they were the fabricators, He said: ﴿Rather, they denied what they did not encompass in knowledge, and its ta'wil had not yet come to them﴾ [Yunus: 39]. So He distinguished between encompassing its knowledge and the coming of its ta'wil.

Thus it becomes clear that people of knowledge and faith can encompass its knowledge while its ta'wil has not yet come to them, and that encompassing the knowledge of the Qur'an is not the coming of its ta'wil. For encompassing its knowledge is knowing the meanings of the speech completely, while the coming of the ta'wil is the actual occurrence of what is reported. There is a difference between knowing the report and knowing what is reported. Knowing the report is knowing the tafsir (exegesis) of the Qur'an, and knowing what is reported is knowing its ta'wil. This is what we explained earlier.

Indeed, Allah only sent down the Qur'an so that its clear and its ambiguous parts may be known, understood, comprehended, pondered and reflected upon, even if its ta'wil is not known. What makes this clear is that Allah says concerning the disbelievers: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a concealed barrier﴾ [al-Isra': 45]. ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness. And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn away in aversion﴾ [al-Isra': 46]. So He informed, as a rebuke of the polytheists, that when the Qur'an is recited to them, He places a concealed barrier between their sight and the Messenger, and places coverings over their hearts lest they understand it, and deafness in their ears. So if people of knowledge and faith had coverings over their hearts such that they could not understand part of it, they would share with them in that. His saying: ﴿lest they understand it﴾ [al-Isra': 46] refers to the entire Qur'an. Thus it is known that Allah loves that it be understood. For this reason al-Hasan al-Basri said: "Allah has not sent down a verse except that He loves it to be known what it was revealed for and what is meant by it." And nothing is excluded from that, neither the ambiguous nor other than it. Mujahid said: "I presented the mushaf to Ibn 'Abbas from its beginning to its end several times, stopping at every verse and asking him about it (p-761)." So this is Ibn 'Abbas, the scholar (hibr) of the Ummah, and he is one of those who said: "None knows its ta'wil except Allah." He answered Mujahid about every verse in the Qur'an. This is what led Mujahid and whoever agreed with him, such as Ibn Qutaybah, to make the pause at His saying: ﴿and those firm in knowledge﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7], so they made those firm in knowledge know the ta'wil. For Mujahid learned from Ibn 'Abbas the tafsir of the entire Qur'an and the explanation of its meanings. So he thought that this is the ta'wil that is negated from other than Allah. The root of this is that the word ta'wil, by which reference is made, differs between what Allah meant in the Qur'an, what groups of the early generations used it for, and the technical usage of groups of later scholars. So because of the shared usage of the word "ta'wil," everyone who understood from it a meaning according to his own language believed that this is what is mentioned in the Qur'an.

Mujahid is the imam of tafsir. al-Thawri said: "If tafsir reaches you from Mujahid, that is enough for you."

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 7 (part 3 of 6):

As for ta'wil (interpretation, in the sense of ultimate meaning), it is a different matter. What makes this clear is that none of the Companions or the Successors refrained from explaining a verse of the Book of Allah, saying, "This is among the mutashabih (ambiguous verses) whose meaning is not known." Nor did any of the predecessors of this community or any of the imams who were followed ever say: "There are verses in the Qur'an whose meaning is not known and which neither the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) nor all the people of knowledge and faith understand." What is said is that the knowledge of some of these verses may be denied for some people, and this is beyond doubt. This question was raised by the later sects, because of their discussion of the verses about the divine attributes, the verses about divine decree, and other matters. They gave it a title: "Is it permissible that the Qur'an should contain what has no known meaning, and that we be commanded to recite its letters without understanding?" Some groups who held to the apparent sense of this verse permitted this, and [argued] that Allah tests His servants with whatever He wills. Other groups forbade it, in order to reach by this their corrupt interpretations, which are "distorting words from their places" (tahrif al-kalim). Error predominates in both groups. The first group falls short in understanding the Qur'an, like the one of whom it was said: ﴿And among them are unlettered people who do not know the Book except wishful thinking, and they only assume﴾ [al-Baqarah: 78]. The second group transgresses, like those who distort words from their places. Among the later scholars there is one who put the question under a shameful label, saying: "It is not permissible for Allah to speak with words and not intend any meaning by them," (this being) in opposition to the Hashwiyya (literalist extremists). No Muslim has said this: that Allah speaks with what has no meaning. The dispute is only whether He speaks with what its meaning is not understood. There is a great difference between denying meaning on the part of the speaker and denying understanding on the part of the addressee. Then he argued from what follows from his own principle, saying: "This is futility (ʿabath), and futility is impossible for Allah." In his view, nothing ugly can be attributed to Allah at all; rather, He may do anything whatsoever, and He cannot be described with futility as a deficiency. Thus it is denied of Him, because the dispute concerns letters, and these in his view are created among the acts, and in his view an act may comprise every attribute. So there is neither clear transmission nor sound reason.

The source of the strife between the two groups and the bewilderment of their minds is that those who claim ta'wil erred in their assertion that the scholars know the ta'wil, and in their claim that ta'wil is their ta'wil, which is the distortion of words from their places. The earlier scholars, through their knowledge of the Qur'an and the Sunnah, the soundness of their intellects, their knowledge of the words of the predecessors and the speech of the Arabs, knew with certainty that the ta'wil claimed by these people is not the meaning of the Qur'an. They distorted words from their places, and became various degrees between the Qaramita and the Batiniyya, who interpret the reports and the commands, and between the Sabians and the philosophers, who interpret nearly all reports about Allah and the Last Day, even most of what concerns the states of the prophets. Between the Jahmiyya and the Mu'tazila, they interpret some of what came about the Last Day and the verses of divine decree, and they interpret the verses of the attributes. Some of the later Ash'ariyya agreed with them on some of what came concerning the attributes, and some of them on some of what came concerning the Last Day. Others from among the categories of this community, although the Sunnah predominates among them, may also interpret places where their interpretation is from the distortion of words from their places.

Those who claimed knowledge of ta'wil, such as a group of the predecessors and the People of the Sunnah, and most of the people of kalam (speculative theology) and innovation, also saw that the texts indicate knowledge of the meanings of the Qur'an. They regarded it as incapacity, a defect, and an ugliness for Allah to address His servants with speech that they read and recite while they do not understand it. They were correct in what they argued from transmission and reason, but they erred in the meaning of ta'wil that Allah denied, and in the ta'wil that they affirmed, through which their innovators climbed up to the distortion of words from their places. The earlier ones came closer to silence and safety with a kind of ignorance, while the later ones became more verbose and contentious, but with a slander against Allah, saying about Him what they do not know, and deviating in His names and His signs. So this is that.

The origin of the confusion is the homonymy in the term ta'wil. In the usage of the later jurists, theologians, traditionists, Sufis and their like, ta'wil is: turning a word away from its prevailing meaning to a less prevalent meaning because of an indicator that accompanies it. This is the ta'wil about which they speak in the principles of jurisprudence and the questions of disagreement. So when one of them says: "This hadith or this text is interpreted (mu'awwal), or it is understood to mean such-and-such," the other says: "This is a type of ta'wil, and ta'wil needs proof." The one who interprets has two tasks: to show that the word admits the meaning he claims, and to show the indicator that requires turning it away from the apparent meaning. This is the ta'wil over which they dispute in the questions of the attributes, when some of them write in refutation of ta'wil or in censure of ta'wil, or one of them says: "The verses of the attributes are not to be interpreted," and another says: "Rather, it is obligatory to interpret them," and a third says: "Rather, ta'wil is permissible, done when there is benefit and left when there is benefit, or it is valid for the scholars only and not for others," and so on through the other statements and disputes.

* *

As for the word ta'wil in the language of the predecessors, it has two meanings:

The first: the explanation of speech and the clarification of its meaning, whether it agrees with its apparent sense or contradicts it. Thus ta'wil and tafsir (exegesis) are close or synonymous in their view. This, Allah knows best, is what Mujahid meant when he said that the scholars know its ta'wil. Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari says in his tafsir: "The discussion on the ta'wil of His saying such-and-such," and "The people of ta'wil differed regarding this verse," and similar expressions, and what he means is tafsir.

The second meaning in the language of the predecessors, which is the third of the designations of ta'wil in general, is the very reality intended by the speech. If the speech is a command, its ta'wil is the very act commanded. If it is a report, its ta'wil is the very thing reported. Between this meaning and the one before it there is a great difference. In the former, ta'wil belongs to the category of knowledge and speech, like tafsir, explanation and clarification, and the existence of ta'wil is in the heart and the tongue; it has mental, verbal and written existence. But in this second meaning, the ta'wil is the very realities existing outside the mind, whether they are past or future.

So when one says "the sun rose," its ta'wil is the very rising. This is the usage and custom.

The third meaning is the language of the Qur'an in which it was revealed, and we have already explained this. Among its examples is the saying of Ya'qub (peace be upon him) to Yusuf: ﴿And thus your Lord will choose you and teach you of the interpretation of events and complete His favor upon you﴾ [Yusuf: 6]. And His saying: ﴿And there entered with him into prison two young men. One of them said, "Indeed, I have seen myself pressing wine," and the other said, "Indeed, I have seen myself carrying bread on my head, and birds are eating from it. Inform us of its interpretation; indeed, we see you are of the doers of good."﴾ [Yusuf: 36]. ﴿He said, "No food will come to you which you are given but I will inform you of its interpretation before it reaches you."﴾ [Yusuf: 37]. And the saying of the council: ﴿"A confusion of dreams; and we are not knowledgeable in the interpretation of dreams."﴾ [Yusuf: 44]. ﴿And the one who was saved of the two and remembered after a time said, "I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me forth."﴾ [Yusuf: 45]. And the saying of Yusuf when they entered upon him in Egypt and he sheltered his parents to himself and said: ﴿"Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, in security."﴾ [Yusuf: 99] ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him prostrating. And he said, "O my father, this is the interpretation of my vision from before; my Lord has made it true."﴾ [Yusuf: 100].

So the ta'wil of the events that are dream visions is the very thing they signify, to which they are turned, as Yusuf said: ﴿This is the interpretation of my vision from before﴾ [Yusuf: 100]. And the one who knows their ta'wil is the one who reports it, as Yusuf said: ﴿No food will come to you which you are given﴾ [Yusuf: 37], that is, in the dream, ﴿but I will inform you of its interpretation before it reaches you﴾ [Yusuf: 37], that is, before the ta'wil reaches you. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you should believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is best and most suitable in result﴾ [al-Nisa': 59]. They said: "Best in outcome and final destination." So the ta'wil here is the ta'wil of their action, which is referring to the Book and the Sunnah. The ta'wil in Surah Yusuf is the ta'wil of dream reports, and the ta'wil in al-A'raf and Yunus is the ta'wil of the Qur'an, and likewise in Surah Al 'Imran. And Allah the Exalted said in the story of Musa and the scholar: ﴿He said, "This is the separation between me and you. I will inform you of the interpretation of that over which you could not have patience."﴾ [al-Kahf: 78] up to His saying: ﴿"And I did it not of my own accord. That is the interpretation of that over which you could not have patience."﴾ [al-Kahf: 82].

So here the ta'wil is the ta'wil of the actions which the scholar did (p-766): tearing the ship without the permission of its owner, killing the boy, and rebuilding the wall. It is the ta'wil of an action, not the ta'wil of speech. This is so because ta'wil is the verbal noun of awwala yu'awwilu ta'wilan, like hawwala tahwilan and 'awwala ta'wilan. And awwala yu'awwilu is the transitive form of ala yaulu awlan, like hala yahulu hawlan. The saying "ala yaulu" means: he returned to such-and-such and came back to it. From it comes al-ma'al, which is what a thing returns to. The mawil shares this derivation, for it is wa'ala, and this is from awwala. Al-mawil means the place of return, as Allah said: ﴿They will not find besides Him any refuge (mawil)﴾ [al-Kahf: 58].

Among what agrees with it in its smaller derivation is al-al (family), for the family of a person is those who return to him. For this reason it is used only for a great person, such that the one added to it is one to whom the family may return, like the family of Ibrahim, the family of Lut and the family of Fir'awn. This is unlike ahl (people). The word awwal is af'al, because they said in its feminine form ula, as they said Jumada al-Ula. In the stories: ﴿To Him is praise in the first and the last﴾ [al-Qasas: 70]. Some people say it is fawʿal and say (awwalahu), but this requires a witness from the speech of the Arabs. Rather, its not taking nunation indicates that it is af'al and not fawʿal, for fawʿal, like kawthar and jawhar, takes nunation. It was named "first" (awwal), Allah knows best, because what follows it returns to it and is built upon it. It is a foundation for what follows and a base for it. The form is a superlative form, like akbar and kubra, asghar and sughra, and not like ahmar and hamra'. For this reason they say: "I came to him before yesterday" (awwal min amsi). And He said: ﴿From the first day﴾ [al-Tawbah: 108], ﴿And I am the first of the Muslims﴾ [al-An'am: 163], ﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41] (p-767), and like: "This is the first of these."

That which is preferred over them in the first sense is because each one returns to what came before him, relying upon it, and this one is the foremost to whom everyone returns. For whoever precedes in an action, and others follow his example in it, is the foremost to whom everyone returns. So the first has the quality of leadership and being followed. The word awwal (first) implies return and recurrence, and "first" (awwal) implies beginning. The one who begins is the opposite of the one who returns, because he is only "first" in relation to what follows him. It is said: "the first of the Muslims" and "the first day," so the meaning of return and recurrence that is in it belongs to the thing added to it, not to the thing to which it is added. When we say "the family of so-and-so" (al fulan), the returning is in the thing added, because this is a superlative form in being a final destination and a return for others, since its being preferred indicates that it is a final destination and a place of return, not one that merely returns or is returned to, for there is no preference in a thing's being returned to something else. The preference lies in its being that to which things return and are referred. When the form is a superlative form, it indicates that it is preferred in being a final destination and a place of return, and absolute preference in this implies that it is the foremost and the one who begins. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 7 (part 4 of 6):**

(p. 768) The *ta'wil* (ultimate meaning or final reality) of a speech is what the speaker intended by it, or what the speech leads to, or what the speaker interpreted it as. The superlative-form verbal noun is used without an act behind it, as in His saying: ﴿And devote yourself to Him with complete devotion﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 8]. So it is permissible to say: "He interpreted the speech to this meaning, *ta'wilan*." The verbal noun here stands in the position of an adjective, since a verbal noun can function as an adjective meaning the doer, as in *'adl* (just), *sawm* (fasting) and *fitr* (breaking the fast), and meaning the object, as in *dirham darb al-amir* (a dirham minted by the ruler) and *hadha khalq Allah* (this is the creation of God). Thus *al-ta'wil* is that to which the speech has been interpreted, or that to which it is interpreted, or that to which the interpreter himself has interpreted it. A speech only returns, reverts, settles, arrives at and is interpreted into its reality, which is the very thing intended by it. This is as some of the early scholars (*salaf*) said regarding His saying: ﴿For every news there is a fixed time, and you will come to know it﴾ [al-An'am: 67]: "It is the reality." If the speech is a report, then it arrives at and returns to the reality reported; otherwise it would have no reality, no final outcome and no return, and would be a lie. If the speech is a command or prohibition, then it arrives at the reality demanded; otherwise its intended object would not exist or be realized. And when the speech is a promise or a threat, (p. 768) it arrives at the awaited reality that is demanded. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he recited this verse: ﴿Say: He is the One able to send upon you a punishment from above you or from beneath your feet, or to confuse you into sects﴾ [al-An'am: 65], and said: "It has occurred, and its *ta'wil* has not yet come."

**Section**

As for placing the names and attributes of God, or some of them, among the *mutashabih* (ambiguous verses) whose *ta'wil* none knows but God, or believing that this is the *mutashabih* whose knowledge of interpretation God has reserved for Himself, as each of the two positions is held by groups among our companions and others, then although they are right in much of what they say and have been spared from innovations into which others fell, the discussion on this matter has two aspects:

The first: Whoever says that this is ambiguous and that its meaning cannot be understood, what is the evidence for that? I do not know of anyone from the early community (*salaf al-ummah*) or of the Imams, neither Ahmad ibn Hanbal nor anyone else, who made this part of the ambiguous verses included in this verse, or who denied that anyone knows its meaning. They treated the names and attributes of God as being like a non-Arabic speech that cannot be understood. Nor did they say that God sends down a speech whose meaning no one understands. Rather, they said: "These are words that have correct meanings." They said regarding the hadiths on the attributes: "Let them pass as they came," and they forbade and rejected and nullified the interpretations of the Jahmiyya, whose content is the nullification (*ta'til*) of the texts from what they indicate. The explicit statements of Ahmad and the Imams before him make clear that they used to refute the interpretations of the Jahmiyya, affirm the texts with their indicated meanings, and understand from them part of what they indicate, just as they understand that in all texts of promise, threat, virtues and others. Ahmad also said, regarding non-attribute hadiths: "Let them pass as they came," (p. 769) concerning hadiths of promise, such as: "Whoever deceives us is not one of us," and hadiths of virtues. His intention by this was that a hadith should not be distorted entirely from its places, as does the one who distorts it and calls his distortion *ta'wil* according to the later usage.

The interpretation of these later scholars is, according to the Imams, a false distortion. Likewise Ahmad stated in his book *al-Radd 'ala al-Zanadiqa al-Jahmiyya* that they clung to the ambiguous verses of the Qur'an. Ahmad discussed that ambiguity and explained its meaning and its tafsir in a way that contradicts the *ta'wil* of the Jahmiyya, and he followed in this the path of the Imams before him. This is an agreement of the Imams that they know the meaning of this ambiguity, that it is not to be kept silent about, and that it must be clarified and explained, without distortion, on its proper places. Thus there is agreement among the Imams without distortion of it from its places or deviation regarding the names of God and His signs.

What clarifies for you the confusion that occurred here is that the People of the Sunna agree on nullifying the interpretations of the Jahmiyya and similar deviant, atheistic people. The rejected *ta'wil* is turning a speech away from its apparent meaning toward what contradicts that apparent meaning. So if it were said that this is the *ta'wil* mentioned in the verse, and that none knows it except God, this would concede to the Jahmiyya that the verse has an interpretation contrary to its indication, though only God knows it. This is not the doctrine of the *salaf* and the Imams. Their doctrine is the negation and rejection of these interpretations, not suspension regarding them. For them, reciting the verse and the hadith is its tafsir, and they are allowed to pass as they came, indicating their meanings, not distorted and not deviated from.

The proof that this is not ambiguous and that its meaning cannot be known is that you say: There is no doubt that God named Himself in the Qur'an with names such as *al-Rahman* (the Most Merciful), *al-Wadud* (the Most Loving), *al-'Aziz* (the Mighty), *al-Jabbar* (the Compeller), *al-Qadir* (the Able), *al-Ra'uf* (the Kind), and similar, and described Himself with attributes, such as Surat al-Ikhlas, the Verse of the Throne, the beginning of al-Hadid and the end of al-Hashr, and His saying: (Indeed God is Knowing of all things), and: (Over all things is Able), and: ﴿Indeed, God loves those who fear Him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 76], and: (the just), and: (the good-doers), and that He is pleased with those who believed and did righteous deeds, (p. 770) and: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took retribution from them and drowned them all﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 55], ﴿That is because they followed what angered God﴾ [Muhammad: 28], ﴿But God disliked their being sent forth﴾ [al-Tawbah: 46], ﴿The Most Merciful established Himself above the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5], ﴿then He established Himself above the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], ﴿He knows what enters into the earth and what comes out of it, and what descends from the sky and what ascends into it, and He is with you wherever you are﴾ [al-Hadid: 4], ﴿And He is the one in the heaven a god and in the earth a god, and He is the Wise, the Knowing﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 84], ﴿To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deed raises it﴾ [Fatir: 10], ﴿Indeed I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ [Ta-Ha: 46], (p. 771) ﴿And He is God in the heavens and in the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 3], ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?﴾ [Sad: 75], ﴿Rather, both His hands are outspread; He spends however He wills﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64], ﴿And there will remain the face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor﴾ [al-Rahman: 27], ﴿They desire His face﴾ [al-Kahf: 28], ﴿And that you may be raised under My eye﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39], and the like of these. So it is said to whoever claims in this matter that it is ambiguous and its meaning cannot be known: Do you say this of everything God named and described Himself with, or of only some of it? If you say: This is for all of it, then this is manifest obstinacy and denial of what is known by necessity from the religion of Islam, indeed clear disbelief. For we understand from His saying: (Indeed God is Knowing of all things) a meaning. And we understand from His saying: (p. 772) (Indeed God is Able over all things) a meaning which is not the first. And we understand from His saying: ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ [al-A'raf: 156] a meaning, and we understand from His saying: ﴿Indeed God is Mighty, Owner of Retribution﴾ [Ibrahim: 47] a meaning. The children of the Muslims, indeed every rational person, understands this.

I have seen some of those who innovated and denied from the people of the Maghrib, who attributed themselves to hadith, but whom corrupt philosophy had affected, who says: "We name God the Merciful, the Compassionate, the Knowing, the Able, as a pure knowledge without understanding from it any meaning that indicates anything at all. Likewise in His saying: ﴿And they encompass not a thing of His knowledge﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], this word is used without our saying that He has knowledge." This excess in the apparent is of the same kind as the excess of the Qaramita in the hidden. But this is drier and that is more disbelieving.

Then it is said to this obstinate person: Are these names indicative of the God who is worshipped, or of a real existing Truth, or not? If he says: No, then he is a pure *mu'attil* (denier of attributes). I do not know of any Muslim who says this. If he says: Yes, it is said to him: Have you understood from them their indication of the Essence of the Lord, but not their indication of the meanings in them of mercy and knowledge, though both are equal in indication? He must say: Because the affirmation of attributes is impossible in reason, as it entails composition or origination, unlike the Essence.

He is then addressed with what the second group is addressed with, as we will mention. That group is the one who admits understanding some of the meaning of these names and attributes but not some others. It is said to them: What is the difference between what you affirmed and what you negated, or what you kept silent about affirming and negating? The difference is either from the side of revelation (*sam'*), because one of the two texts indicates decisively or apparently, unlike the other; or from the side of reason, that one of the two meanings is permissible or obligatory to affirm and the other is not. Both aspects (p. 773) are false in most places. As for the first, the Qur'an's indication that He is Merciful, Compassionate, Loving, Hearing, Seeing, High, Great, is like its indication that He is Knowing and Able; there is no difference between them from the side of the text. Likewise, His mention of His mercy, His love and His highness is like His mention of His will and His volition.

As for the second, it is said to whoever affirms one thing and negates another: Why did you negate, for example, the reality of His mercy and His love, and return them to His will?

If he says: Because the meaning understood from mercy in our case is a tenderness that is impossible for God, it is said to him: The meaning understood from will in our case is an inclination that is impossible for God. If he says: His will is not of the kind of the will of His creation, it is said to him: Nor is His mercy of the kind of the mercy of His creation. Likewise His love. If he says (and this is the reality of his position): I did not affirm will and other attributes by revelation; rather I affirmed knowledge, power and will by reason. Likewise hearing, seeing and speech by one of two methods, because the act indicates power, the perfection indicates knowledge, and the specification indicates will; it is said to him: The answer is from three aspects:

The first: Bestowal, benefaction and the removal of harm also indicate mercy, just as the specification indicates will and bringing near. The kinds of specification that could only come from one who loves indicate love, or the unrestricted specification indicates will. As for specification by bestowal, it is a particular specification, and specification by bringing near and selection is a particular nearness, and what he took in the path of will is taken in the like of this.

The second: It is said to him: Suppose reason does not indicate this. Then it does not negate it except by the same means by which it negates will, while revelation is an independent proof by itself. Rather, reliance on it in these narrow matters is greater and its indication is more complete. So for what reason did you negate its indicated meaning, or hold back, and return all these attributes to will? Although the texts distinguish between them. Thus he does not cite a proof except that it is countered by its like in his affirmation of will over and above the act.

The third: It is said to him: If the Jahmi says to you: "Will has no meaning except the absence of compulsion, or the act itself and the command to it," and claims that affirming a will entails a prohibited consequence whether one says it is eternal or that it is originated.

(p. 774) Here the Mu'tazila were confused. For they do not say that there is an eternal will, because an eternal attribute is impossible for them. Nor do they say that an attribute of Him is renewed, because for most of them it is impossible for originated events to inhere in Him, while contradicting themselves.

So they became two parties:

The Baghdadis: They are the most extreme in innovation regarding the attributes and regarding divine decree (*qadar*). They denied the reality of will. Al-Hafiz said: "It has no meaning except the absence of compulsion." Al-Ka'bi said: "It has no meaning except the act itself when it relates to His act, and the command itself when it relates to the obedience of His servants."

The Basrans: Like Abu 'Ali and Abu Hashim. They said: "A will occurs not in a locus, so there is no will." Thus they committed to the origination of an originated thing that is not willed, and to an attribute subsisting without a locus, and both of these are known by immediate recognition to be corrupt in reason. Their answer was that what they claimed to be impossible, namely the affirmation of attributes, is not impossible, and the text has indicated it, and so has the act. So when the opponent disputes the indication of the text or of reason, he is labeled a sophist or a Qarmati, and this same thing exists regarding mercy and love, for their opponents dispute with them about the indication of revelation and reason on them with decisive certainty.

Then it is said to his opponents: "By what have you established that He is All-Knowing and All-Powerful?" Whatever they establish with respect to this, whether by revelation (sam') or reason ('aql), then by that very same means the will (irada) is established. Whatever doubts (shubah) they raise in opposition, they are answered with its like concerning the All-Knowing and the All-Powerful. When the matter reaches the establishment of the attributes (ma'ani) and their necessitating origination (huduth), composition (tarkib) and dependence (iftiqar), the answer is what we have settled elsewhere, for these do not necessitate origination, nor a composition that requires need of another.

They also argue back with what the people of ta'til (those who deny the attributes, mu'attilah) use to negate the divine essence (dhat) of false doubts. And they are held to the existence of the Lord, the Creator, which is known through the innate nature (fitrah khalqiyyah), the necessary rational truths (darurah 'aqliyyah), the decisive rational proofs (qawati' 'aqliyyah), the consensus of nations, and other evidences. Then they are asked for an existence of the kind we are accustomed to, or an existence whose modality they know. They will inevitably have to flee to affirming something whose reality resembles realities. So the discussion regarding everything He named and described Himself with is like the discussion regarding His own Essence, glorified and exalted is He.

(p. 775) The essence of this discourse is that most of those who negate or affirm something of what the Book and the Sunnah indicate must affirm a thing when the requirement (muqtada) is present and the impediment (mani') is absent. And they negate a thing either because an impediment exists, or because the requirement is absent, or they suspend judgment when there is neither requirement nor impediment. Then it is shown to them that the requirement in what they negated exists, just as it exists in what they affirmed, either in every respect, or in a respect that necessitates affirmation. If the requirement there is true, then it is likewise here; otherwise, repelling that requirement is of the same kind as repelling this one. As for the impediment, it is shown that the impediment that they imagined in what they negated is of the same kind as the impediment they imagined in what they affirmed. If that supposed impossible impediment exists under both assumptions, then they are not saved from its consequence by affirming one and negating the other. For if it is true, it negates both; and if it is false, it negates neither. So they must treat both matters equally in affirmation and negation, and there is no way to negation, so affirmation is determined. This is the essence of the argument of necessity against whoever affirms something. And there is no one who does not necessarily affirm something, or for whom affirming it is obligatory. This gives you, in general terms, that the necessary implications which they claim require negation are invalid imaginings, even if their corruption is not known in detail. As for the detailed level, the corruption of the impediment and the presence of the requirement is shown, as he has settled this more than once.

If someone says: "Those attributes that are in us accidents (a'rad), such as life, knowledge and power, are affirmed for Him, but what in us are parts (ab'ad), such as the hand and the foot, are not affirmed, because these are parts and components that necessitate composition and corporeality (tajsim)." It is said to him: "Those are accidents which necessitate corporeality and rational composition, just as these necessitate sensory composition according to you. If you affirm those in a way in which they are not accidents, or their being called accidents does not prevent their affirmation, then it is said to him: 'And we affirm these in a way in which they are not composition and parts, or their being called composition and parts does not prevent their affirmation.'"

If he says: "These [parts] are only understood as parts," it is said to him: "And those [attributes] are only understood as accidents."

If he says: "The accident is that which does not endure, and the attributes of the Lord endure," it is said: "And the part is that which can be separated from the whole, and that is impossible with respect to Allah. So the separation of the eternal attributes is impossible with respect to Allah, the Exalted, absolutely, while the created being may be separated from its accidents and parts."

(p. 776) If he says: "That is corporeality, and corporeality is negated," it is said: "This too is corporeality, and corporeality is negated."

If he says: "I understand an attribute that is not an accident, without being localized (mutahayyiz), even if it has no analogue in the observable world," it is said to him: "Then understand an attribute which for us is a part, without being localized, even if it has no analogue in the observable world."

If he denies the understanding of this, he denies the understanding of that, even though there is some difference between them, but it is a difference that does not affect the point of dispute. For this reason the Jahmiyyah, the mu'attilah, deny everything, but that also necessitates denying the Essence. And whoever affirms these attributes of the reports (sifat khabariyyah) from among the like of these, explicitly states that they are attributes subsisting in Him like knowledge and power. This too is not the literal meaning of the text, nor the indication of reason; rather, necessity forced them into these narrow passages.

The root of this is that they introduced terms that are not in the Book or the Sunnah, and these are ambiguous terms, such as mutahayyiz (localized), muhaddad (bounded), jism (body), murakkab (composite), and the like. They negated their meanings and made that a premise accepted among them, and they indicated it by a kind of syllogism (qiyas). That syllogism led them astray through a method they followed in establishing the origination of the world through the origination of accidents, or in establishing the contingency (imkan) of the body through its composition from parts. So it became obligatory to extend the proof of origination and contingency to everything this proof included, since a decisive proof does not admit abandonment because of a stronger opposing argument. They saw that this caused them trouble from the texts on one side and from reason on another, so they became factions. At times they favored the first syllogism and rejected what opposed it, and they were the Mu'tazilah. At times they favored the second syllogism and rejected the first, like Hisham ibn al-Hakam the Rafidi (Rafidi, a Shi'i sect), for it has been said: "The first discussion about the body, in negation and affirmation, took place in the time of Hisham ibn al-Hakam and Abu al-Hudhayl al-'Allaf." For Abu al-Hudhayl and his like among the early Mu'tazilah negated the body because of the syllogism they followed. Hisham opposed them and affirmed the body because of the syllogism they followed. The first group considered the affirmation of it impossible, and this group considered its negation impossible. At times they combine the texts and the syllogism with a combination in which impossibility and contradiction become apparent.

I know of no one among those who departed from the Book and the Sunnah, from all the champions of kalam and philosophy, except that he must contradict himself, declaring impossible what he made obligatory in a similar case, and making obligatory what he declared impossible in a similar case, since their speech is from (p. 777) other than Allah. Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿And had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [An-Nisa: 82].

The correct position is that of the leaders of guidance, namely that Allah is described with what He described Himself with, or what His Messenger described Him with, without going beyond the Qur'an and the hadith. In this one follows the ways of the righteous predecessors (al-Salaf al-Salih), the people of knowledge and faith. The meanings understood from the Book and the Sunnah are not rejected by doubts, so that it becomes a case of "distorting words from their places"; nor are they turned away from, so that it becomes a case of those who, when reminded of the signs of their Lord, do not fall upon them deaf and blind; nor is contemplation of the Qur'an abandoned, so that it becomes a case of those who know not the Book except as wishful fancies. This is one of the two aspects, namely the denial that these are from the mutashabih (ambiguous verses).

* *

The second aspect: if it is said that these are from the mutashabih, or that some of them are from the mutashabih, as has been transmitted from some of the Imams that he called some of what the Jahmiyyah cited as evidence "mutashabih," then it is said: What is in the Qur'an is that none knows its ta'wil (ultimate interpretation) except Allah, whether this refers to the mutashabih or to the entire Book, as has preceded. Negating knowledge of its ta'wil is not negating knowledge of its meaning, as we have previously stated concerning the Resurrection and the matters of the Resurrection. This aspect is strong if the hadith of Ibn Ishaq concerning the delegation of Najran is authentic, that they argued against the Prophet ﷺ with his saying: "We and you..." and similar. It is also supported by the fact that it is established that the Qur'an contains mutashabih, which is what admits two meanings, and that among the attributes there is something of this kind, just as that is the case in matters of the Return (ma'ad), and more so. For negating ambiguity between Allah and His creation is greater than negating ambiguity between the promised Paradise and the existing world. The essence of the answer is what we presented first: that negating knowledge of the ta'wil is not a negation of knowledge of the meaning. We add further confirmation: Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿And We have certainly presented for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, that they may be reminded﴾ [Az-Zumar: 27]. ﴿An Arabic Qur'an, without any deviance﴾ [Az-Zumar: 28]. And He, the Exalted, said: (p. 778) ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the clear Book﴾ [Yusuf: 1]. ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an that you may understand﴾ [Yusuf: 2]. So He informed that He sent it down so that they would understand it, and that He sought their remembrance. He also said: ﴿And these examples We present to the people; perhaps they will give thought﴾ [Al-Hashr: 21]. So He urged contemplation of it, understanding of it, reason regarding it, remembrance by it, and reflection upon it, and He excepted nothing from that. Rather, multiple texts explicitly state its generality, such as His saying: ﴿Then do they not contemplate the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ [Muhammad: 24], and His saying: ﴿Then do they not contemplate the Qur'an? And if it had been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [An-Nisa: 82]. It is known that negating contradiction from it is only possible through contemplating all of it, for otherwise contemplating part of it does not necessitate a judgment negating the opposition of what was not contemplated to what was contemplated. 'Ali, peace be upon him, said when he was asked: "Did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ leave anything with you?" He said: "No, by the One who split the grain and created the soul, except an understanding that Allah bestows upon a servant regarding the Book, and what is in this sheet." So he informed that understanding of it differs among the Ummah, and understanding is more specific than knowledge and judgment. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Solomon (p. 779) and to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 79]. The Prophet ﷺ said: "May a conveyor of knowledge be more retentive than a hearer," and he said: "Convey from me, even if it is a single verse."

Furthermore, the early generations of the Companions, the Successors and the rest of the Ummah have spoken about all the texts of the Qur'an, the verses of the attributes and others, and have interpreted them in accordance with their indication, and they transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ many hadiths that agree with the Qur'an. The leading Companions in this are greater than others, such as 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who used to say: "If I knew of someone more knowledgeable of the Book of Allah than me, reachable by camels' flanks, I would go to him." And 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, for whom the Prophet ﷺ made supplication and who was the scholar of the Ummah and the interpreter of the Qur'an. He and his companions were among the greatest of the Companions and the Successors in affirming the attributes and transmitting them from the Prophet ﷺ. Whoever has experience with hadith and tafsir knows this. Among the Successors there is none greater than the companions of these two masters; indeed, the third of them, among the eminent Successors of their kind or close to them in rank, are the companions of Zayd ibn Thabit. But his companions, despite their eminence, were not exclusively his, for they also took from others, such as 'Umar, Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas. Had the meanings of these verses been negated or left silent about, the rabbaniyyun (learned masters) of the Companions, who were the people of knowledge of the Book and the Sunnah, would not have spoken about them more. Moreover, the Companions transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ that they used to learn the tafsir from him along with the recitation, and none of them ever reported that he refrained from explaining any verse.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami said: "Those who used to teach us recitation, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and others, told us that when they learned ten verses from the Prophet ﷺ, they would not go beyond them until they had learned what was in them of knowledge and action. They said: 'So we learned the Qur'an, the knowledge and the action together.'" Likewise, the Imams, when asked about any of these matters, did not negate their meaning, but affirmed the meaning and negated the modality (kayfiyyah). Such as the statement of Malik ibn Anas when he was asked about the words of the Exalted: ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5], "How is He established?" He said: "The istiwa' (establishment) is known, the modality is unknown, belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation (bid'ah)." Likewise Rabi'ah before him. And people have received this statement with acceptance.

فَلَيْسَ في أهْلِ السُّنَّةِ (Ahl al-Sunna, the Sunni community) مَن يُنْكِرُهُ. وقَدْ بَيَّنَ أنَّ الِاسْتِواءَ مَعْلُومٌ، كَما أنَّ سائِرَ ما أخْبَرَ بِهِ مَعْلُومٌ، ولَكِنَّ الكَيْفِيَّةَ لا تُعْلَمُ، ولا يَجُوزُ السُّؤالُ عَنْها، لا يُقالُ: كَيْفَ اسْتَوى؟ ولَمْ يَقُلْ مالِكٌ: الكَيْفُ مَعْدُومٌ، وإنَّما قالَ: الكَيْفُ مَجْهُولٌ. وهَذا فِيهِ نِزاعٌ بَيْنَ أصْحابِنا وغَيْرِهِمْ مِن أهْلِ السُّنَّةِ، غَيْرَ أنَّ أكْثَرَهم يَقُولُونَ: لا تَخْطُرُ كَيْفِيَّتُهُ بِبالٍ، ولا تَجْرِي ماهِيَّتُهُ في مَقالٍ. ومِنهم مَن يَقُولُ: لَيْسَ لَهُ كَيْفِيَّةٌ ولا ماهِيَّةٌ. فَإنْ قِيلَ: مَعْنى قَوْلِهِ: الِاسْتِواءُ مَعْلُومٌ أنَّ وُرُودَ هَذا اللَّفْظِ في القُرْآنِ مَعْلُومٌ كَما قالَهُ بَعْضُ أصْحابِنا الَّذِينَ يَجْعَلُونَ مَعْرِفَةَ مَعانِيها مِنَ التَّأْوِيلِ (ta'wil, interpretation) الَّذِي اسْتَأْثَرَ اللَّهُ بِعِلْمِهِ، قِيلَ: هَذا ضَعِيفٌ، فَإنَّ هَذا (p-٧٨١) مِن بابِ تَحْصِيلِ الحاصِلِ، فَإنَّ السّائِلَ قَدْ عَلِمَ أنَّ هَذا مَوْجُودٌ في القُرْآنِ، وقَدْ تَلا الآيَةَ، وأيْضًا فَلَمْ يَقُلْ: ذُكِرَ الِاسْتِواءُ في القُرْآنِ، ولا إخْبارُ اللَّهِ بِالِاسْتِواءِ، وإنَّما قالَ: الِاسْتِواءُ مَعْلُومٌ، فَأخْبَرَ عَنْ الِاسْمِ المُفْرَدِ أنَّهُ مَعْلُومٌ، لَمْ يُخْبِرْ عَنْ الجُمْلَةِ، وأيْضًا فَإنَّهُ قالَ: والكَيْفُ مَجْهُولٌ، ولَوْ أرادَ ذَلِكَ لَقالَ: مَعْنى الِاسْتِواءِ مَجْهُولٌ، أوْ تَفْسِيرُ الِاسْتِواءِ مَجْهُولٌ، أوْ بَيانُ الِاسْتِواءِ غَيْرُ مَعْلُومٍ، فَلَمْ يَنْفِ إلّا العِلْمَ بِكَيْفِيَّةِ الِاسْتِواءِ، لا العِلْمَ بِنَفْسِ الِاسْتِواءِ، وهَذا شَأْنُ جَمِيعِ ما وصَفَ اللَّهُ بِهِ نَفْسَهُ. لَوْ قالَ في قَوْلِهِ: ﴿إنَّنِي مَعَكُما أسْمَعُ وأرى﴾ كَيْفَ يَسْمَعُ وكَيْفَ يَرى؟ لَقُلْنا: السَّمْعُ والرُّؤْيَةُ مَعْلُومٌ والكَيْفُ مَجْهُولٌ. ولَوْ قالَ: كَيْفَ كَلَّمَ مُوسى تَكْلِيمًا؟ لَقُلْنا: التَّكْلِيمُ مَعْلُومٌ والكَيْفُ غَيْرُ مَعْلُومٍ. وأيْضًا فَإنَّ مَن قالَ هَذا مِن أصْحابِنا وغَيْرِهِمْ مِن أهْلِ السُّنَّةِ يُقِرُّونَ بِأنَّ اللَّهَ فَوْقَ العَرْشِ حَقِيقَةً، وأنَّ ذاتَهُ فَوْقَ ذاتِ العَرْشِ، لا يُنْكِرُونَ مَعْنى الِاسْتِواءِ، ولا يَرَوْنَ هَذا مِنَ المُتَشابِهِ (mutashabih, ambiguous verses) الَّذِي لا يُعْلَمُ مَعْناهُ بِالكُلِّيَّةِ. ثُمَّ السَّلَفُ (al-Salaf, the early generations) مُتَّفِقُونَ عَلى تَفْسِيرِهِ بِما هو مَذْهَبُ أهْلِ السُّنَّةِ. قالَ بَعْضُهم: ارْتَفَعَ عَلى العَرْشِ: عَلا عَلى العَرْشِ. وقالَ بَعْضُهم عِباراتٍ أُخْرى. وهَذِهِ ثابِتَةٌ عَنْ السَّلَفِ. وقَدْ ذَكَرَ البُخارِيُّ في صَحِيحِهِ بَعْضَها في آخِرِهِ، في كِتابِ الرَّدِّ عَلى الجَهْمِيَّةِ (al-Jahmiyya, a early theological sect).

وأمّا التَّأْوِيلاتُ المُحَرَّفَةُ مِثْلَ اسْتَوْلى وغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ، فَهي مِنَ التَّأْوِيلاتِ المُبْتَدَعَةِ لَمّا ظَهَرَتْ الجَهْمِيَّةُ. وأيْضًا قَدْ ثَبَتَ أنَّ اتِّباعَ المُتَشابِهِ لَيْسَ في خُصُوصِ الصِّفاتِ، بَلْ في صَحِيحِ البُخارِيِّ (p-٧٨٢) أنَّ النَّبِيَّ (ﷺ) قالَ لِعائِشَةَ: «يا عائِشَةُ! إذا رَأيْتِ الَّذِينَ يَتَّبِعُونَ ما تَشابَهَ مِنهُ؛ فَأُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ سَمّى اللَّهُ، فاحْذَرِيهِمْ»، وهَذا عامٌّ. وقِصَّةُ صَبِيغِ بْنِ عَسَلٍ مَعَ عُمَرَ بْنِ الخَطّابِ مِن أشْهَرِ القَضايا، فَإنَّهُ بَلَغَهُ أنَّهُ يَسْألُ عَنْ مُتَشابِهِ القُرْآنِ حَتّى رَآهُ عُمَرُ، فَسَألَ عُمَرَ عَنْ: ﴿والذّارِياتِ ذَرْوًا﴾ فَقالَ: ما اسْمُكَ؟ قالَ: عَبْدُ اللَّهِ صَبِيغٌ، فَقالَ: وأنا عَبْدُ اللَّهِ عُمَرُ، وضَرَبَهُ الضَّرْبَ الشَّدِيدَ. وكانَ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ إذا ألَحَّ عَلَيْهِ رَجُلٌ في مَسْألَةٍ مِن هَذا الجِنْسِ يَقُولُ: ما أحْوَجَكَ أنْ يُصْنَعَ بِكَ كَما صَنَعَ عُمَرُ بِصَبِيغٍ. وهَذا لِأنَّهم رَأوْا أنَّ غَرَضَ السّائِلِ ابْتِغاءُ الفِتْنَةِ لا الِاسْتِرْشادُ والِاسْتِفْهامُ، كَما قالَ النَّبِيُّ عَلَيْهِ الصَّلاةُ والسَّلامُ: «إذا رَأيْتِ الَّذِينَ يَتَّبِعُونَ ما تَشابَهَ مِنهُ ...». وكَما قالَ تَعالى: ﴿فَأمّا الَّذِينَ في قُلُوبِهِمْ زَيْغٌ فَيَتَّبِعُونَ ما تَشابَهَ مِنهُ ابْتِغاءَ الفِتْنَةِ﴾ فَعاقِبُوهم عَلى هَذا القَصْدِ الفاسِدِ، كاَلَّذِي يُعارِضُ بَيْنَ آياتِ القُرْآنِ. وقَدْ نَهى النَّبِيُّ (ﷺ) عَنْ ذَلِكَ وقالَ: لا تَضْرِبُوا كِتابَ اللَّهِ بَعْضَهُ بِبَعْضٍ فَإنَّ ذَلِكَ يُوقِعُ الشَّكَّ في قُلُوبِهِمْ (p-٧٨٣) ومَعَ ابْتِغاءِ الفِتْنَةِ ابْتِغاءُ تَأْوِيلِهِ الَّذِي لا يَعْلَمُهُ إلّا اللَّهُ، فَكانَ مَقْصُودُهم مَذْمُومًا، ومَطْلُوبُهم مُتَعَذِّرًا، مِثْلَ أُغْلُوطاتِ المَسائِلِ الَّتِي نَهى رَسُولُ اللَّهِ (ﷺ) عَنْها. ومِمّا يُبَيِّنُ الفَرْقَ بَيْنَ المَعْنى والتَّأْوِيلِ أنْ صَبِيغًا سَألَ عَنْ الذّارِياتِ ولَيْسَتْ مِنَ الصِّفاتِ. وقَدْ تَكَلَّمَ الصَّحابَةُ في تَفْسِيرِها مِثْلَ عَلِيِّ بْنِ أبِي طالِبٍ مَعَ ابْنِ الكَوّاءِ لَمّا سَألَهُ عَنْها، كَرِهَ سُؤالَهُ، لِما رَآهُ مِن قَصْدِهِ، لَكِنْ عَلِيٌّ كانَ رَعِيَّتُهُ مُلْتَوِيَةً عَلَيْهِ، لَمْ يَكُنْ مُطاعًا فِيهِمْ طاعَةَ عُمَرَ حَتّى يُؤَدِّبَهُ. والذّارِياتِ والحامِلاتِ والجارِياتِ والمُقَسِّماتِ فِيها اشْتِباهٌ، لِأنَّ اللَّفْظَ يَحْتَمِلُ الرِّياحَ والسَّحابَ والنُّجُومَ والمَلائِكَةَ ويَحْتَمِلُ غَيْرَ ذَلِكَ، إذْ لَيْسَ في اللَّفْظِ ذِكْرُ المَوْصُوفِ. والتَّأْوِيلُ الَّذِي لا يَعْلَمُهُ إلّا اللَّهُ هو أعْيانُ الرِّياحِ ومَقادِيرُها وصِفاتُها وأعْيانُ السَّحابِ وما تَحْمِلُهُ مِنَ الأمْطارِ ومَتى يَنْزِلُ المَطَرُ. وكَذَلِكَ في الجارِياتِ والمُقَسِّماتِ، فَهَذا لا يَعْلَمُهُ إلّا اللَّهُ تَعالى. وكَذَلِكَ في قَوْلِهِ: (إنّا ونَحْنُ) ونَحْوِهِما مِن أسْماءِ اللَّهِ الَّتِي فِيها مَعْنى الجَمْعِ كَما اتَّبَعَتْهُ النَّصارى، فَإنَّ مَعْناهُ مَعْلُومٌ وهو اللَّهُ سُبْحانَهُ، لَكِنَّ اسْمَ الجَمْعِ يَدُلُّ عَلى تَعَدُّدِ المَعانِي بِمَنزِلَةِ الأسْماءِ المُتَعَدِّدَةِ، مِثْلَ العَلِيمِ والقَدِيرِ والسَّمِيعِ والبَصِيرِ، فَإنَّ المُسَمّى واحِدٌ، ومَعانِيَ الأسْماءِ مُتَعَدِّدَةٌ، فَهَكَذا الِاسْمُ الَّذِي لَفْظُهُ الجَمْعُ. وأمّا التَّأْوِيلُ الَّذِي اخْتَصَّ اللَّهُ بِهِ، فَحَقِيقَةُ ذاتِهِ وصِفاتِهِ، كَما قالَ مالِكٌ: والكَيْفُ مَجْهُولٌ. فَإذا قالُوا: ما حَقِيقَةُ عِلْمِهِ وقُدْرَتِهِ وسَمْعِهِ وبَصَرِهِ؟ قِيلَ: هَذا هو التَّأْوِيلُ الَّذِي لا يَعْلَمُهُ إلّا اللَّهُ. وما أحْسَنَ ما يُعادُ التَّأْوِيلُ إلى القُرْآنِ كُلِّهِ.
