Whoever fulfils his covenant and is mindful of God—indeed, God loves the mindful.﴾ Know that (bala, "yes") is either used to affirm what they denied concerning there being no blame upon them regarding the unlettered (ummiyyin), meaning: "Yes, there is blame upon them." In that case, the pause on (bala) is a complete pause (waqf al-tamam), and His saying, ﴿whoever fulfils his covenant﴾, is a sentence confirming the sentence which (bala) has taken the place of. Or it is used to begin a new sentence without regard to it being a response to the preceding negation; for the word (bala) may be mentioned at the beginning of one speech that is followed by another, as al-Razi reported. This is the view I prefer, although al-Kashshaf and those who follow it limited themselves to the first view. They have mentioned concerning (na'am, "yes") that it comes for emphasis when placed at the beginning, as in: "Na'am, these are their ruins" (na'am hadhihi atlaluhum). So let (bala) be likewise, for they are siblings, even if they differ in some forms. Accordingly, it is not good to pause on (bala). The pronoun in ﴿his covenant﴾ either refers to the name of God in His saying ﴿and they speak falsely against God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75], in the sense: whoever fulfils God's covenant and is mindful of Him by abstaining from treachery and deceit, God loves him. Or it refers to ﴿whoever fulfils﴾, in the sense that whoever fulfils what he has pledged and is mindful of God, He loves him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "This is general, and it seems that even if the People of the Book fulfilled their covenants and abstained from betrayal, they would earn God's love," I say: Indeed, for when they fulfil covenants, they first fulfil the greatest covenant, which is what was taken from them in their Scripture concerning belief in a messenger confirming what is with them. And if they were mindful of God in abstaining from betrayal, they would be mindful of Him in abstaining from lying against God and distorting His words. End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 77:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[77] ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price — those will have no share in the Hereafter, and Allah will not speak to them or look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, and they will have a painful punishment.﴾

﴿Indeed, those who sell﴾ i.e., who exchange (yastabdilūn): ﴿the covenant of Allah﴾ i.e., what He took from them in His Book, or what they pledged to Him of belief in the Messenger who confirms what is with them: ﴿and their oaths﴾ i.e., those they bound themselves to by committing to follow the truth upon the tongues of the messengers: ﴿for a small price﴾ from the transient, base worldly life, the whole of which bears no comparison to the least of what they forfeited. ﴿Those will have no share﴾ i.e., no portion of reward: ﴿in the Hereafter, and Allah will not speak to them, nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection﴾, and that is due to their being veiled from the stations of His nearness, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿No! Indeed they, that Day, will be veiled from their Lord﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 15]. ﴿Nor will He purify them﴾ i.e., nor will He praise them as He praises His friends, or He will not cleanse them from the defilement of their sins through forgiveness: ﴿and they will have a painful punishment﴾ i.e., in the Fire. Know that in this verse there are several issues:

The first: Some of the commentators of the Zaydiyya said: the fruit of the verse is that whoever breaks a covenant with Allah for a worldly purpose, or swears falsely, has committed a major sin (kabira).

The second: On reconciling His saying here, ﴿and Allah will not speak to them﴾, with His saying: ﴿By your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 92], al-Qaffal said: the purpose of this verse is to show the intensity of Allah's wrath against them, for whoever withholds his speech from another does so out of anger toward him; when a person is angry with another he says to him, "I will not speak to you," and he may order that he be kept away from him, saying, "I do not wish to see the face of so-and-so," and when his name is mentioned he does not mention him with good. Thus it is established that the verse is a metaphor for the intensity of anger; we seek refuge in Allah from it. Others said: it is not far-fetched that Allah, majestic is His majesty, makes His friends hear His speech without a messenger, as a lofty honor particular to His friends, while He does not speak to these disbelievers and sinners, and the reckoning with them is through the speech of the angels. Others said: the meaning of the verse is that He will not speak to them with speech that would gladden them or benefit them, and all of these are good.

The third: Al-Shaykhan related from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever swears an oath to take the property of a Muslim man without right will meet Allah while He is angry with him." Abdullah said: Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited to us its confirmation from the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price﴾ to the end of the verse. In another narration he said: "Whoever swears a perjurious oath (yamin sabr) by which he seizes the property of a Muslim man will meet Allah while He is angry with him." So Allah revealed the confirmation of that: ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price﴾, the verse. Then al-Ash'ath ibn Qays al-Kindi entered and said: "What is Abu Abd al-Rahman (Ibn Mas'ud) narrating to you?" We said: "Such and such." He said: "He has spoken the truth; it was revealed concerning me. There was a dispute between me and a man over a well, so we brought it before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Your two witnesses, or his oath.' I said: 'He will swear and not care.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever swears a perjurious oath by which he seizes the property of a Muslim man, while he is a wrongdoer in it, will meet Allah while He is angry with him.' And it was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price﴾ to the end of the verse."

Al-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud also narrated it and said: the dispute was between al-Ash'ath and a Jewish man.

Al-Bukhari related from Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa that a man displayed a commodity in the market and swore by Allah that he had been offered for it what he had not been offered, in order to deceive a Muslim man into it, so this verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price﴾ to the end of the verse. We have previously mentioned, in the introduction to the tafsir in the discussion of the occasions of revelation, and in Surat al-Baqara also at the verse ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Jibril﴾ [al-Baqara: 97], what shows how such narrations may be reconciled, and that there is no contradiction. So reflect upon this.

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[78] ﴿Among them is surely a group who distort their tongues with the Scripture, so that you may think it is from the Scripture, but it is not from the Scripture. And they say, "It is from God," but it is not from God. And they tell lies against God while they know it.﴾

﴿Among them is surely a group who distort their tongues with the Scripture, so that you may think it is from the Scripture, but it is not from the Scripture. And they say, "It is from God," but it is not from God. And they tell lies against God while they know it.﴾

The Imam Ibn Kathir said: He, exalted is He, informs about the Jews, may the curses of God be upon them, that among them is a group who alter the words from their places, change the speech of God, and remove it from its intended meaning, in order to deceive the ignorant into thinking that it is in the Book of God in that form, and they attribute it to God. This is a lie against God, while they know within themselves that they have lied and fabricated in all of that. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they tell lies against God while they know it.﴾

Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "distort their tongues with the Scripture" (p-872) means they alter it. Thus al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that they alter it and remove it. No one removes the wording of a Book from the Books of God, Mighty and Majestic, but they distort it: they interpret it in other than its true interpretation.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: The Torah and the Gospel, as God, exalted is He, sent them down, have not had a single letter changed from them, but they go astray through distortion and interpretation, and through books they used to write from their own selves, saying, "It is from God," and it is not from God. As for the Books of God, they are preserved and cannot be altered. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it.

Ibn Kathir said: If Wahb meant what is in their hands of that, then there is no doubt that alteration, distortion, addition and omission have entered it. As for the translation of that witnessed text into Arabic, there is in it a great error, many additions, deficiencies and gross delusion. It falls under the category of interpreting a translated text that conveys meaning loosely, and the understanding of many of them is corrupt. But if he meant the Books of God which are His own Books sent from Him, then those, as he said, are preserved and nothing has entered them. End of quote. We have already discussed this in the introduction to the tafsir when speaking of the Isra'iliyyat (narratives of Israelite origin), and also in Surat al-Baqarah at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you hope that they will believe in you, while a group of them used to hear the speech of God and then distort it?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 75].

When He, exalted is He, had made clear their lies against Him, exalted is His remembrance, He made clear their fabrication against His messengers, for they claimed that 'Isa, peace be upon him, commanded them to take him as a lord. So He, glorified is He, answered them with His saying:

(p-873)

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[79] ﴿It is not for a human being that Allah should give him the Scripture, the judgment, and prophethood, and then he should say to the people, "Be servants to me rather than to Allah." Rather, [he would say], "Be rabbaniyyin (devoted to the Lord) because of what you have been teaching of the Scripture and what you have been studying."﴾

﴿Ma kana li-bashar﴾ means: it is not valid and not proper. The use of "bashar" (human being) hints at the reason for the ruling, since humanness is incompatible with what they attributed to him. ﴿An yu'tiyahu Allah al-kitab wal-hukm﴾ means the understanding and knowledge, or wisdom. ﴿Wal-nubuwwah﴾ means the report from Him, Exalted is He, so that he calls people to Allah by abandoning rivals. ﴿Thumma yaqula lil-nas﴾ means to those whom Allah sent him to, to call them to worship Him alone. ﴿Kunu 'ibadan li﴾ means take me as a lord. ﴿Min dun Allah. Wa lakin﴾ he says to them, ﴿kunu rabbaniyyin﴾, i.e., attributed to the Lord, because lordship has taken possession of them and humanness has been effaced, by virtue of their being knowledgeable, active, teaching, and reciting the books of Allah. That is, be worshippers who are disciplined through knowledge, action, and persistence in acts of obedience, until you become rabbaniyyin through the light overcoming the darkness. (This was conveyed by al-Qashani.) ﴿Bima kuntum tu'allimuna al-kitab wa-bima kuntum tadrusun﴾ means because of your perseverance in teaching people the Scripture and studying it, i.e., reading it. For that leads you to Allah, Exalted is He, through sincerity in His worship.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying:

[80] ﴿Nor would He command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords. Would He command you to disbelief after you have submitted [to Allah]?﴾

﴿Nor would He command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords; would He command you to disbelief﴾ means: to return to it, when he was sent to erase polytheism. ﴿After you have submitted﴾ means: after your firm establishment in Islam.

(p-874) Points of note (tanbihat):

The first: If what is mentioned in the verse is not befitting for a prophet or a messenger, then it is even less befitting for anyone else among people, by way of a fortiori reasoning.

For this reason al-Hasan al-Basri said: "It is not fitting for a believer that he command people to worship him." He said: "That is because the people used to worship one another," meaning the People of the Book. "They worshipped their rabbis and monks, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 31]." In Jami' al-Tirmidhi, as will come, it is narrated that 'Adi ibn Hatim said: "O Messenger of Allah, they did not worship them." He said: "Yes, they made lawful for them the unlawful and made unlawful for them the lawful, so they followed them; that is their worship of them." So the ignorant among the rabbis and monks and the leaders of misguidance enter into this censure and rebuke, unlike the messengers and their followers among the scholars who act, for they only command what Allah commands, which the noble messengers conveyed to them, and they only forbid what Allah forbade, which His noble messengers conveyed to them. Said by Ibn Kathir.

The second: In this verse is the greatest incentive for one who has knowledge to act upon it, and among the greatest acts of acting upon knowledge is teaching it, and sincerity to Allah, glorified is He. Dirasah (study, here: mutual review of knowledge and jurisprudence) indicates that knowledge, teaching and study make a person rabbani (a devoted, godly scholar). Whoever engages in them without this aim has wasted his effort and his work has failed. His example is that of one who plants a beautiful, splendid tree, pleasing to the eye, yet with no benefit in its fruit. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We seek refuge in Allah from knowledge that does not benefit and a heart that does not humble itself." Thus is it in Fath al-Bayan and in al-Razi.

(p-875) The third: In the seven canonical readings, ﴿wa-la ya'murakum﴾ is read with raf' (nominative) as a new sentence (isti'naf), meaning: "and Allah or the Prophet does not command you." It is also read with nasb (accusative) as conjoined to ثُمَّ يَقُولَ (thumma yaqula, "then he says"), and wa-la (ولا) is extra (mazidah), added to emphasize the meaning of negation.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[81] ﴿And when God took the covenant of the Prophets: "Whatever I have given you of the Book and wisdom, and then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and you must support him." He said, "Do you affirm and accept My commitment on that condition?" They said, "We affirm." He said, "Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses."﴾

[The scholar, may God have mercy on him, did not explain this verse]

The discussion of God's words, the Exalted:

[ 82 ] ﴿Whoever turns away after that, those are the defiant transgressors.﴾

﴿Whoever turns away after that, those are the defiant transgressors.﴾ Know that the purpose of these verses is to enumerate matters well known to the People of the Book which testify to the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), in order to cut off their excuse and to expose their obstinacy. Among them is what God, the Exalted, mentions in this verse: that He, the Exalted, took a covenant from the prophets to whom He had given the Book and wisdom, that whenever a messenger came to them confirming what was with them, even if he abrogated some of their rulings (as wisdom required, given the demands of the time), they would believe in him and support him, as a further emphasis on making his matter famous. Their knowledge, prophethood, and following of the law, and their support, would not prevent them from this. He informed that they accepted this, and He ruled that whoever turned away from it was among the defiant transgressors.

It has been read in the seven canonical readings with the lam of ﴿what I have given you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81] pronounced with a fatha and also with a kasra. On the first reading, it serves as a preface to an oath, because taking a covenant means making someone swear, and the ma (ما) in this case may be conditional. The ﴿you shall certainly believe in him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81] stands in place of the answer to both the oath and the condition. It may also be relative, meaning: "that which I have given you, you shall certainly believe in it." On the second reading, namely the kasra of the lam, the ma is either a verbal noun (maṣdariyya), meaning: "because of My giving you the Book, and then because of the coming of a confirming messenger to you who does not oppose you, God took the covenant that you shall believe in him and support him." Or it is relative, and the meaning is: his taking of the covenant concerns what I have given you, and a confirming messenger of it has come to you. As for His words ﴿then bear witness﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81], meaning: O prophets, bear witness against one another by acknowledgment. And in His words ﴿and I am with you among the witnesses﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81] there is an affirmation upon them. Whoever considers the course of this verse will know that this covenant has been emphasized to the utmost degree. If this obligation is upon the prophets, then it is all the more so upon their communities.

It has been narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: "God never sent a prophet among the prophets without taking a covenant from him: if God sends Muhammad while he is alive, he shall certainly believe in him and support him." He also commanded him to take the covenant from his community: "If Muhammad is sent while they are alive, they shall certainly believe in him and support him." Ibn Kathir said: "This does not contradict what Tawus, al-Hasan, and Qatada said: God took the covenant of the prophets that some of them would confirm others. Rather, it implies and necessitates it. For this reason, Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Ma'mar, from Ibn Tawus, from his father, the same as the statement of Ali and Ibn Abbas." — End of quote.

Some scholars understood this covenant to be specific to our Prophet (ﷺ), as al-Qadi Iyad reported in al-Shifa' from Abu al-Hasan al-Qabisi, who said: "God specially chose Muhammad (ﷺ) with a merit that He gave to no one else, which distinguished him, namely what He mentioned in this verse." — End of quote. You have now understood the intended meaning.

It remains to note that Imam Abu Muslim al-Isfahani held that in His words ﴿the covenant of the prophets﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81] there is an elision of a modifier, meaning: "their communities." His wording is: "The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that those from whom God took the covenant are obligated to believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) at the time of his mission, and all the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, will be among the dead at the time of Muhammad's mission, and the dead are not under obligation. Since those upon whom the covenant was taken are obligated to believe in Muhammad, peace be upon him, at the time of his mission, and it is impossible to impose belief upon the prophets at the time of Muhammad's mission, we know that those upon whom the covenant was taken are not the prophets themselves, but rather the communities of the prophets." He said: "What confirms this is that God ruled that those upon whom the covenant was taken, if they turned away, would be defiant transgressors, and this description does not befit the prophets, peace be upon them, but befits the communities." Al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, answered: "Why could it not be that the meaning of the verse is: if the prophets were alive, it would be obligatory upon them to believe in Muhammad, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him?" Its parallel is His words: ﴿If you associate others with God, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar: 65], though God knew that he would never associate anything with Him; rather, this statement came in the manner of supposition and hypothesis. So too here. He also said: ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have severed his aorta﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44–46]. And He said concerning the angels: ﴿And whoever among them says, "I am a god besides Him," We will repay him with Hell. Thus do We repay the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 29], although He informed about them that ﴿they do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ [al-Anbiya': 27], and that ﴿they fear their Lord above them and do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Nahl: 50]. All of this came in the manner of supposition and hypothesis, so too here.

We say: He named them defiant transgressors on the supposition of turning away, for the name of defiance is no more grave than the name of polytheism, and He mentioned, in the manner of supposition and hypothesis, His words: ﴿If you associate others with God, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. So too here. — Related by al-Razi.

When God, the Exalted, made clear that belief in the Prophet (ﷺ) is a law that He legislated and made obligatory upon all the prophets and communities who came before, it follows that whoever dislikes this is seeking a religion other than the religion of God. Therefore He said:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[83] ﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah, while to Him has submitted whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly, and to Him they will be returned?﴾

﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah, while to Him has submitted whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly﴾ That is: whoever is in them has submitted to Him, by humbling themselves and yielding to His will and proceeding under His decree, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly, and their shadows at morning and evening﴾ [al-Ra'd: 15]. ﴿Have they not considered what things Allah has created, whose shadows incline to the right and the left, prostrating to Allah while they are humbled?﴾ [al-Nahl: 48]. ﴿And to Allah prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures, and the angels, and they are not arrogant﴾ [al-Nahl: 49].

So the believer submits to Allah with his heart and his body, while the disbeliever submits to Him unwillingly, for he is under His subjugation, compulsion, and great authority, which cannot be opposed or resisted. This is what Ibn Kathir stated. ﴿And to Him they will be returned﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, when He will recompense each one for his deeds. The sentence was brought for the purpose of threat and warning.

(p-٨٧٩)

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 84:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[84] ﴿Say: "We believe in God, and in what has been revealed to us, and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the tribes, and what was given to Moses and Jesus and the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submitting."﴾

﴿Say: "We believe in God, and in what has been revealed to us, and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the tribes"﴾, i.e., the sons of Jacob; ﴿and what was given to Moses and Jesus and the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them﴾ by believing in some and disbelieving in others, as the Jews and the Christians do; ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾, i.e., we are obedient, so we do not take lords besides Him.

A subtlety:

The reason for the plural in His saying "We believe" (āmannā), after the singular in "Say" (qul), is that the command is general, and the singular is to honor him, peace be upon him, and to signal that he is the foundation of this matter. Or the command is specific to informing about his own pure self only, and the plural is to show the greatness of his rank and the elevation of his station with his command, by speaking of himself in the manner of kings.

A second point:

The verb anzala is here followed by the preposition ʿalā (indicating elevation), while in al-Baqarah it is followed by ilā (indicating destination), because both meanings exist: revelation descends from above and ends at the Messenger. So sometimes one of the two meanings is used and sometimes the other. The author of al-Lubab said: the address in al-Baqarah is to the community, due to His saying "Say" (qūlū) in the plural, so only ilā was correct, because the books reach the prophets and all their communities. Here He said "Say" (qul), which is an address to the Prophet ﷺ alone, not to his community, so the fitting preposition is ʿalā, because the books were sent down upon him and the community has no share in them.

There is consideration in this, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Believe in what has been revealed to those who believed﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 72]. This was noted by al-Nasafi.

(p-880)

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 85:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[85] ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him, and he will be, in the Hereafter, among the losers.﴾

﴿And whoever seeks﴾ i.e., desires, seeks: ﴿other than Islam as a religion﴾ i.e., other than monotheism and submission to the judgment of God, exalted is He. Like the practice of the polytheists openly, and those who claim to be monotheists while associating partners with Him, like the People of the Two Scriptures: ﴿it will never be accepted from him﴾ because he has not submitted to the command of God. And in the authentic hadith: "Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our command, it is rejected" (ﷺ): ﴿and he will be, in the Hereafter, among the losers﴾ because of his losing the guidance-paths in this world.

The scholar Abu al-Su'ud said: The meaning is that the one who turns away from Islam and seeks other than it is devoid of benefit, and falls into loss, by nullifying the sound natural disposition (fitrah) upon which people were created. And in the arrangement of rejection and loss upon the mere act of seeking is an indication that the condition of one who adopts a religion other than Islam and is content with it is more gruesome and more ugly. End of quote.

Commentary on His words, exalted is He:

﴿How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief, and had testified that the Messenger is true, and after clear evidences had come to them? And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

This is an expression of astonishment at how Allah would guide them to what is right and grant them success. The one who deviates from the truth after it has become clear to him is immersed in error and far from rectitude. It has also been said that this is a negation and a denial, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and wronged - never would Allah forgive them or guide them to a path(p-881) except the path of Hell﴾ [An-Nisa: 168-169].

The one meant by this verse is either the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab), and the intended meaning is their disbelief in the Messenger (ﷺ) when he came to them, after having believed in him before his coming, as they saw him in their scriptures, and they used to seek victory through him over the polytheists. It also refers to their testimony to the truth of his message, since they recognised him as they recognise their own sons. And there came to them clear evidences of his truthfulness, by which they believed in the like of them and in what is less than them, through Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both. Thus they wronged his right, which was established by his evidences and by their confirmation of the heavenly scriptures. Or the one meant by the verse is he who apostatised after his belief, as has been related concerning that, as we will mention.

Then Allah, exalted is He, explained the threat upon each of them with His saying:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[87] ﴿Those—their recompense is that upon them is the curse of Allah, and of the angels, and of mankind, all together.﴾

﴿Those﴾, i.e., those described by what preceded: ﴿their recompense is that upon them is the curse of Allah﴾, i.e., His expulsion (from mercy) and His anger. ﴿And of the angels and of mankind, all together﴾. The meaning of "mankind" is either the believers, or it is general, for the disbeliever also curses the one who denies the truth and apostatizes from it, and so he has cursed himself.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[88] ﴿Abiding therein; the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved.﴾

﴿Abiding therein﴾ means: in the curse, or the punishment, or the Fire, even though none of them has been mentioned, since the context points to them. Abiding in the curse, on the first reading, means that on the Day of Resurrection the angels, the believers, and those with them will continue to curse them in the Fire, so that none of their states is free from being cursed by one of these. Or it means abiding in the consequence of the curse, since the curse requires punishment, so the abiding of the consequence of the curse is expressed as the abiding of the curse itself. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever turns away from it, he will bear on the Day of Resurrection a burden﴾ [Ta-Ha: 100] ﴿abiding therein﴾ [Ta-Ha: 101]. This was stated by al-Razi: ﴿the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved﴾, meaning: they will not be given respite, or they will not be awaited so that they may offer an excuse, or they will not be looked upon with a merciful gaze.

(p-٨٨٢)

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[89] ﴿Except those who repent after that and make amends, for indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

﴿Except those who repent after that﴾: i.e., after disbelief following belief. ﴿And make amends﴾: i.e., they add righteous deeds to repentance. In this is the point that repentance alone is not sufficient until righteous deeds are added to it. ﴿For indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: so He accepts their repentance and bestows His favor upon them. This is from His kindness, His beneficence, His compassion, and His generosity towards His creation: whoever turns to Him in repentance, He turns to him in forgiveness. Ibn Jarir related from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: A man from the Ansar had embraced Islam, then apostatized and joined the polytheists. Then he regretted it and sent to his people: "Send to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ [asking]: Is there any repentance for me?" So this was revealed: ﴿How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief?﴾ [Al ʿImran: 86] up to His saying: ﴿For indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ So his people sent to him, and he embraced Islam. Likewise al-Nasai, al-Hakim, and Ibn Hibban related it. Al-Hakim said: "Its chain is sound, but they (al-Bukhari and Muslim) did not record it." ʿAbd al-Razzaq related from Mujahid, who said: al-Harith ibn Suwayd came and embraced Islam with the Prophet ﷺ, then al-Harith disbelieved and returned to his people. Then Allah revealed concerning him: ﴿How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief?﴾ [Al ʿImran: 86] up to His saying: ﴿Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ He said: A man from his people carried it to him and recited it to him. Al-Harith said: "By Allah, as far as I know, you are truthful, and the Messenger of Allah is more truthful than you, and Allah is more truthful than the three of you." So al-Harith returned and embraced Islam, and his Islam was good.

Ibn Salamah said: "Thus it became a repentance for him, and for every regretful person until the Day of Resurrection."

Note:

Some of the exegetes of the Zaydiyyah said: The fruit of the verse is the permissibility of cursing disbelievers, whether the disbeliever is specified or unspecified, according to the apparent evidences. Al-Nawawi said: The apparent meaning of the hadiths is that it is not forbidden. Al-Ghazali pointed to its prohibition, except regarding one whom Allah has informed us died upon disbelief, such as Abu Lahab, Abu Jahl, Pharaoh, Haman, and their like. He said: Because one does not know what will be the end of his life. As for those whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ cursed by name, it is possible that the Prophet ﷺ knew that they died upon disbelief. As for what has come in al-Tirmidhi from him ﷺ: "The believer is not a slanderer, nor a curser, nor one who is obscene or foul-mouthed." It was said: "Al-laʿan" (the one who curses habitually) is like "al-darrab" (the one who strikes much), for emphasis, and the meaning is: he does not make cursing a habit to the point of frequently doing it.

Among the fruits of the verse is the validity of repentance from disbelief and from sins such as apostasy and others, and this is a consensus (ijmaʿ, scholarly agreement). Except the repentance of the apostate: regarding it there is an anomalous dispute. According to the majority of scholars, his repentance is accepted by this verse and others. According to Ibn Hanbal, his repentance is not accepted; he related this from him in (Sharh al-Ibanah). It was said: This is an error. Also, by this verse and by His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Nisaa: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed﴾ [al-Nisaa: 137], where He affirmed belief after disbelief that was preceded by belief. If apostasy is repeated from him, his repentance is also valid according to the majority of scholars, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: If they cease, they will be forgiven what has already passed﴾ [al-Anfal: 38]. Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said: If he apostatizes a third time, his repentance is not accepted after that, i.e., by the apparent meaning of the verse of al-Nisaa. End quote. I say: In (Zad al-Mustaqniʿ) and its commentary, from the jurisprudence of the Hanbalis, is the following text: "The repentance of one whose apostasy is repeated is not accepted, rather he is killed, because that indicates the corruption of his belief and his lack of concern for Islam." End quote. This is close to the school of Ishaq. And in (Fath al-Bari) he related the same from al-Layth and from Abu Ishaq al-Marwazi, one of the imams of the Shafiʿis.

(p-884)

The discussion of the words of His exalted saying:

[90] ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved after their belief and then increased in disbelief - their repentance will never be accepted. And those are the ones who are astray.﴾

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved after their belief and then increased in disbelief - their repentance will never be accepted. And those are the ones who are astray.﴾ That is: those who strayed from the path of truth and erred from its way. The saying of the Exalted, ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾, has been a difficulty for many, since repentance is accepted according to the majority, as in the verse before it, and in His glorified saying: ﴿And it is He who accepts repentance from His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 25], and other than that. So they answered: the meaning is at the time of the presence of death. Al-Wahidi said in (al-Wajiz): "Their repentance will never be accepted, because they do not repent except at the presence of death, and that repentance is not accepted." - End of quote. That is, as the Exalted said: ﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death comes to one of them﴾ [al-Nisa': 18], etc.

It was also said: the non-acceptance of their repentance is a metaphor for their not repenting, i.e., they do not repent, like His saying: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6]. He expressed it this way to emphasize their condition and to display their state in the form of the state of those despairing of mercy. It was also said: because their repentance would only be hypocrisy, given their apostasy and their increase in disbelief. There remain for the exegetes other opinions, which in interpretation are further than what has been mentioned.

I see this verse as nothing other than the verse of al-Nisa': ﴿Indeed, those who believed and then disbelieved﴾ [al-Nisa': 137], etc. Both of them clearly indicate that whoever's apostasy is repeated, his repentance is not accepted, and this is the view taken by Ishaq and Ahmad, as we have mentioned earlier, because of his firm entrenchment in disbelief.

Al-Qashani has pointed out that this verse together with the one before it indicates that disbelievers are of two types in the matter of obstinacy. His expression at the saying of the Exalted: ﴿How will Allah guide a people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 86] is: He, the Exalted, denied His guidance to a people whom He had already guided first by the innate light of readiness toward faith, then by the light of faith, until they witnessed the truth of the Messenger and became certain, such that there remained for them (sic). The rational proof through the clear evidences was joined to this. Then, after all these signs, their souls manifested obstinacy and contentiousness, and veiled the lights of their hearts, their intellects and their spirits, which all three bear witness to the truth for the sake of the truth, because of the ill omen of their wrongdoing and the strength of the domination of their commanding souls over them, which is the utmost of wrongdoing. So He said: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 86], because of the thickness of their veil and their profound distance from the truth and from accepting the light. They are of two types:

One type, in whom the state of domination of the commanding souls over their hearts has become firmly rooted and established, and they have gone to the extreme of error and corruption, and persisted in distance and obstinacy, until that became a fixed disposition that does not depart. And another type, in whom that has not yet become firmly rooted, and has not yet become a seal (rayn) upon their hearts, and there remains behind the veil of the soul a remnant of the light of their readiness, perhaps mercy from Allah and success will overtake them, so they will regret and respond by the judgment of the innate disposition of their intellects. He indicated the first type by His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved after their belief﴾ to its end, and the second by His saying: ﴿except those who repent after that and make amends﴾ [Al 'Imran: 89], through persistence in righteous deeds and disciplines, to undo what they had corrupted. - End of quote.

[ ٩١ ] ﴿(Indeed, those who disbelieved and died while they were disbelievers, never will be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold, even if he were to ransom himself with it. For those is a painful punishment, and they will have no helpers.)﴾

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and died while they were disbelievers, never will be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold, even if he were to ransom himself with it. For those is a painful punishment, and they will have no helpers.﴾ This verse is similar to His saying in Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved - if they had all that is on the earth and the like of it with it, to ransom themselves thereby from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 36]. Imam Ahmad and the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Anas ibn Malik that the Prophet ﷺ said: "It will be said to a man from the people of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection: 'Tell me, if you had whatever is on the earth, would you have ransomed yourself with it?' He will say: 'Yes.' Allah will say: 'I wanted from you something easier than that, when you were in the loins of your father Adam: that you should not associate anything with Me. But you refused except to associate.'"

In a narration of Imam Ahmad from Anas, he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A man from the people of Paradise will be brought, and He will say to him: 'O son of Adam! How did you find your abode?' He will say: 'O Lord, the best of abodes.' He will say: 'Ask and wish.' He will say: 'I ask for nothing and wish for nothing except that You return me to the world so that I may be killed in Your cause ten times' - because of what he sees of the excellence of martyrdom. And a man from the people of the Fire will be brought, and He will say to him: 'O son of Adam! How did you find your abode?' He will say: 'O Lord, the worst of abodes.' He will say to him: 'Would you ransom yourself from it with the fill of the earth in gold?' He will say: 'O Lord, yes.' He will say: 'You have lied! I asked you for less than that and easier, and you did not do it,' and he will be returned to the Fire."

Therefore He said: ﴿For those is a painful punishment, and they will have no helpers﴾, meaning: no rescuer from the punishment of Allah, and no protector from the painful retribution of His punishment.

A subtle point (lafifah):

Regarding His saying: ﴿even if he were to ransom himself with it﴾, the author of al-Intisaf (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: This wa- (وَاو) accompanying the conditional (شرط) requires another condition, to which the conditional that is joined with it is necessarily coordinated. The custom in such cases is that what is stated alerts to what is left unstated by way of a stronger inference (طريق الأولى). Example: your saying: "Honour Zayd even if he does wrong." This wa- coordinated the mentioned with an omitted element whose estimate is: "Honour Zayd, even if he does wrong," except that you alerted by the obligation of honouring him even if he does wrong, that honouring him if he does good is a stronger inference. From it is His saying: ﴿Be persistent in upholding justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 135]. Its meaning - and Allah knows best - is: even if the truth is against others or against you, but He mentioned what is more difficult for them, so He made it obligatory, alerting to what is easier and more deserving of obligation. When the import of the wa- in such places becomes clear, you find this verse of Al 'Imran apparently contrary to this pattern, because His saying: ﴿even if he were to ransom himself with it﴾ requires another omitted condition, of which this mentioned case alerts by stronger inference. This mentioned situation, namely their ransoming themselves with the fill of the earth in gold, is the situation most worthy of acceptance of ransom, and there is no situation beyond it that would be more deserving of acceptance than it. Therefore al-Zamakhshari estimated the sentence to mean: "Never will a ransom be accepted from any of them, even if he ransom with the fill of the earth in gold," until another situation becomes evident in which ransoming specifically with the fill of the earth in gold would be more deserving of acceptance than it; so when it is negated where it is most deserving, then it is negated all the more in what is other than this situation by stronger inference. All of this is an explanation of what motivated him to the mentioned estimate. As for applying the verse to it, it is very difficult, so the better course is to mention an aspect by which the verse can be applied in the easiest way and nearest understanding, if Allah wills. We say: The acceptance of a ransom which is the fill of the earth in gold occurs in several states:

Among them: that it is taken from him by compulsion as a ransom for his self, as blood-money (diyah) is taken by compulsion from the property of the killer according to one opinion.

Among them: that the one ransoming says in supposition: "I ransom myself with such-and-such," though he may not do it.

Among them: that he says this statement and actually fulfils the amount with which he ransoms himself, and makes it present and ready, and he may hand it over, for example, to someone he trusts to accept his ransom.

When the states are multiple, what is meant in the verse is the most emphatic of the states and the most deserving of acceptance, which is that he ransoms himself with the fill of the earth in gold in a verified ransom, by being able to do this great thing, handing it over and fulfilling it by choice, and yet it is not accepted from him. Thus merely his saying: "I will spend the wealth and I am able to do so," or what runs in this direction by stronger inference, would then have the wa- in its proper function, alerting that there are other states in which acceptance would not benefit by stronger inference in relation to the mentioned state. This meaning has appeared plainly in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved - if they had all that is on the earth and the like of it with it, to ransom themselves thereby from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 36] - and Allah knows best. All of this is a confirmation that there is no escape and no deliverance for them from the threat; otherwise, it is known that they are more incapable of even a fils on that day. An example of this estimate is that a speaker says: "I will not sell you this garment for a thousand dinars, even if you hand them to me in my hand here." So reflect on this consideration, for it is of the "easy yet impossible" kind. And Allah is the Granter of success. (End.)

There is a second aspect: that what is meant is: "even if he ransoms with its like with it," as stated explicitly in that other verse. The meaning then is: the fill of the earth is not accepted as a ransom, even if its like is added to it. The "like" (مِثْل) is often omitted in their speech, as in your saying: "I struck him the striking of Zayd" (ضَرَبْتُهُ ضَرْبَ زَيْدٍ), meaning: "the like of his striking." And "Abu Yusuf Abu Hanifa" (أَبُو يُوسُفَ أَبُو حَنِيفَةَ), meaning: "his like." And the phrase "there is no question and no Abu Hasan for it" (وَقَضِيَّةٌ وَلا أَبَا حَسَنٍ لَها), meaning: "nor the like of Abu Hasan." Likewise it is intended in such expressions as their saying: "The like of you does not do such a thing," meaning: "you." That is because the two like things stand in for one another, so they are in the ruling of one thing. On this aspect, the speech proceeds according to the earlier interpretation, because by alerting that the fill of the earth in gold twice is not accepted, it alerts by stronger inference that filling it once is not accepted.

[p. 889] A third aspect: that "the fill of the earth" (مِلْءُ الأرْضِ) is not first taken to mean ransoming, but rather almsgiving (تَصَدُّق). The stated condition would then not be among what is intended to emphasize the preceding ruling, but rather a conditional whose answer is omitted, and the meaning becomes: "There will not be accepted from him the fill of the earth in gold, which he gives in charity; and even if he ransoms with it, it will not be accepted from him either." The pronoun in "with it" (بِهِ) refers to the wealth, without considering the attribute of giving in charity.

A fourth aspect: that the wa- was added to emphasize the negation. So reflect.

The commentary on His words, the Exalted:

[92] ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love. And whatever you spend, indeed Allah is Knowing of it.﴾

﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾ This is a resumed address to the believers, brought to explain what benefits them and is accepted from them, following the explanation of what does not benefit the disbelievers and is not accepted from them. That is: you will never reach the reality of righteousness (al-birr) and join the company of the righteous (al-abrar), based on the understanding that the definite article in al-birr is generic (lil-jins). Or: you will never attain the righteousness of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, which is His reward and His Garden, if the article is for a specific reference (lil-ahd), until you spend in the way of Allah from what you love, that is, what you desire and what pleases you of your noble wealth, as in His words: ﴿Spend of the good things you have earned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 267]. The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Anas ibn Malik who said: "Abu Talhah was the richest of the Ansar of Madinah in palm trees, and the most beloved of his property to him was Bayruha', and it faced the mosque, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to enter it and drink from its pleasant water." Anas said: "When this verse was revealed: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾, Abu Talhah came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: 'O Messenger of Allah! Indeed Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says in His Book: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾, and indeed the most beloved of my property to me is Bayruha', and it is a charity for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, I hope for its righteousness and its reserve with Allah. So place it, O Messenger of Allah, where Allah shows you.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Bakh bakh! That is a profitable property, that is a profitable property. I have heard what you said, and I think you should give it to the nearest relatives.' Abu Talhah said: 'I will do that, O Messenger of Allah.' So Abu Talhah distributed it among his relatives and the sons of his paternal uncle." (Bayruha' is narrated with a kasra or fatha on the ba', a fatha or damma on the ra', and with both mad and qasr; it is the name of a garden in Madinah. In al-Fa'iq it is said that it is fay'alá from al-barah, which is the open land. Bakh bakh is an expression of approval and praise, repeated for emphasis. Rabih with a single ba' means "possessing profit"; with a ya' underneath it means "its benefit and reward will return to you.")

In the two Sahihs it is also narrated that Umar said: "O Messenger of Allah! I have never acquired property more precious to me than my share at Khaybar, so what do you command me concerning it?" He said: "Keep the principal and dedicate the fruit."

Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr al-Bazzar narrated that Abdullah ibn Umar said: "This verse came to my mind: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾, so I considered what Allah had given me, and I found nothing more beloved to me than a Roman slave-girl of mine. So I said: 'She is free for the sake of Allah.' Then if I were to return to something I had dedicated to Allah, I would marry her." That is, I would marry her.

Note:

Al-Qashani said: In this verse, every act that brings its doer closer to Allah is righteousness, and approach to Him is not possible except by disassociating from all else. Whoever loves something has been veiled from Allah, the Exalted, by it, and has committed a hidden shirk, because his love is attached to other than Allah, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And among the people are those who take other than Allah as equals, loving them as they love Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165]. And whoever prefers himself with it over Allah has distanced himself from Allah in three respects: the love of other than the Truth, shirk, and preferring the self over the Truth. But if he prefers Allah with it over himself and gives it in charity and removes it from his hand, the distance has ceased and nearness has been attained; otherwise he remains veiled. And if he spends from other property many times its value, he has not attained righteousness, because of His knowledge of what he spends and his being veiled by other than it.

﴿And whatever you spend, indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾ That is: He will recompense you for it, whether it is little or much, good or otherwise.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 93:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[93] ﴿All food was lawful to the Children of Israel, except what Israel had made unlawful for himself before the Torah was revealed. Say: "Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful."﴾

﴿All food was lawful to the Children of Israel, except what Israel had made unlawful for himself before the Torah was revealed﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is that all foods had remained lawful to the Children of Israel from before the revelation of the Torah. And the prohibition of what was forbidden to them from them was because of their wrongdoing and their transgression. Nothing from them had been forbidden before that, except the single food item which their forefather Israel made unlawful for himself, so they followed him in its prohibition.

Notes (tanbihat):

The first: It is related concerning what Israel made unlawful for himself that it was the flesh of camels and their milk. Imam Ahmad related it in a narration, and al-Tirmidhi said: hasan gharib. It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and others, as statements traced to them (mawquf), that it was the sinew (al-'uruq). They said: he was afflicted with sciatica (ʿirq al-nasa) at night, which disturbed him, so he vowed that if he recovered he would not eat a sinew, and his descendants would not eat any flesh that had a sinew. So his sons followed him in removing the sinews from the meat (p-892), taking him as an example and following his path. Al-Razi said: Al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him, transmitted from the translation of the Torah that when Jacob left Haran for Canaan, he sent messengers to his brother Esau in the land of Seir. The messenger returned to him and said: Esau is coming to meet you, and with him are four hundred men. Jacob was alarmed and greatly grieved, so he prayed and supplicated, and he sent gifts to his brother, and he mentioned the story, until he mentioned the angel who met him in the form of a man. That man came close, and placed his finger on the place of the sciatic sinew, so that sinew became numb and dried up. Because of this, the Children of Israel do not eat sinews. End of quote. I say: The story is recorded in the Book of Genesis of the Torah, in chapter thirty-two.

The second: The prohibition mentioned, according to the first narration, namely the flesh of camels and their milk, was an act of piety, worship, asceticism and discipline of the self, seeking the pleasure of the Exalted Truth. According to the second, it was either fulfilment of a vow, or treatment, or because his soul found it repugnant, and Allah knows best. So the prohibition here means abstention.

The third: Al-Zamakhshari said: The verse is a refutation of the Jews and a denial of them, where they wished to clear themselves of what was censured against them in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws, and of cattle and sheep We forbade them their fat﴾ [al-An'am: 146], up to His saying: ﴿That is how We repaid them for their rebellion﴾ [al-An'am: 146]. They denied what angered them and what they recoiled from and resented, of what the Qur'an declared, namely the forbidding of good things to them because of their rebellion and wrongdoing. So they said: We are not the first to whom it was forbidden, and this is nothing but an ancient prohibition, which was forbidden to Noah and to Abraham and to those after them among the Children of Israel, and so on, until the prohibition reached us, so it was forbidden to us as it was forbidden to those before us (p-893). Their aim was to deny Allah's testimony against them of rebellion, wrongdoing, hindering from the way of Allah, consuming usury, taking people's wealth falsely, and the other evils He enumerated. End of quote.

﴿Say: "Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful."﴾ That is, in your claim that it is an ancient prohibition. In His command to the Prophet ﷺ to argue with them from their own Book and to confound them with what it states, that the prohibition of what was forbidden to them is recent, not ancient, as they claim, is the greatest proof of his truthfulness and their falsehood, since they did not dare to bring out the Torah. So they were confounded, and they turned back humbled.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 94:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[94] ﴿So whoever fabricates a lie against Allah after that, it is those who are the wrongdoers.﴾

﴿So whoever fabricates﴾ i.e., deliberately: ﴿a lie against Allah﴾ i.e., concerning the matter of foods and other things: ﴿after that, it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾ because they expose themselves to Allah's exposing them and punishing them.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[95] ﴿Say: "Allah has spoken the truth. So follow the religion of Abraham, inclining toward truth, and he was not one of the polytheists."﴾

﴿Say: Allah has spoken the truth﴾ is an indirect rebuke of their lying, meaning: it is established that Allah is truthful in what He has revealed, and you are the liars. ﴿So follow the religion of Abraham﴾, i.e., the religion of Islam upon which Muhammad (ﷺ) and those who believed with him stand, and which is in origin the religion of Abraham (peace be upon him), so that you may free yourselves from Judaism, which has entangled you in the corruption of your religion and your worldly affairs, since it has compelled you to distort the Book of Allah in order to make your aims agree, and has obliged you to forbid the good things that Allah made lawful for Abraham and for those who followed him. ﴿Inclining toward truth﴾, i.e., turning away from false religions. ﴿And he was not one of the polytheists﴾ is an indirect allusion to the shirk within Judaism and Christianity, namely ascribing a son to Allah or divinity to Jesus. How, then, do they claim to be upon his religion, when he called only to monotheism and to disavowal of every object of worship other than Allah, the Exalted, which is what Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent with?!

(p. 894)

The discussion concerning His saying, exalted is He:

[96] ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds.﴾

﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind﴾ — that is, for their rites and acts of worship. ﴿That at Bakkah﴾ — that is, "the House which is at Bakkah," i.e., in it. Omitting the noun it qualifies carries a grandeur that is not hidden. Bakkah is a dialectal variant of Makkah, for the Arabs interchange the letters bāʾ and mīm, as in their saying "ḍarbatu lāzibin wa lāzimin" (a blow that cleaves to), and "al-namīṭ and al-nabīṭ" as the name of a place in al-Dahnāʾ, and their saying "amrun rātibun wa rātimun" (a constant matter), and "aghbaṭat al-ḥummā wa aghmaṭat" (the fever subsided). It has also been said: Makkah is the town, and Bakkah is the place of the mosque. It was so named because it crushes (daqqihā) the necks of tyrants, so that no tyrant intends it except that God, exalted is He, breaks him; or because of the crowding (izdiḥām) of people there, from bakka, meaning to disperse and put down, and to press against. Likewise Makkah derives from makka, meaning to destroy and diminish, because it destroys whoever wrongs and profanes in it, and diminishes sins or annihilates them, as in the Qamus. Some have held that Makkah is "Mīshā" or "Māsā," mentioned in the Torah, and others that it is derived from the name of one of the sons of Ishmael, who was Massā. ﴿Blessed﴾ — that is, abundant in good, because of what accrues to one who performs the pilgrimage, the lesser pilgrimage, and seclusion there, and circumambulates it, of reward and expiation of sins. ﴿And a guidance for the worlds﴾ — because it is their qiblah and place of worship.

Note:

Some exegetes mentioned that the meaning of "first" is that it was the first to be laid out and built, and they related reports on this, among them that God created this House before He created any of the earths; and among them that God sent angels to build a House on earth in the likeness of the Bayt al-Ma'mur, and that was before the creation of Adam; and among them that it was the first House set down upon the surface of the water at the creation of the heavens and the earth, and that it was created two thousand years before the earth. There is no sound report in these narrations on which one may rely. What is definite is that the meaning is: the first house established as a mosque, as clarified by the narration of Ibn Abi Hatim from Ali, may God be pleased with him, concerning this verse, who said: "The houses existed before it, but it was the first house established for the worship of God, exalted is He." (p. 895) In the Two Sahihs, from Abu Dharr, may God be pleased with him, who said: "I said: O Messenger of God, which mosque was established on earth first? He said: 'The Sacred Mosque.' I said: Then which? He said: 'The Farthest Mosque.' I said: How long was between them? He said: 'Forty years. Then wherever prayer overtakes you, pray there, for the merit is in it.'"

Ibn al-Qayyim said in Zad al-Ma'ad: This hadith has caused confusion for those who do not know its meaning, and said: It is known that Sulayman ibn Dawud (Solomon) built the Farthest Mosque, and between him and Ibrahim there are more than a thousand years. This is from the ignorance of the speaker, for Sulayman only had of the Farthest Mosque its renewal, not its founding; and the one who founded it was Ya'qub ibn Ishaq, may God's peace and blessings be upon them both, after Ibrahim, peace be upon him, built it by this measure of time. End.

**The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:**

[97] ﴿In it are clear signs: the Station of Abraham. And whoever enters it is safe. And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by people who are able to make their way there. And whoever disbelieves, then Allah is Free of need from the worlds.﴾

﴿In it are clear signs: the Station of Abraham﴾: it is the stone on which he stood when he raised the foundations of the House. Ibn Kathir said: It was stuck to the wall of the House until Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), during his caliphate, moved it to the east, so that those performing circumambulation (tawaf) could reach it and so that people would not disturb those praying beside it after the tawaf, since Allah, exalted is He, had commanded us to pray there when He said: ﴿And take the Station of Abraham as a place of prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125]. The discussion of this has already been covered in Surat al-Baqarah. The exegetes said: The fruit of the verse is encouragement to visit the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) and to perform acts of obedience within it, because He, exalted is He, described it with blessing and guidance and made in it clear signs. (p-٨٩٦)

A subtle point (latifah, a refined observation):
"The Station of Abraham" is a subject whose predicate has been omitted, meaning: "Among them is the Station of Abraham." Or it is a substitute (badal) for "signs," a substitution of part for whole. Or it is an explanatory apposition (atf bayan). This is either taken singly, in view of its standing as many signs, because of the clarity of its significance and the strength of its indication of Allah's power and of the prophethood of Abraham, peace be upon him, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation, devoutly obedient﴾ [al-Nahl: 120]. Or it is taken in view of its containing many signs. They said: Each of the two footprints in a solid rock, his sinking into it up to the ankles, the softening of some rocks and not others, its preservation apart from the rest of the signs of the prophets, peace be upon them, and its being kept safe for thousands of years despite the great number of enemies, is an independent sign. This is supported by the reading (ayah bayyinah, "a clear sign") in the singular. Or it is understood from His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:
﴿And whoever enters it is safe﴾. Even if it is an independent initial or conditional sentence, it carries the sense of saying: "And he who enters its precinct is safe," so that in meaning and outcome it is coordinated with "the Station of Abraham." It is not hidden that the two are a kind of plurality, so this suffices. Or it is taken that he mentioned two of those signs and omitted mention of the rest, indicating their abundance. This was stated by Abu al-Su'ud. (p-٨٩٧)

Al-Mahayimi said: ﴿In it are clear signs﴾: the throwing of the birds at the People of the Elephant with stones of baked clay; the swift punishment of whoever transgressed within it; the answering of the supplication of whoever prayed beneath its water spout; and the submission of souls to its honour without any restrainer. Among its greatest signs is: the Station of Abraham, which is the stone on which he stood when he raised the foundations of the House. Whenever the wall rose, the stone rose into the air, then it became soft, so that his feet sank into it as though into mud, and its trace remained until the Day of Resurrection. Among its signs also: whoever enters it is safe from the plundering and fighting of the Arabs, and its game and trees are safe. End of quote.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The meaning of the safety of one who enters it is his safety from being molested, as in His saying: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a secure sanctuary, while people are being snatched away from around them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 67]. This was by the supplication of Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure land﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126]. If a man committed every offence and then sought refuge in the Sacred Precinct, he would not be pursued. And from Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): "If I found the slayer of al-Khattab (his father) within it, I would not touch him until he left it." End of quote.

A notice (tanbih):
What the verse establishes of safety for one who enters is only by its legal sanctity, which the verses revealed and which the hadiths and reports explained. In the two Sahihs, and the wording is that of Muslim, from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said on the day of the Conquest of Makkah: "There is no migration (hijrah) after the Conquest, but there is jihad and good intention, and when you are called to march forth, then march forth." He also said on the day of the Conquest of Makkah: "Indeed, this land, Allah made it sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth, so it is sacred by Allah's sanctity until the Day of Resurrection. Its thorny plants may not be cut, its game may not be startled, and its lost property may not be picked up except by one who will announce it, and its grass may not be cut." Al-Abbas said: "O Messenger of Allah, except for idhkhir (a fragrant grass), for it is used by their smiths and for their houses." He said: "Except for idhkhir." And the two have from Abu Hurayrah something similar or close to it. (p-٨٩٨)

Also in the two, and the wording is that of Muslim too, from Abu Shurayh al-Adawi, that he said to Amr ibn Sa'id, while he was dispatching armies to Makkah: "Permit me, O Amir, to relate to you a saying which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) uttered on the day after the Conquest. My ears heard it, my heart retained it, and my eyes saw him when he spoke it. He praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: 'Indeed Makkah, Allah made it sacred, and people did not make it sacred. So it is not lawful for a person who believes in Allah and the Last Day to shed blood in it or to cut a tree in it. If anyone takes permission from the fighting of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in it, say to him: Indeed Allah permitted His Prophet but did not permit you, and He only permitted me in it for an hour of the day, and its sanctity has returned today as it was yesterday. So let the one present inform the absent.'" It was said to Abu Shurayh: "What did he say to you?" He said: "I know that better than you, O Abu Shurayh. The Sacred Precinct does not protect a disobedient person, nor a fugitive with blood guilt, nor a fugitive with theft (kharbah)."

Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in Zad al-Ma'ad: His saying "it is not lawful for anyone to shed blood in it" refers to the prohibition of shedding blood that is specific to it, which is permitted elsewhere but forbidden there because it is a sanctuary. Just as the prohibition of cutting its trees, of startling its game, and of picking up its lost property is specific to it and permitted elsewhere, since all of them are in one statement and one system; otherwise the purpose of the specification would be void. These are of several kinds:

The first, and it is the one for which Abu Shurayh al-Adawi related the hadith: that a group that refuses to pledge allegiance to the Imam within it may not be fought, especially if it has an interpretation (ta'wil). Just as the people of Makkah refused to pledge allegiance to Yazid and pledged to Ibn al-Zubayr. Therefore, their fighting, the setting up of the catapult against them, and the violation of Allah's sanctuary was not permissible by text and consensus (ijma', the agreement of scholars). Only Amr ibn Sa'id the wicked and his faction opposed this, and opposed the text of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with his opinion and desire, saying: "The Sacred Precinct does not protect a disobedient person." It is said to him: It does not protect a disobedient person from the punishment of Allah. And if it did not protect him from having his blood shed, it would not be a sanctuary in relation to human beings, though it would be a sanctuary in relation to birds and animals. It has continued to protect disobedient persons since the time of Abraham, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, and Islam established this. The reason that Maqis ibn Subabah and Ibn Khatal and those named with them did not gain protection is that at that hour it was not a sanctuary but lawful ground. When the hour of war ended, it returned to what it had been upon the day Allah created the heavens and the earth. In the Jahiliyyah the Arabs would see the slayer of his father or his son within the sanctuary and would not disturb him, and this was among them specifically in the sanctuary that had become sacred. Then Islam came and confirmed and strengthened this. The Prophet (ﷺ) knew that among the community there would be those who would imitate him in making fighting and killing lawful there, so he cut off the analogy and said to his companions: "If anyone takes permission to fight the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), say: Indeed Allah permitted His Messenger but did not permit you." Based on this, whoever commits a hadd (prescribed punishment) or qisas (retaliation) outside the Sacred Precinct that requires execution, and then seeks refuge in it, may not have it carried out upon him within it.

Imam Ahmad reported from Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "If I found in it the slayer of al-Khattab, I would not touch him until he leaves it." It was also mentioned from Abdullah ibn Umar that he said: "If I found in it the slayer of Umar, I would not strike him." And from Ibn Abbas that he said: "If I met the slayer of my father in the Sacred Precinct, I would not harm him until he leaves it." This is the view of the majority of the Successors (tabi'un) and those after them. Indeed, nothing is preserved from any Successor or Companion contrary to it. Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) and whoever agreed with him from the people of Iraq went to this, as did Imam Ahmad and whoever agreed with him from the people of hadith. Malik and al-Shafi'i held that retaliation is carried out within it just as it is carried out outside it. This was also the choice of Ibn al-Mundhir. The argument for this view is the generality of the texts establishing the execution of hudud and qisas in every place and time, and that the Prophet (ﷺ) killed Ibn Khatal while he was clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah, and by what is narrated (p-٩٠٠) from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed the Sacred Precinct does not protect a disobedient person, nor a fugitive with blood guilt, nor a fugitive with theft (kharbah)." And because if the hudud and qisas concerned lesser matters than life, the sanctuary would not protect him nor prevent their execution upon him. And because if he committed within it something that requires a hadd or qisas, the sanctuary would not protect him nor prevent its execution, so likewise if he commits it outside and then seeks refuge in it, since its being a sanctuary for the purpose of protection does not differ between the two situations. And because he is an animal whose killing is permitted due to its corruption, so the situation does not differ between killing him after he has taken refuge in the sanctuary and his having committed what made his killing permissible within it, like the snake, the kite and the rabid dog. And because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Five are wicked creatures that are to be killed in the lawful area and in the sanctuary." So by mentioning their killing in the lawful area and the sanctuary he drew attention to the cause, which is their wickedness, and did not make their seeking refuge in the sanctuary a barrier to their being killed. Likewise the wicked son of Adam who has deserved execution.

The first group said: There is nothing in this that contradicts the evidences we have mentioned, especially His saying: ﴿And whoever enters it is safe﴾. This is either a report in the sense of a command, since it is impossible for Allah's report to be broken; or a report about His law and religion which He legislated in His sanctuary; or an announcement of the customary, continuous matter within His sanctuary in the Jahiliyyah and in Islam, as He said: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a secure sanctuary, while people are being snatched away from around them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 67], and His saying: ﴿And they say: If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched away from our land. Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary to which are brought the fruits of all things?﴾ [al-Qasas: 57].

Whatever lies outside this from the false opinions should not be considered, such as the saying of some: "Whoever enters it is safe from the Fire," and the saying of some: "He is safe from death while not in Islam," and similar claims. For how many have entered it while in the depths of Hellfire?

As for the general texts (al-'umumat) that indicate the implementation of the prescribed punishments (hudud) and retaliation (qisas) in every time and place, it is said first: those general texts make no reference to the time of implementation or its place, just as they make no reference to its conditions or the absence of its impediments. The wording does not indicate these by its literal form (wad') or by its implication (tadammun). It is therefore unrestricted (mutlaq) with respect to them. For this reason, when a ruling has a condition or an impediment, it is not said that the dependence of the ruling upon it is a specification (takhsis) of that general text. So no one who analyses (muhassil) says that His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], is specified by a woman who is in her waiting period ('iddah), or by marriage without the permission of her guardian, or without witnesses. Likewise, the general texts on the implementation of the prescribed punishments and retaliation make no reference to their time, their place, their condition, or their impediment. And even if the wording were supposed to include these, it would be necessary to specify it by the evidences that indicate prohibition, so that their effect would not be nullified; and it would be necessary to apply the general wording to what lies beyond them, like its counterparts. Now, if you specify those general texts by the pregnant woman, the nursing woman, the sick person whose recovery is hoped for, and the states that make implementation unlawful, such as severe illness, extreme cold, or extreme heat, then what prevents specifying them by these evidences? And if you say: this is not a specification but a restriction (taqyid) of their unrestricted form, then: "Take this measure of ours, [it is] equal for equal" (p. 902).

As for the killing of Ibn Khatal, it has already been mentioned that it occurred at the time of permissibility, and that the Prophet (ﷺ) cut off the extension of the ruling and stated that this was among his special privileges. His saying (ﷺ): "Indeed it was made lawful for me only for an hour of a day," is explicit that what was made lawful for him was the shedding of blood, which is lawful outside the Sacred Precinct (Haram), only during that hour specifically. For if it were lawful at every time, it would not have been restricted to that hour. This is explicit that lawful blood at other times is forbidden during it, apart from that hour.

As for his saying: "The Haram does not shelter a sinner," this is a saying of the corrupt man 'Amr ibn Sa'id al-Ashdaq, by which he rejects the hadith of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when Abu Shurayh al-Ka'bi narrated this hadith to him, as has been clarified in the Sahih. How then can it be preferred over the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?

As for your saying: "If the hadd and qisas were for lesser than the soul, the Haram would not protect the one who committed it from it," this question has two opinions among the scholars, and these are two reports explicitly attributed to Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him. Whoever prevents implementation looks to the general evidences that protect, with respect to the soul and what is below it. And whoever distinguishes says: the shedding of blood refers to killing, and its prohibition within the Haram does not necessitate the prohibition of what is below it, because the sanctity of the soul is greater and violation by killing is more severe. They said: also, the hadd by flogging or amputation operates as a form of discipline, so it is not prevented from it, like a master's disciplining of his slave. The apparent view of this school is that there is no difference between the soul and what is below it in this matter. Abu Bakr said: I found this issue in the report of Hanbal from his paternal uncle: that all the hudud are implemented in the Haram except killing. He said: and the practice is that every offender who enters the Haram is not subjected to the hadd until he leaves it. They said: and in that case we answer you with a compound answer. If there is a significant distinction between the soul and what is below it in this matter, then the objection is void. And if there is no significant distinction between them, then we equate them in the ruling and the objection is nullified. Its invalidity is therefore established under both assumptions.

They said: As for your saying that the Haram does not shelter one who violates its sanctity by committing what requires the hadd, the same applies to one who seeks refuge in it, then this is combining what Allah, His Messenger, and the Companions distinguished between. Imam Ahmad narrated: 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us from Ma'mar, from Ibn Tawus, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Whoever steals or kills in a hadd offence and then enters the Haram, he is not to be sat with, spoken to, or sheltered, until he leaves it and is seized, and the hadd is implemented upon him.
