And if he steals or kills within the Haram, it is implemented upon him within the Haram." Al-Athram mentioned, from (p. 903) Ibn 'Abbas also: "Whoever commits an offence within the Haram, the consequence of what he committed there is implemented upon him." Allah, glorified is He, has commanded the killing of whoever fights in the Haram, saying: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you there; but if they fight you, then kill them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191]. The distinction between one who seeks refuge and one who violates the sanctity there is in several respects:

First: the offender there is one who violates its sanctity by committing the crime within it. This contrasts with one who committed an offence outside it and then sought refuge in it, for he magnifies its sanctity and is conscious of it by taking refuge in it. Therefore analogizing one to the other is invalid.

Second: the offender within it is like one who corrupts on the carpet of the king in his house and sanctuary. One who committed an offence outside it and then sought refuge in it is like one who committed an offence outside the king's carpet and sanctuary, then entered his sanctuary seeking protection.

Third: the offender in the Haram has violated the sanctity of Allah, glorified is He, and the sanctity of His House and sanctuary. So he violates two sanctities, unlike anyone else.

Fourth: if the hadd were not implemented upon the criminals in the Haram, corruption would spread and evil would grow in the sanctuary of Allah. For the people of the Haram are like others in their need for their souls, their wealth, and their honour. And if the hadd were not legislated against those who committed crimes in the Haram, the hudud of Allah would be suspended and harm would spread to the Haram and its people.

Fifth: one who seeks refuge in the Haram is like the repentant, humble one who seeks refuge at the House of the Lord, may He be exalted, clinging to its curtains. Therefore it is not fitting for his situation, nor for the situation of His House and sanctuary, that he be disturbed. This contrasts with one who proceeds to violate its sanctity.

The secret of the distinction has become clear, and it has become evident that what Ibn 'Abbas said is pure jurisprudence (fiqh). As for your saying that it is a harmful animal, so its killing is permitted both inside and outside the Haram, like the rabid dog, then the analogy is not valid. For the rabid dog's nature is harm, so the Haram did not forbid killing it in order to repel its harm from its people. As for the human being, the origin with respect to him is inviolability, and his sanctity is great. He is permitted only by an external cause, so he resembles the aggressor among the permitted animals that are lawfully eaten, for the Haram protects those. Moreover, the people of the Haram need to kill the rabid dog, the snake, and the kite just as the people outside the Haram need it, equally. So if the Haram protected them, harm to the people would be great because of them. End. (From Part 2, from page 177 to page 180.)

When Allah, may He be exalted, mentioned the virtues and merits of the House, He followed it with the mention of the obligation of the pilgrimage (hajj), saying: ﴿And due to Allah from the people is the pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to make his way to it.﴾ The lam in "al-bayt" (the House) indicates a known referent (li-l-'ahd). Its hajj means: intending it for visitation with the known rite of worship (nusuk). The vowelling of the ha' with kasra and with fatha are two dialects, and they are two Sab'i (canonically recognised) readings. In the verse there are several discussions:

The first: concerning its grammatical analysis (i'rab). Abu al-Su'ud said regarding the beginning of the verse: it is a sentence consisting of a subject, which is ﴿hajj al-bayt﴾ (the pilgrimage to the House), and a predicate, which is "for Allah" (li-llah). His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿upon the people﴾ is attached to what the predicate is attached to of stability (istiqrar), or to an omitted element which is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun implicit in the preposition, the governing element of which is that stability. It is also permitted that "upon the people" be the predicate, and "for Allah" attached to what the predicate is attached to. Then he said regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿for whoever is able to make his way to it﴾, that it is in the position of the predicate, as a substitution (badal) from "the people," a partial substitution (badal al-ba'd min al-kull) specifying its generality. Thus the pronoun returning to the substituted noun is omitted, meaning: whoever among them is able. It was also said: a substitution of the whole (badal al-kull), on the basis that what is meant by "the people" is the able part, so there is no need for the pronoun. It was also said: it is in the position of nominative case (raf'), as the predicate of an implied subject, meaning: they are whoever is able. It was also said: it is in the place of accusative case (nasb) by the estimate: "I mean" (a'ni).

The second: this verse is the verse of the obligation of the hajj according to the majority. It was also said: rather it is His saying: ﴿And complete the hajj and the 'umrah for Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196]. The first is more apparent. In Fath al-Bayan: the lam in His saying "li-llah" is what is called the lam of obligation and binding (lam al-ijab wa-l-ilzam). Then the particle "'ala" (upon) increased this meaning with emphasis, for it is among the clearest indicators of obligation according to the Arabs, as when a speaker says: "I owe so-and-so such-and-such." So Allah, glorified is He, mentioned it in the most emphatic expression indicating obligation, to affirm His right and to magnify its sanctity. Numerous hadiths have been related that it is one of the pillars of Islam, its supports, and its foundations, and the Muslims have agreed upon this with a necessary consensus (ijma' darurri).

The third: the hajj is obligatory upon the accountable person (mukallaf) once in a lifetime, by the text and by consensus. Imam Ahmad, Muslim, and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed us and said: 'O people, Allah has enjoined upon you the hajj, so perform it.' A man said: 'Every year, O Messenger of Allah?' He remained silent, until he said it three times. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'If I had said yes, it would have become obligatory, and you would not have been able to do it.' Then he said: 'Leave me as I have left you, for those before you were destroyed by their abundance of questions and their disputing with their prophets. So when I command you with something, do of it what you are able, and when I forbid you from something, avoid it.'" Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed us and said: 'O people! Indeed Allah has prescribed for you the hajj.' Al-Aqra' ibn Habis stood up and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is it every year?' He said: 'If I had said yes, it would have become obligatory; and if it had become obligatory, you would not have acted upon it, and you would not be able to act upon it. The hajj is once. Whoever does more, it is voluntary.'"

(p. 906) The fourth: the ability to make the way (istita'at al-sabil) is an expression for the possibility of reaching it. Ibn al-Mundhir said: The scholars differed concerning His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿for whoever is able to make his way to it﴾. One group said: the verse is general, for we do not know of any established report from the Prophet (ﷺ), nor any consensus of the people of knowledge, that requires us to exclude any part from the apparent meaning of the verse. So the hajj is obligatory upon every able person who finds a way to it, by whatever means the ability is achieved, according to the apparent meaning of the verse. He said: And we have related from 'Ikrimah that he said: "The ability is health." And al-Dahhak said: "If he is a healthy young man who has no wealth, he should hire himself out for his food and his dependants until he completes his rite." Someone said to him: "Did Allah obligate people to walk to the House?" He said: "If some of them had an inheritance in Makkah, would he leave it?" He said: "No, rather he would set out toward it even if crawling." He said: "Likewise, the pilgrimage to the House is obligatory upon him." Malik said: "Ability is the capacity of people: a man who finds the provisions and the mount but is not able to walk, and another who is able to walk on his feet." Another group said: "Ability is provisions and mount." This is what al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said, and they relied on the hadith of Ibn 'Umar: "A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what makes the hajj obligatory?' He said: 'Provisions and a mount.'" Related by al-Tirmidhi, and in its chain is al-Khuzi, concerning whom there is criticism. Ibn Kathir said: "But others have corroborated him." The hafiz Abu Bakr ibn Mardawayh was keen to collect the routes of this hadith. Al-Hakim related it from the hadith of Qatadah, from Anas: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿for whoever is able to make his way to it﴾. It was said: 'What is the way?' He said: 'Provisions and a mount.'" Then he said: "It is sound according to the condition of Muslim, though they did not record it."

The fifth: Imam Ibn al-Qayyim al-Dimashqi, may Allah be pleased with him, said in Zad al-Ma'ad, in the context of the Prophet's (ﷺ) guidance in his pilgrimage: There is no disagreement that after his migration to Madinah he performed only one pilgrimage, which is the Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajjat al-Wada'), and there is no disagreement that it was in the tenth year. There is disagreement over whether he performed hajj before the migration.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 97 (part 3 of 3):

(p-907) Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) performed Hajj three times: two Hajjs before he migrated, and one Hajj after he migrated, along with which was an 'umrah." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib hadith from the narration of Sufyan." He said: "I asked Muhammad (i.e., al-Bukhari) about this, and he did not recognize it from the narration of al-Thawri." In another narration: "This hadith is not considered preserved (mahfuz)."

When the obligation of Hajj was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) hastened to perform Hajj without delay, for the obligation of Hajj was delayed until the ninth or tenth year. As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'umrah for Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196], although it was revealed in the sixth year at the time of al-Hudaybiyah, it does not contain the obligation of Hajj; rather it contains the command to complete it and to complete the 'umrah once one has embarked upon them, and that does not require the obligation of beginning them. If it is said: "From where do you derive that the revelation of its obligation was delayed until the ninth or tenth year?" It is said: "Because the beginning of Surah Al 'Imran was revealed in the Year of the Delegations (ʿam al-wufud), and in it the delegation of Najran came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and he made a treaty with them concerning the payment of the jizyah. The jizyah was only revealed in the Year of Tabuk, the ninth year, and in it the beginning of Surah Al 'Imran was revealed, and he debated with the People of the Book and invited them to monotheism and to mubahalah." This is indicated by the fact that the people of Makkah felt in their souls a loss of the trade with the polytheists when Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, indeed the polytheists are unclean, so let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram after this, their year﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28], so Allah the Exalted compensated them for that with the jizyah. The revelation of these verses and their proclamation took place in the ninth year. He sent al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr) to proclaim this in Makkah at the seasons of Hajj, and he sent 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) after him. What we have mentioned has been said by more than one of the early scholars (al-salaf), and Allah knows best. As for the words of the Exalted:
﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is Free of need from the worlds﴾ — it is either a new sentence (mustanaf) announcing the threat against whoever disbelieves in Him, Exalted, with no connection to what precedes it; or it is connected to what precedes it and is included with it, and this is more apparent and more eloquent. The disbelief (kufr) here is either in the sense of denying the obligation of Hajj, or in the sense of abandoning what was previously commanded. Its parallel in the Sunnah is what al-Nasa'i and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Buraydah, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The covenant between us and them is the prayer; whoever abandons it has disbelieved." (p-908) And from Abdullah ibn Shaqiq, who said: "The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not regard abandoning any of the deeds as disbelief except the prayer" — related by al-Tirmidhi. And Abu Dawud has from Jabir, raised: "Between the servant and disbelief is the abandoning of the prayer." The wording of Muslim is: "Between a man and polytheism is the abandoning of the prayer." Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever possesses provision and a mount that conveys him to the House of Allah and does not perform Hajj, then it makes no difference to him whether he dies as a Jew or a Christian; and that is because Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And due to Allah from the people is pilgrimage to the House — for whoever is able to find thereto a way﴾." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hasan gharib hadith; we do not know it except through this route, and there is criticism (maqal) in its isnad." Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr al-Isma'ili narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "Whoever is able to perform Hajj but does not perform it, it makes no difference to him whether he dies as a Jew or a Christian." Ibn Kathir said: "Its isnad to Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) is sound." Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated in his Sunan from al-Hasan al-Basri, who said: Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I have considered sending a man to these regions, so that they may look at every person who has means (jidah) but does not perform Hajj, and impose the jizyah upon them; they are not Muslims, they are not Muslims." Al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: Ibn Habib has used the apparent meaning of the verse to argue that whoever abandons Hajj, even if he does not deny it, has disbelieved. Then he said: Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Umar: "Whoever is able and is wealthy and healthy but does not perform Hajj, his mark between his eyes will be (that of) a disbeliever," then he recited this verse.

(p-909) Reminder:
This noble verse has gathered, from the various kinds of considerations that express the utmost concern with the matter of Hajj and the severe warning against one who abandons it, what admits of no further addition. Among them: the use of the preposition lam and ʿalā in His saying ﴿And due to Allah from the people is pilgrimage to the House﴾, meaning that it is a right obligatory upon the necks of people owed to Allah, from which they cannot be released until they fulfill it and discharge their duty. Among them: that He mentioned "the people" and then replaced it with ﴿for whoever is able to find thereto a way﴾, and in this there are two kinds of emphasis:
One of them: that the substitution is a repetition and a reiteration of the intended meaning.
The second: that clarification after ambiguity and detail after generality is presentation of it in two different forms.
Among them: His saying ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ in place of "whoever does not perform Hajj," as a strengthening against the one who abandons Hajj.
Among them: the mention of being free of need from it, which indicates abhorrence, wrath and forsaking.
Among them: His saying ﴿from the worlds﴾ and not "from it." What it contains of indication of independence from it by proof: for when He is free of need from the worlds, independence from it is necessarily included; and because it indicates complete independence, it is more indicative of the magnitude of the wrath, which is expressed by this phrase. Al-Zamakhshari pointed to this. Then the Exalted rebuked the disbelieving People of the Book for their obstinacy against the truth with His saying:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[98] ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah, while Allah is Witness over what you do?"﴾

﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah"﴾ i.e., those that indicate the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). His saying ﴿while Allah is Witness over what you do﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) serving to intensify the rebuke, and the naming of Allah (al-Jalālah) in the place where a pronoun would be expected serves to instill humiliation and to magnify the gravity of the matter. The intensive form in (shahīd, "Witness") serves to confirm the warning, and all of this necessitates that they not dare to do what they are doing. Then, may He be exalted, following the denunciation of them for their misguidance, rebuked them for their leading others astray, saying:

(p-910)

**[The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:]**

[99] ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, why do you avert from the way of Allah those who believe, seeking to make it crooked, while you are witnesses? And Allah is not unaware of what you do."﴾

﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, why do you avert from the way of Allah"﴾: that is, from His religion. They would scheme to turn people away from Islam. ﴿Those who believe﴾ is the object of ﴿you avert﴾, and the prepositional phrase was placed before it for emphasis. ﴿You seek it﴾ is according to ḥadhf wa-iṣāl (omission of the preposition and its attachment to the verb), meaning: you seek for it, that is, for the way of Allah, which is the most upright of ways. ﴿Crooked﴾ means: crookedness, deviation, and distortion.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The verb *baghā* (to seek) takes a single object when it is not accompanied by the preposition *lām*, as in your saying: *baghaytu al-māl* (I sought the wealth), *al-ajr* (the reward), and *al-thawāb* (the recompense). Here the intended sense is: "you seek for it crookedness," and then the *lām* was dropped, as they said: *wahabtuka dirhaman* (I gave you a dirham), meaning *wahabtu laka dirhaman* (I gave to you a dirham). Similarly: *ṣidtuka ẓabyan* (I hunted a gazelle for you), meaning *ṣidtu laka ẓabyan* (I hunted for you a gazelle). And he recited:

*So their servant turned away, then called out: "Shall I hunt for you an oryx, or a donkey?"*

He meant: *aṣīdu lakum* (I hunt for you).

Al-Razi said: There is another interpretation of the verse, namely that ﴿crooked﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*). The meaning would be: you seek it while going astray, since they used to claim that they were upon the religion and way of Allah. So He, exalted is He, said: You seek the way of Allah while going astray. According to this view, there is no need for ḥadhf wa-iṣāl.

Nasir al-Din mentioned in *al-Intisaf* another interpretation, saying: "It is more complete in meaning, namely that you make the pronoun (*hā'*) the direct object, and ﴿crooked﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier in which the verbal noun that is ﴿crooked﴾ occupies the place of a noun. In this grammatical construction there is an exaggeration: they seek for the straight path to become crookedness itself, following the mode of exaggeration in such expressions as *rajulun ṣawm* (a man who is all fasting). This would be more forceful in condemning them and rebuking them, and Allah knows best."

﴿While you are witnesses﴾ that it is the way of Allah, and averting from it is misguidance and leading others astray. ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ is a threat and a warning.

(p-٩١١)

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[100] ﴿O you who have believed, if you obey a faction of those who were given the Scripture, they will return you, after your belief, to disbelievers.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, if you obey a faction of those who were given the Scripture﴾, i.e., by your good opinion of them because they are the People of the Book: ﴿they will return you after your belief﴾, i.e., in monotheism and prophethood: ﴿to disbelievers﴾, because they envy the believers for what Allah has given them of His bounty, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Many of the People of the Scripture wish they could return you to disbelief after your belief, out of envy from themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 109], and the verse.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 101:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[101] ﴿And how can you disbelieve while the verses of Allah are recited to you and among you is His Messenger? And whoever holds fast to Allah has already been guided to a straight path.﴾

﴿And how can you disbelieve﴾: the meaning of the interrogative here is denunciation and wonder. The meaning is: from where could disbelief reach you? ﴿while the verses of Allah are recited to you﴾, which is the Qur'an, the inimitable (al-Mu'jiz), which is greater than the signs that were recited to those before them; ﴿and among you is His Messenger﴾, who admonishes you, exhorts you, and removes your doubts, and who has guided you from error and rescued you from ignorance. ﴿And whoever holds fast to Allah has already been guided to a straight path﴾, that is: whoever adheres to His true religion, which He has made clear through His signs upon the tongue of His Messenger, namely Islam and monotheism, which is expressed as the Way of Allah. Then he is upon guidance and his follower will not go astray. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible that this be an exhortation for them to take refuge in Him in repelling the evils and schemes of the disbelievers" — end of quotation. Then the sentence, in that case (p-912), is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to His saying: ﴿O you who believe, if you obey a party of those who were given the Scripture...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 100] and so on, because its implication is that if you obey them out of fear of their evils and schemes, then do not fear them, and take refuge in Allah in repelling that, for whoever takes refuge in Him, He suffices him.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[102] ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah as He should be feared, and do not die except as Muslims.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah as He should be feared﴾ That is, as He deserves to be feared (ḥaqq taqātih), and this is by continuing in fear of Him, outwardly and inwardly, and acting in accordance with what it requires. Al-Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Abī Ḥātim related, with a sound chain of narration, from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd that he said concerning the meaning of the verse: it is that He is obeyed and not disobeyed, that He is remembered and not forgotten, and that He is thanked and not ungrateful to Him. Ibn Mardawayh and al-Ḥākim also related it as a marfūʿ (traced to the Prophet ﷺ) report, and al-Ḥākim said: "It is sound according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhārī and Muslim), though they did not record it."

Ibn Kathīr said: "The more apparent view is that it is a mawqūf (ending with a Companion) report, and Allah knows best."

It is also related from Anas that he said: "A servant does not fear Allah as He should be feared until he guards his tongue." ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah related from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning the verse: that they strive in the way of Allah with the striving due to Him, and that the blame of any blamer does not seize them concerning Allah, and that they stand firm in justice even against themselves, their fathers and their sons.

I say: All that has been related, insofar as the verse includes it in its generality, is not contradictory.

Note:

Some claimed that this clause of the verse is abrogated by the verse ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghābun: 16], interpreting "as He should be feared" to mean that the servant must perform everything due to Allah and that He deserves. He said: "This would render the servant unable to fulfill it, so attaining it is impossible." This claim did not hit the mark, for each of the two verses was brought in a specific sense of its own, so it cannot be conceived that this clause demands an impossible degree of taqwā. Rather, what is meant by it is the continuance of turning to Him, the fear of Him, and recognition of His majesty and greatness, in heart and body, as we have explained. This is within the capacity of everyone who turns to Him. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghābun: 16], is a command to worship Him to the extent of capacity, without imposing what cannot be borne, since ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. It is evident that whoever does what he is able of the worship of Him, Exalted is He, turns to His majesty, sincerely purifies his deeds, and is solicitous in his acts of obedience, has indeed feared Allah as He should be feared. ﴿And do not die except as Muslims﴾, that is, sincerely devoting your souls to Allah, Exalted is He, not allowing any association with anything else in them at all, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 125]. This is an exceptive construction (istithnāʾ mufarragh) from the most general of states, meaning: do not die in any state except the state of the realization of your Islam and your steadfastness upon it, as the nominal sentence indicates. Had it been said "except as Muslims," it would not have conveyed its benefit.

The governing element of the state (al-ʿāmil fī al-ḥāl) is what precedes illā after the negation. The apparent sense of the noble wording, although it is a prohibition against dying under a certain condition, is being in any state other than the state of Islam; but the intended meaning is the prohibition of that condition at the moment of death, which necessarily implies a command to its opposite, which is being in the state of Islam at that time. Since the address is to the believers, the intended meaning is the obligation of steadfastness upon Islam until death. Directing the prohibition at death is for emphasis in prohibiting its mentioned condition, for the prohibition of a qualified thing of this kind is a prohibition of the qualification and a complete removal of it at its root, conveying what the prohibition of the qualification itself does not convey. For your saying: "Do not pray except while you are (khāshiʿ)," conveys, in emphasizing the obligation of humility in prayer, what your saying "Do not abandon humility in prayer" does not convey; because the latter is a prohibition only against abandoning humility, whereas the former is a prohibition against it and against what accompanies it, and it indicates that humility is the foundation of prayer, and that prayer without it should not be performed. In this there is a kind of warning against what lies beyond death, as Abū al-Suʿūd conveyed.

The discussion of another aspect of the eloquent secret of this clause has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah.

**The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[103] ﴿And hold fast, all together, to the rope of Allah, and do not separate. And remember the favour of Allah upon you when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became, by His favour, brothers. And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it. Thus does Allah make clear to you His signs that you may be guided.﴾

﴿And hold fast, all together, to the rope of Allah, and do not separate.﴾ The "rope" (al-habl) may mean the covenant, as He said in the verse after it: ﴿Humiliation is decreed upon them wherever they are found, except with a rope from Allah and a rope from the people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 112], meaning, with a covenant and a pledge. It may also mean the Qur'an, as in Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Zayd ibn Arqam, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: (p-915) "Verily, I am leaving among you two weighty things: the first is the Book of Allah, which is the rope of Allah. Whoever follows it is upon guidance, and whoever abandons it is upon misguidance..." The hadith continues. The two meanings are close, for His covenant, that is, His law, His religion and His Book, is a safeguard for the one who holds fast to it against misguidance, like a rope that one grips for fear of falling.

His saying ﴿and do not separate﴾ means: do not turn away from the truth by falling into disagreement among yourselves, as the Jews and Christians disagreed, or as you were divided in the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam), turning your backs on one another, with some of you opposing and fighting others. Or it means: do not bring about (p-916) that which leads to division and to the loss of the unity and harmony you now have, which is contrary to what your Unifier, who brought you together, desires, namely following the truth and holding fast to Islam. This is the explanation given by al-Zamakhshari.

﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became, by His favour, brothers.﴾

Al-Zamakhshari said: In the Jahiliyyah there were among them grudges, enmities and continuous wars. Then Allah brought their hearts together through Islam, cast love into them, and they became loving, agreeing, merciful and sincerely counselling brothers, united upon one matter, which arranged their affairs among them and removed disagreement. This is the brotherhood in Allah.

﴿And you were on the brink,﴾ that is, on the edge, ﴿of a pit of the Fire,﴾ because of the state of Jahiliyyah you were in, ﴿and He saved you from it,﴾ that is, through Islam.

Ibn Kathir said: This context concerns the Aws and the Khazraj, for among them there were many wars in the Jahiliyyah, intense enmity, rancour and grudges, and their fighting and battles lasted a long time because of them. When Allah brought Islam, and those among them who entered it did so, they became brothers who loved one another for the majesty of Allah, who were closely bound together for the sake of Allah, and who helped one another in righteousness and piety. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He it is who supported you with His help and with the believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 62] ﴿and brought their hearts together﴾ [al-Anfal: 63], and the verse continues. They had been on the brink of a pit of the Fire because of their disbelief, and Allah saved them from it when He guided them to faith. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reminded them of this favour on the day he distributed the spoils of Hunayn. Some of them found fault, because of what he had preferred for others in the distribution, according to what Allah had shown him. So he addressed them, saying: "O assembly of the Ansar! Did I not find you astray, and Allah guided you through me? Were you not divided, and Allah united you through me? Were you not poor, and Allah made you rich through me?" Whenever he said something, they replied: "Allah and His Messenger are most gracious." End of Ibn Kathir's words.

(p-917) **A subtle point:**

Al-Zamakhshari said: The pronoun in ﴿from it﴾ refers either to the pit, or to the Fire, or to the brink. It is feminine because it is attached to "pit", and it refers to the brink as in the line of poetry:

*"As the spear's shaft was soaked with blood."*

End of his words.

(p-918) Abu Hayyan said: It is only good for the pronoun to refer to the brink, because that is what is being spoken of. End of his words.

In al-Intisaf (by Ibn al-Munayyir) it is said: The pronoun may refer to the pit, and so there is no need for the interpretation mentioned above, just as you say: "I honoured the servant of Hind and treated her well." The meaning is more complete if it refers to the pit, for it is from the pit that deliverance is truly a favour. As for being favoured with deliverance from the brink, this is because being on the brink usually entails falling into the pit, so deliverance from the brink is deliverance from the pit into which one was about to fall. Thus, attributing the favour to deliverance from the pit is more eloquent and more striking. Moreover, Abu 'Ali in al-Ta'aliq regarded the acquisition of feminine gender from the genitive noun as a poetic necessity, contrary to his view in al-Idah, as reported by Ibn Yas'un.

What led al-Zamakhshari to refer the pronoun to the brink is only that the brink is where they were; they had not been in the pit so that He could favour them with deliverance from it. Yet I have shown, in the course of this discussion, what justifies the favour of deliverance from the pit, for they were usually heading toward it had it not been for the Lord's deliverance. Do you not see the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The one who grazes around the sanctuary is about to fall into it," and the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Is one who founded his building upon the brink of a crumbling, collapsing bank, so it collapsed with him into the fire of Hell?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 109]? (p-919) Consider how Allah the Exalted made the building's standing on the brink a cause leading to its collapse into the Fire of Hell, emphasising this with His saying ﴿collapsing﴾ [al-Tawbah: 109]. And Allah knows best. End of his words.

Then al-Zamakhshari said: The brink of a pit, and its lip (shafa and shafah), is its edge, whether masculine or feminine. Its final radical is a waw, but in the masculine form it is transposed, and in the feminine it is elided. Similarly, al-Shafa and al-Shafah are like al-Janib and al-Janibah (side). End of his words.

Al-Zajjaj reported the dual of shafa as shafawan. Al-Akhfash said: Since imala (vowel inclination toward the i-sound) is not permitted in it, it is known to derive from waw, because imala is from ya'. Thus it is in al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari).

Then al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: how were they placed on the edge of a pit of the Fire? I say: had they died in the state they were in, they would have fallen into the Fire. So their life, after which falling into the Fire was expected, is depicted as sitting on its edge, on the verge of falling into it.

Al-Razi said: This contains an indication of the insignificance of the duration of life, for between life and death, which necessarily leads to falling into the pit, there is no more than the distance between the edge of a thing and that thing itself.

﴿Thus﴾ means: like that clarification, ﴿does Allah make clear to you His signs﴾ in every place, to deliver you from misguidance in it, ﴿that you may be guided﴾ to your religious and worldly right direction in it. Then he pointed out that just as He saved you from the Fire and from misguidance by sending the Messengers and sending down the verses, so there should be among you those who save their brothers. Thus he said: (p-920)

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 104:**

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[104] ﴿Let there be among you a community who call to good, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong. Those are the successful.﴾

﴿Let there be among you a community﴾: i.e., a group. It is called *umma* because people flock to it (*yawummuhā*), meaning they seek it out and follow it. ﴿who call to good﴾, which is what contains religious and worldly welfare. ﴿and enjoin what is right﴾, i.e., every kind of what is right, whether obligatory or recommended, which brings them closer to Paradise and keeps them far from the Fire. ﴿and forbid what is wrong﴾, i.e., every kind of what is wrong, whether forbidden or disliked, which brings them closer to the Fire and keeps them far from Paradise. ﴿Those﴾, the callers, enjoiners and forbidders, ﴿are the successful﴾, the ones who win the rewards of their deeds and the deeds of those who follow them.

Some scholars said: *al-falāḥ* (success) is attaining victory and reaching the desired goal. Worldly success is attaining the happiness by which life is made pleasant, while otherworldly success consists of four things: lasting without perishing, honour without humiliation, wealth without poverty, and knowledge without ignorance.

**Subtle Point:**

It has been said that the conjunction in ﴿and enjoin﴾ (*wa-ya'murūna*) on what precedes it is the conjunction of the specific upon the general (*'aṭf al-khāṣṣ 'alā al-'āmm*). This is what al-Zamakhshari said, and he was challenged on it in (*al-Intiṣāf*). His wording is: The conjunction of the specific upon the general indicates greater attention to the specific, without doubt, when it is restricted to some of the things the general covers, like His saying: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [al-Baqara: 98], and His saying: ﴿In them are fruit and palm trees and pomegranates﴾ [al-Rahman: 68], and His saying: ﴿Guard over the prayers and the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqara: 238], and similar examples, because restricting to specifying what is singled out by mention gives it distinction from the rest of what the general covers. As for this verse, after the general term *al-khayr* (good), everything it covers has been mentioned, since the good being called to is either the doing of something commanded or the leaving of something forbidden, and it does not exceed one of these two. So for the specification to distinguish it from the rest of what the general covers, the better view is that the purpose of this specification is to mention the calling to good first in general and then in detail. In this there is an admonition that mention in two ways has what is not hidden of care (God knows best). Unless a custom is established that restricts enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong to some kinds of good, in which case al-Zamakhshari's intention is complete. I do not consider this custom to exist, and God knows best. End.

**Notice:**

The verse indicates the obligation of enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. Its obligation is established by the Book and the Sunna, and it is among the greatest duties of the pure Shari'a, a great foundation of its foundations, a firm pillar of its pillars, and through it its order is perfected and its summit is raised. So says (*Fath al-Bayan*).

Al-Ghazali, may God be pleased with him, said: This verse contains a clear statement of obligation. His exalted saying ﴿Let there be﴾ is a command, and the apparent meaning of a command is obligation. It also shows that success is bound to it, since He restricted it, saying: ﴿Those are the successful﴾. It also shows that it is a collective obligation (*farḍ kifāya*) and not an individual obligation (*farḍ 'ayn*), and that when a community undertakes it, the obligation falls from the others. For He did not say: "Let all of you be enjoiners of what is right," but rather: ﴿Let there be among you a community﴾. Therefore, whenever one person or a group undertakes it, the burden is lifted from the others, and success belongs specifically to those who undertake it directly. But if all of creation neglects it, the burden necessarily covers all who are able to do it. End.

If you say: Who is to carry it out? The answer is: every Muslim who is able to do it, and who does not think it likely that if he denounces it he will suffer great harm, or that his prohibition will have no effect, because that would be futile. Nevertheless, it is recommended for displaying the emblem of Islam and reminding people of the matter of religion. If you say: Who is to be commanded and forbidden? I say: every person obligated (*mukallaf*) and not obligated, if he intends to harm someone else he is prevented, such as children and the insane. Children are forbidden from prohibited things so they do not become accustomed to them, just as they are made to pray so they become trained in it. This was mentioned by al-Zamakhshari.

(p-922) The detailed discussion of this matter is in (*al-Ihya*) of al-Ghazali, may his secret be sanctified. At the beginning of that discussion he said, may his secret be sanctified, the following text: Enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong is the greatest pole in religion, and it is the important matter for which God sent all the prophets. If its carpet were folded up and its work neglected, prophethood would be rendered inoperative, religion would be obliterated, slackness would prevail, error would spread, ignorance would be widespread, corruption would become rampant, the breach would widen, lands would be ruined, and servants would perish, even if they did not perceive the destruction until the Day of Calling Out. What we feared would happen has happened: to God we belong and to Him we return. For the work and knowledge of this pole have been effaced, its reality and form have been entirely wiped out, the flattery of creatures has taken hold of hearts, awareness of the Creator has been erased from them, and people have indulged in following desires and passions as cattle do. A sincere believer who is not deterred by the blame of any blamer in God's cause has become rare on the face of the earth. So whoever strives to remedy this slackness and close this gap, either by taking on its work or by undertaking its execution, renewing this effaced practice and rising to bear its burdens and exerting himself to revive it, he will be singled out among creation for reviving a practice which time has led to its extinction, and he will have exclusive possession of a devotion whose ranks of nearness are dwarfed beside its summit. End.

**Commentary on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:**

[105] ﴿And do not be like those who became divided and differed after the clear proofs had come to them. And those will have a great punishment.﴾

﴿And do not be like those who became divided and differed after the clear proofs had come to them. And those will have a great punishment.﴾ Exalted is He forbids His servants from being like the Jews in their splitting into sects and their deviation from the truth through following desire, obeying the self, and envy, to the point that each group among them affirmed some of the prophets and denied others, and called to what it had innovated in its religion. Thus they came to enmity and division after the manifest signs had come to them, which clarify the truth and necessitate agreement upon one word, which is the word of truth. The prohibition is therefore directed primarily at those who take up the call to the religion, and secondarily at their followers. In His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And those will have a great punishment﴾, there is emphasis and intensification in threatening those who divide, and severity in warning those who resemble them, which is not hidden.

**Notes (tanbihat):**

**The first:** Fakhr al-Din al-Razi mentioned, among the aspects of His saying ﴿differed﴾, that is, that each one of them claimed that he was upon the truth and that his companion was upon falsehood. Then he said: "I say that if you are fair, you will know that most of the scholars of this age have come to be described by this attribute. So we ask Allah for pardon and mercy." End of his words. His saying "this age" indicates that this condition did not exist among the scholars of the early generations (al-salaf). They continued to differ in the subsidiary matters (furu') and in legal rulings according to what proof had become clear to them and what their ijtihad (independent reasoning) led them to. None of them misguided another, and none claimed that he was upon the correct position that admits no error while his opponent was upon an error that admits no correctness. This only arose from the rigidity of the later imitators (muqallidun), their partisanship, and their belief in the infallibility of their school. "Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return." The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spread across the lands, and each people had knowledge that differed from what the others had, yet they remained united and supportive of one another.

**The second:** al-Qashani said: By "the signs" he means the rational and legal proofs that necessitate unity of direction and agreement of word. For people have different natures, instincts, desires, scattered inclinations, and varied customs and conduct, derived from their temperaments and their passions. From this arise divergent understandings and hostile characters. If they have no model to follow and no leader, whose beliefs, secrets and opinions they unite upon by following him, and whose words, customs and desires they harmonize upon by loving and obeying him, they remain neglected and scattered, prey for Satan, like a flock's stray sheep that becomes the wolf's. For this reason, the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: "People must have an imam, righteous or wicked." The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) never sent two men or more on any matter without appointing one of them over the other and ordering the other to obey and follow him, so that the affair would be unified and organized. Otherwise, chaos and confusion would occur, the affairs of religion and worldly life would be disturbed, and the order of livelihood and the Hereafter would be disrupted. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever separates from the community by a span has not smelled the fragrance of Paradise." And he said: "Allah is with the community." Do you not see that human society, when it is not governed by the leadership of the heart and obedience of the intellect, how its order is disrupted and it leads to corruption and division, which necessitates the loss of this world and the Hereafter? When His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And this is My straight path, so follow it, and do not follow other ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾ [al-An'am: 153] was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) drew a line and said: "This is the path of guidance." Then he drew lines to its right and left and said: "These are paths; upon each path is a devil calling to it."

**The third:** Shaykh al-Islam Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyya, may his secret be sanctified, said at the beginning of his book (Raf' al-Malam 'an al-A'immah al-A'lam): Let it be known that there is none of the generally accepted imams among the Ummah who believes in opposing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in any part of his Sunnah, subtle or major, for they are in certain agreement upon the obligation to follow the Messenger, and that every person's words are taken and left except those of the Messenger (ﷺ). But if one of them has a statement, while a sound hadith has come contrary to it, he must have an excuse for leaving it. The excuses in sum are three kinds:

One of them: that he did not believe the Prophet (ﷺ) said it.

The second: that he did not believe he intended that matter by that statement.

The third: that he believed that ruling was abrogated (mansukh).

These three kinds branch into multiple causes. Then he expanded the discussion on that.

He also mentioned, may his secret be sanctified, in some of his fatawa (legal opinions), that the early generations (al-salaf), the four imams, and the majority say: the proofs are, in reality, some stronger than others. A person must strive and seek the stronger. When he sees a proof stronger than another, and sees nothing opposing it, he acts upon it, and Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. If what is in reality more correct is something else, he is mistaken yet excused, and he has a reward for his ijtihad and his action according to what has become clear to him as preponderant, and his error is forgiven. That reality is the ruling, but on condition of the ability to know it. Whoever is unable to know it will not be held accountable for leaving it. If by error is meant sin, then the mujtahid is not in error; rather every mujtahid is correct, obedient to Allah, doing what Allah commanded him. If what is meant is the lack of knowledge of the truth in reality, then the one who is correct is one, and he has two rewards. This is like the mujtahids regarding the direction of the Ka'bah, when they pray facing four directions: the one who hits the Ka'bah is one, and he has two rewards, because his ijtihad and his action were more complete than others'. The strong believer is more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, and whoever Allah increases in knowledge and action, Allah increases him in reward by what He added of knowledge and action. He, Exalted, said: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people. We raise by degrees whom We will. Indeed your Lord is Wise and Knowing﴾ [al-An'am: 83]. Malik said, narrating from Zayd ibn Aslam: "by knowledge." Likewise He said about the story of Joseph: ﴿He could not have taken his brother within the king's religion except that Allah willed. We raise by degrees whom We will, and over every possessor of knowledge is one more knowing﴾ [Yusuf: 76]. It has thus become clear that all mujtahids spoke with knowledge and followed knowledge, that jurisprudence (fiqh) is among the noblest sciences, and that they are not among those who follow only conjecture. But some of them may have knowledge that the other does not have, either by having heard what the other did not hear, or by understanding what the other did not understand, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field when the sheep of the people grazed in it, and We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ [al-Anbiya': 78]. ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Solomon, and to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾ [al-Anbiya': 79]. This is the condition of the people of ijtihad, reflection and deduction, in the fundamentals (usul) and in the subsidiary matters (furu').

Then he said: When a person reflects upon the disputes of people, he finds that each group has knowledge that the other does not have, as in matters of rulings. Yet none has fully comprehended the truth except one who follows the Muhajirun and the Ansar and believes in all that the Messenger brought as it was intended. These are the people of mercy who do not differ. End of his words.

Thus it is known that the differences among the Companions, the Successors (tabi'un) and the mujtahids in the subsidiary matters are not what this verse encompasses, for what is meant by it is differing from the truth after its clarity, by rejecting it. How far apart the two kinds of difference are! Then the seeker of truth must use his reasoning regarding these differences of opinion, so that whatever he finds to be the strongest in proof he adopts, and otherwise he leaves it. In that case he is among those about whom Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿So give good tidings to My servants﴾ [al-Zumar: 17] ﴿who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾ [al-Zumar: 18]. And if something about which there is disagreement becomes unclear to him, let him supplicate with what Muslim narrated in his Sahih from A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say when he stood to pray at night: "O Allah, Lord of Jibril, Mika'il and Israfil, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You judge between Your servants concerning that in which they differ. Guide me, by Your permission, to the truth in what they have differed about, for You guide whom You will to a straight path." For Allah, Exalted, said in what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) narrated from Him: "O My servants, all of you are astray except whom I have guided, so seek guidance from Me and I will guide you." End of his words.

**The fourth:** Some of the exegetes mentioned here what is narrated in the hadith: "The difference of my Ummah is a mercy," but no sound chain of narration is known for it. Al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in (al-Madkhal) narrated it with a weak chain from Ibn Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Some of the verifiers said: It contradicts the texts of the verses and hadiths, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they will continue to differ﴾ [Hud: 118] ﴿except those upon whom your Lord has mercy﴾ [Hud: 119]. Similar to it is His saying (ﷺ): "Do not differ, lest your hearts differ," and other numerous hadiths. What is decisively established is that agreement is better than disagreement. End of his words.

Imam Ahmad and Abu Dawud narrated with their chains from Abu Amir Abd Allah ibn Yahya, who said: "We performed Hajj with Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan. When we arrived at Makkah, he stood after praying the Zuhr prayer and said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The People of the Two Scriptures split into seventy-two sects in their religion, and this Ummah will split into seventy-three sects,' meaning the desires (al-ahwa'), 'all of them in the Fire except one, and that is the community (al-jama'ah). Among my Ummah will come out peoples into whom those desires will seep, as rabies seeps into its victim, not leaving a vein or joint without entering it. By Allah, O assembly of Arabs, if you do not uphold what your Prophet (ﷺ) brought, then others among the people are more worthy of not upholding it.'" Ibn Kathir said: This hadith has been narrated through multiple routes. End of his words.

**A summary on the beginning of the difference in this Ummah among the people of desires:**

Imam Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, mentioned in the book (al-Furqan bayn al-Haqq wal-Batil) that the Muslims, during the caliphate of Abu Bakr and Umar, and the early part of the caliphate of Uthman in the first year of his rule, were in agreement with no dispute among them. Then at the end of Uthman's caliphate, matters occurred that necessitated a kind of division, and a group of people of sedition and oppression arose and killed Uthman, and the Muslims became divided after the killing of Uthman. When the Muslims fought at Siffin and agreed to appoint two arbitrators, the Kharijites came out against the Commander of the Faithful Ali ibn Abi Talib, separated from him and separated from the community of the Muslims. In his time the Shi'ah also arose, but they were concealed in their belief, not showing it to Ali and his followers, and they were three groups:

The first group: said that he is God. When this became known to him, he burned them with fire.

The second: the reviling ones (al-sabbah), for he had heard that Abu al-Sawda was reviling Abu Bakr and Umar, so he sought him. It was said that he sought him in order to kill him, so he fled from him.

The third: the preferentialists (al-mufaddilah), who preferred him over the two shaykhs, and it has been widely transmitted from him that he said: "The best of this Ummah after its Prophet is Abu Bakr and Umar." Al-Bukhari narrated that in his Sahih.

Then, at the end of the era of the Companions, the Qadariyya (those who deny divine decree) arose, and then the Murji'a (the Murji'ah, those who postpone judgment on the matter of faith) arose. Then he said: People, in ordering the heretics (ahl al-ahwa', "people of desires"), have divided into categories. Some order them according to the time of their emergence, so they begin with the Khawarij. Others order them according to the lightness or severity of their matter, so they begin with the Murji'a and end with the Jahmiyya, as many of the companions of Ahmad (may Allah be pleased with him) did, such as his son 'Abd Allah and others like him, al-Khallal, Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Batta and their likes, and Abu al-Faraj al-Maqdisi. Both groups end with the Jahmiyya, because they are the most severe of innovations. Likewise al-Bukhari in his Sahih: he began with the Book of Faith and the refutation of the Murji'a, and concluded with the Book of Tawhid and the refutation of the zanadiqa (heretics who conceal disbelief) and the Jahmiyya.

Then he said, may his secret be sanctified: The early generations held fast to the Qur'an and faith. When there occurred in the Ummah what occurred of division and disagreement, the people of division and disagreement became sects (shi'a), and their reliance inwardly was not upon the Qur'an and faith, but upon principles their shaykhs had innovated, upon which they depend concerning tawhid, the attributes, qadar, belief in the Messenger, and other matters. Then whatever they thought agreed with these principles from the Qur'an, they argued with it, and whatever contradicted them, they interpreted away. Therefore, when you find them arguing with the Qur'an and the Hadith, they do not take care to determine the precise meaning of their indications, nor do they examine all that the Qur'an contains of that meaning, since their actual reliance was upon something other than that. The verses that oppose them, they set about interpreting in the manner of one who intends to reject them however he can. His aim is not to understand the intent of the Messenger, but to repel his opponent from arguing with them. Then he said, may his secret be sanctified: It is incumbent upon every believer not to speak about anything of the religion except by following what the Messenger brought, and not to go ahead of him, but (p-931) to look at what he said, so that his speech follows his speech and his knowledge follows his command, just as the Companions and those who followed their path among the Successors (tabi'un) who follow them in goodness, and the Imams of the Muslims did. Therefore none of them opposed the texts with his reason, nor whispered a religion other than what the Messenger brought. When one wants to know something of the religion and to speak about it, he looks at what Allah and His Messenger said; from it he learns, with it he speaks, in it he reflects and contemplates, and by it he derives evidence. This is the principle of the People of the Sunnah.

He, may his secret be sanctified, said in his epistle to the community of Shaykh 'Adi ibn Musafir, the following text: This division that occurred within the Ummah, among its scholars, shaykhs, rulers and leaders, is what made the enemies dominate over it, by their abandoning the practice of obedience to Allah and His Messenger, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And from those who say, "We are Christians," We took their covenant, but they forgot a portion of what they were reminded of, so We caused among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection. And Allah will inform them of what they used to do﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 14]. Whenever people abandon some of what Allah has commanded them, enmity and hatred arise among them; when a people separate, they become corrupt and perish, and when they unite, they become righteous and rule. Indeed, unity is mercy, and division is punishment. The sum of this lies in enjoining what is good and forbidding what is evil, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah as He should be feared, and do not die except as Muslims﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 102] ﴿And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 103], up to His saying: ﴿And let there be [arising] from you a nation inviting to good, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong. And those are the successful﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 104]. Among enjoining what is good is enjoining harmony, unity and togetherness, and forbidding disagreement and division; and among forbidding what is evil is establishing the prescribed punishments upon those who have left the law of Allah the Exalted. Then he said: It is obligatory upon those in authority, namely the scholars of every group, their rulers and their shaykhs, that they correct their common people, command them to good and forbid them from evil, so they command them with what Allah and His Messenger commanded, and forbid them from what Allah and His Messenger ﷺ forbade. And the saying of Allah the Exalted:
(p-932)

**The explanation of His saying, may He be exalted:**

[106] ﴿On the Day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black. As for those whose faces turn black: "Did you disbelieve after your belief? So taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."﴾

﴿On the Day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black﴾ means: many faces will turn white, and these are the faces of the believers, because they followed the true religion, which is the shining light. Many faces will turn black, and these are the faces of the disbelievers among the People of the Book and the polytheists, because they followed dark misguidance. This is so that by it their faith and their disbelief may be inferred, and each will be recompensed according to the requirement of his state. This verse has parallels, among them His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied against God, their faces blackened. Is there not in Hell an abode for the arrogant?﴾ [Az-Zumar: 60]. Among them is His saying: ﴿And neither humiliation nor darkness will cover their faces﴾ [Yunus: 26]. Among them is His saying: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾ [Abasa: 38], ﴿laughing and joyful﴾ [Abasa: 39], ﴿and faces that Day will have dust upon them﴾ [Abasa: 40], ﴿darkness will cover them﴾ [Abasa: 41]. Among them is His saying: ﴿Faces that Day will be bright﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 22], ﴿looking at their Lord﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 23], ﴿and faces that Day will be frowning﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 24], ﴿expecting that a calamity of the backbreaking kind will be done to them﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 25]. Among them is: ﴿You will recognise in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin: 24], and other than these. The exegetes have two views regarding this whiteness, radiance, dust and darkness:

The first: whiteness is a figurative usage (majaz, figurative sense) for joy and happiness, and blackness for grief. This is a common figurative usage. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿When one of them is given news of a female child, his face darkens, and he is filled with suppressed grief﴾ [An-Nahl: 58]. It is said: "So-and-so has a white hand with me," meaning: a clear and pleasing favour.

The Arabs say of one who attains his aim and succeeds in his objective: "His face has turned white," meaning delight and brightness. When congratulating someone on happiness, they say: "Praise be to God who has whitened your face." It is said of one who has suffered something disagreeable: "His face has darkened and his colour has changed, and his appearance has been transformed." Accordingly, the meaning of the verse is: the believer will be returned on the Day of Resurrection to what his hands have sent forward. If he has good deeds, his face will turn white, meaning he will be delighted with the blessings and grace of God. In the opposite case, when the disbeliever sees his ugly deeds counted, his face will turn black, meaning intense grief and sorrow. This is the view of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani.

The second view: this whiteness and blackness occur in the faces of both the believers and the disbelievers, because the expression is literal (haqiqa, literal sense) in both, and there is no evidence requiring the abandonment of the literal sense, so it is necessary to resort to it. Abu Muslim may reply: the evidence indicates what we have said, because He, may He be exalted, said:

﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾ [Abasa: 38], ﴿laughing and joyful﴾ [Abasa: 39], ﴿and faces that Day will have dust upon them﴾ [Abasa: 40], ﴿darkness will cover them﴾ [Abasa: 41]. He placed dust and darkness in opposition to laughter and joy. So if dust and darkness did not mean the figurative sense we have mentioned, it would not be correct to set them in opposition to it. Thus we know that what is meant by this dust, darkness, grief and sorrow is what makes this opposition correct. This is what al-Razi stated.

**A subtle point (latifa):**

(يَوْمَ) [yawma, "the Day"] is in the accusative case, either as the object of an implied verb addressed to the believers, warning them of the consequence of division after the clear proofs have come, and encouraging them to agree on holding fast to the religion. That is: "Remember the Day when..." etc. Or it is an adverbial complement of time (zarf) for the verb of stability in (لَهم, "for them"), or for (عَظِيمٌ, "great"), or for (عَذابٌ, "a punishment").

﴿As for those whose faces turn black: "Did you disbelieve after your belief? So taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."﴾ This is a detailed account of the states of the two groups after an overall indication of them. The mention of these first is because the context is one of warning against resembling them, together with what it contains of combining the general and the detailed, and leading to ending the discourse with the good state of the believers, as it began with that in the general statement. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿(Did you disbelieve (p-934) after your belief)﴾ is according to the implied "saying" (qawl), meaning: it will be said to them. The interrogative particle (الهمزة, "alif of interrogation") is for reproach and for expressing wonder at their state, as Abu al-Su'ud stated. The meaning is: did you disbelieve after there became clear to you what requires belief, which is the proofs God established for monotheism and prophethood, and what your own conscience confides to you of the truthfulness and validity of this claim and its testimony to its soundness? As He, may He be exalted, said before this verse: ﴿O People of the Book, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God while you are witnesses?﴾ [Al-i-Imran: 70]. He blamed them for disbelief after the signs had become clear. He also said to the believers: ﴿And do not be like those who divided and differed after the clear proofs had come to them; for those there is a great punishment﴾ [Al-i-Imran: 105].

So His saying here, may He be exalted: ﴿Did you disbelieve after your belief?﴾ is to be understood in accordance with what has been mentioned, so that this verse confirms what precedes it, and it is general with regard to all disbelievers.

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[107] ﴿As for those whose faces turn white, they will be in the mercy of Allah, therein they will abide forever.﴾

﴿As for those whose faces turn white, they will be in the mercy of Allah, therein they will abide forever.﴾ What is meant by "the mercy of Allah" is the Garden (al-Jannah). It is expressed by the word "mercy" as a reminder that the believer, even if he spends his entire life in obedience to Allah, Exalted is He, does not enter the Garden except by His mercy, Exalted is He.

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[108] ﴿These are the verses of God, which We recite to you in truth. And God does not desire injustice for the worlds.﴾

﴿These are the verses of God, which We recite to you in truth﴾ The demonstrative refers to what preceded of promise and warning. ﴿And God does not desire injustice for the worlds﴾ That is: He does not will to wrong His servants, by seizing anyone without a crime, or by increasing the punishment of a criminal, or by diminishing the reward of a good-doer. Al-Razi said: The mention of injustice here is fitting because the severe punishment was mentioned previously, and He, glorified and exalted is He, is the most generous of the generous. So it is as if He, exalted is He, is making an excuse for that, and said: They only fell into it because of their own reprehensible deeds. All of this indicates that the side of mercy is predominant. Abu al-Su'ud said: In the construction of the sentence there is a kind of allusion, by way of implication, that the disbelievers are the wrongdoers, who wronged themselves by exposing themselves to everlasting punishment, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, God does not wrong people at all, but people wrong themselves﴾ [Yunus: 44].

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 109:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[109] ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And to Allah are returned all matters.﴾

﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth⁠﴾ meaning: to Him alone, exalted is He, without any partner among what is in them of created beings, in ownership and creation, in giving life and causing death, and in rewarding and punishing. ﴿And to Allah⁠﴾ meaning: to His judgment and decree, ﴿are returned all matters⁠﴾ meaning: their affairs, so that He recompenses each of them according to what He has promised and threatened. There is thus no motive for Him to do wrong, because He is free of need of everything and able over everything.

The discussion of the interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying, the Exalted:

[110] ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind: you enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and believe in Allah. Had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them. Some of them are believers, but most of them are defiant transgressors.﴾

﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ is a new sentence (kalam mustaʾnaf), brought to strengthen the believers in what they are upon: their agreement on the truth and their calling to good. The word ﴿kuntum﴾ may be from *kāna* in its complete sense (al-tāmma), meaning "you were created and brought into being as the best nation," or from *kāna* in its incomplete sense (al-nāqiṣa), meaning "you were in the knowledge of Allah the best nation," or "you were mentioned among the nations that came before you as the best nation." The phrase ﴿brought forth for mankind﴾ is a qualifier of ﴿nation﴾, and the lam is connected to ﴿brought forth﴾, meaning: it was made manifest to them, until it was distinguished, recognised, and separated from others. Then he (Allah) explained the aspect of its excellence by what its totality did not come together for others, in His saying: ﴿you enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and believe in Allah﴾. By these attributes they were preferred over others, of whom He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They used not to forbid one another from wrongs they committed; evil indeed was what they used to do﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 79], and ﴿They say: "We believe in some and disbelieve in others"﴾ [al-Nisa: 150].

Abu al-Su'ud said: ﴿and believe in Allah﴾ means faith connected to everything that must be believed in: messenger, book, reckoning, and recompense. It was not stated in detail because it is evident that this is what the believers believe in, and to indicate that this is truly belief in Allah, the Exalted, and that whatever is devoid of any of that, such as the faith of the People of the Book, is not part of belief in Him at all. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They say: "We believe in some and disbelieve in others," and they wish to adopt a way between that. Those are the disbelievers in truth﴾ [al-Nisa: 150–151]. Belief in Allah was placed after enjoining right and forbidding wrong, although it precedes them both in existence and rank, because the indication of these two on their being the best for mankind is clearer than the indication of belief on it, and so that what follows may be joined to it. End of quotation.

Ibn Jarir narrated that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, saw among the people a lack of restraint, so he recited this verse, ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾, then said: "Whoever is pleased to be of this nation, let him fulfil the condition of Allah concerning it." A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqara: 143], meaning: best, ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾ [al-Baqara: 143], meaning: by enjoining right and forbidding wrong.

Numerous reports have been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the meaning of the verse, among them what Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim narrated from Muʿawiya ibn Haydah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed you complete seventy nations, you are the best of them and the most honoured of them before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." Ibn Kathir said: This is a well-known hadith; al-Tirmidhi graded it as hasan, and it is narrated from the hadith of Muʿadh ibn Jabal, Abu Saʿid and others. This nation attained the prize in good deeds through its Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), for he is the most noble of Allah's creation and the most honoured of the messengers before Allah. Allah sent him with a complete, great law which no prophet before him was given, nor any messenger of the messengers. So acting upon his way and path, a little of it takes the place that the great deeds of others cannot fill. The scholar Hafiz Ibn Kathir mentioned here the hadith of the seventy thousand who enter Paradise without reckoning, and he cited its chains and its compilers, and did well, may Allah, the Exalted, have mercy on him.

﴿And had the People of the Book believed﴾, that is, in what was sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿it would have been better for them﴾, that is, than what they are upon, as an indication of the foolishness of their minds in clinging to what prevented them from belief: the small, transient reward and the paltry leadership, and their abandoning of lasting wealth and dazzling honour. Since this might suggest that none of them believed, he added, as a new sentence: ﴿Some of them are believers﴾, that is, in Allah and in what was sent down to you and what was sent down to them, ﴿but most of them are defiant transgressors﴾. Since opposition by the majority is crushing, He, glory be to Him, consoled His allies by His saying:

The commentary on His saying, Exalted is He:

[111] ﴿They will not harm you, except for some annoyance. And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you; then they will not be helped.﴾

﴿They will not harm you, except for some annoyance﴾ — that is, with their tongues, in which there is nothing to fear of stabbing [criticism] and threats. ﴿And if they fight you﴾ (p-938) — that is, at some time among the times — ﴿they will turn their backs to you﴾, meaning defeated and forsaken. ﴿Then they will not be helped﴾, meaning there will be no victory for them over you; rather, you will be helped over them. God has spoken truly, and who is more truthful in speech than God? They have never fought in any situation without being like this. Ibn Kathir said: On the day of Khaybar, God humiliated them and abased their noses. Likewise those before them among the Jews of Madinah: Banu Qaynuqa', Banu al-Nadir, and Banu Qurayzah — God humiliated them all. Likewise the Christians in al-Sham: the Companions broke them on more than one occasion and stripped them of the dominion of al-Sham forever and ever, for the longest age of ages. The community of Islam will remain standing in al-Sham until ʿIsa ibn Maryam (ʿAlayhi al-Salam) descends, while they are in that state, and he will rule by the religion of Islam and the law of Muhammad (ﷺ), upon whom be the best of prayers and peace. He will break the cross, kill the swine, and abolish the jizyah, accepting nothing but Islam.

Subtleties (lata'if):

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why was the coordinated verb in His saying, ﴿then they will not be helped﴾, not put in the jussive?

I say: He turned it from the rule of the conditional response to the rule of a fresh statement, as if it were said: "Then I inform you that they will not be helped."

If you ask: What is the difference in meaning between its being in the nominative and its being in the jussive?

I say: Had it been jussive, the negation of help would have been restricted to their fighting, like the turning of backs; but when it was in the nominative, the negation of help became an unrestricted promise, as if He said: "Then their affair and their story, which I inform you of and give you good news of after the turning, is that they are forsaken, with help and strength negated from them; they will not rise after it with any wing, and no matter will be set right for them." And it happened as He informed: concerning the state of Banu Qurayzah, al-Nadir, Banu Qaynuqa', and the Jews of Khaybar.

If you ask: What is it that this report is coordinated with?

I say: The clause of condition and response. As if it were said: "I inform you that if they fight you, they will be routed; then I inform you that they will not be helped."

If you ask: What is the meaning of the delay in "thumma" (then)?

(p-939) I say: The delay is in rank, because the report of imposing abandonment upon them is greater than the report of their turning their backs.

Al-Nasir ibn al-Munir said: This is an ascent in the promise from the lesser to the greater, because they were promised that their enemy would turn them to flight upon encounter; then the promise ascended to what is more complete in success, namely that these people will not be helped at all. This ascent is increased by the entry of "thumma" rather than "wa", for it is here borrowed for delay in rank, not in existence, as if he said: "Then here is what is higher in favor and more generous in degrees of kindness: that these are a people who will not be helped whatsoever." And God knows best.

The Explanation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[112] ﴿They have been struck with humiliation wherever they are found, except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people. They have incurred wrath from Allah, and they have been struck with destitution. That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right. That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress.﴾

﴿They have been struck with humiliation wherever they are found, except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people﴾ That is: humiliation and abasement have encompassed them, just as a pitched tent encompasses its occupants, wherever they are found. His words ﴿except under a covenant from Allah﴾ are in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), with the implied sense: except while holding fast to, or clinging to, or bound by a covenant from Allah. This is an exception from the most general of general states, and the meaning is: humiliation has been struck upon them in all circumstances, except in the state of their holding fast to the covenant of Allah and the covenant of the people, that is, the protection (dhimma) of Allah and the protection of the Muslims. In other words, they have no honor at all except this one: their seeking refuge in the protection (dhimma) in exchange for the jizya that they accepted. Thus stated in (al-Kashshaf). ﴿They have incurred wrath from Allah﴾ That is: they have deserved it. ﴿And they have been struck with destitution﴾ That is: poverty, so that with these attributes they would be the most thoroughly marked by abasement. ﴿That﴾ That is: the destitution, the humiliation and the wrath were struck upon them. ﴿That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾ That is: out of arrogance and rebellion. ﴿And kill the prophets﴾ (p-940) That is: those who came to them from Allah in truth.
