And since they were protected in religion and in worldly life, He said ﴿without right﴾, that is, without anything that would permit killing. ﴿That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾ That is: the striking of humiliation and destitution in this world, and the incurring of wrath in the Hereafter, as is explained by their disbelief and their killing of the prophets; it is therefore a consequence of their disobedience and their transgression of the limits of Allah, exalted is He. It has also been said: "That" refers to the cause of the cause, namely disbelief and killing; that is, these arose from them because of their disobedience and transgression, for proceeding into sins and treating the crossing of limits lightly makes disbelief easy. Al-Isfahani said: The people of the science of conduct (muʿāmalāt) have said: whoever is afflicted with abandoning the etiquette (ādāb) falls into abandoning the sunan, whoever is afflicted with abandoning the sunan falls into abandoning the obligations (farāʾiḍ), whoever is afflicted with abandoning the obligations falls into belittling the Sharia, and whoever is afflicted with that falls into disbelief.

Burhan al-Din al-Biqa'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The verse is evidence for holding a son who approves of his father's sin accountable for it, however far back the father goes. This accords with what I have seen in the translation of the Torah that is in their hands, for in the second book it says: "And God spoke all these words, saying: I am the LORD your God who brought you up out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. You shall have no other gods before Me. You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth. You shall not bow down to them or serve them; for I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the third and the fourth generation of those who hate Me, and showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love Me and keep My commandments." — End.

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[113] ﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Scripture is an upright community who recite the verses of God during the night hours while they prostrate.﴾

﴿They are not all alike﴾ is a resumptive sentence, brought as a preface to praise those among the People of the Scripture who turned to the truth and cast off falsehood, not heeding predecessor or successor; and as a reminder of His saying: ﴿Among them are believers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110]. That is: the People of the Scripture are not equal, nor do they share in the same evils. Then He resumed His speech as an explanation of their non-equality: (p-941) ﴿Among the People of the Scripture is an upright community who recite the verses of God during the night hours while they prostrate.﴾

Regarding His saying ﴿upright (qa'imah)﴾ there are several interpretations:

The first: that they are standing in prayer, and He expressed their nightly worship by reciting the Qur'an during the hours of the night, as in His saying: ﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing﴾ [al-Furqan: 64], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand in prayer almost two-thirds of the night﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], and His saying: ﴿Stand [in prayer] the night﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 2], and His saying: ﴿And stand before God in devout obedience﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238].

The second: that they are steadfast in holding to the true religion, constant in it, not wavering in adhering to it, as in His saying: ﴿except as long as you remain standing over him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75], meaning: persistent in demanding, steadfast in insistence. And from this (p-942) is His saying: ﴿standing firmly in justice﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18].

The third: that they are upright and just, from your saying: "I straightened the stick and it stood," meaning "it became straight." Al-anaa' (the hours) is the plural of (ina') like (mi'an) and (am'a'), and (inan) like (nihan) and (anha'). His saying: ﴿while they prostrate﴾ is an independent resumptive sentence, not a circumstantial clause (hal) of the subject of ﴿recite﴾, because of what is authentically established in the Sunnah prohibiting recitation during prostration. This is in what Imam Ahmad and Muslim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both), who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, I have been forbidden to recite the Qur'an while bowing or prostrating. As for bowing, magnify the Lord in it; and as for prostration, strive in supplication, for it is fitting that you be answered."

The meaning of the verse, then, is that they stand at times and prostrate at other times, seeking bounty and mercy, as in His saying: ﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing﴾ [al-Furqan: 64], and His saying: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord?﴾ [al-Zumar: 9]. It is also possible that the meaning is: "while they pray," since prayer is called sujud (prostration) and sajdah (a prostration), just as it is called ruku' (bowing) and rak'ah (a unit of prayer), and tasbih (glorification) and tasbihah. Accordingly, the sentence admits of both interpretations, and the repetition of the predication serves to strengthen and emphasize the ruling.

Then He, exalted is He, described them with other attributes, clarifying their distinction from the Jews in another respect, by His saying:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, the Exalted:

[114] ﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and hasten to good deeds. And those are among the righteous.﴾

﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ means: in the manner that the Sharia has articulated. It is evident that belief in Allah necessarily entails belief in all His prophets and messengers. And belief in the Last Day necessarily entails caution against (p-943) disobedience. These Jews deny the prophets of Allah and do not guard themselves against the disobedience of Allah, so they have not attained belief in the Origin and the Return. ﴿And enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ is an allusion to the Jews' laxity in enjoining good (al-ihtisab), and even more, to their inverting the matter by misleading people and barring them from the path of Allah, for that is enjoining what is wrong and forbidding what is right. His words, the Exalted, ﴿and hasten to good deeds﴾ are another attribute comprising the various kinds of virtues related to the self and to others. Hastening to good (al-musara'a fi'l-khayr) is an excessive eagerness for it. In it there is an allusion to the Jews' sluggishness in these matters, and even more, to their hastening towards evils. ﴿And those﴾ means: those described with these virtuous attributes. ﴿Are among the righteous﴾ means: among the number of those whose conditions have become sound before Allah, the Exalted, and who deserve His good pleasure. The description with righteousness (al-salah) indicates the most perfect ranks, so it is the utmost praise, and for this reason the prophets were described with it in the Revelation.

The discussion of God's words:

[115] ﴿And whatever good they do, they will not be denied it; and God is Knowing of the God-fearing.﴾

﴿And whatever good they do, they will not be denied it﴾ means: they will not be deprived of its reward. The use of the passive form (lan yukfarūhu, "they will not be denied it") follows the customary way of Divine Majesty (kibriyā'). The two verbs have also been read in the second person (takfurūhu, taf'alū... "you"), as a form of address. ﴿And God is Knowing of the God-fearing﴾, so He will repay them their rewards. These described ones are those mentioned at the end of the surah: ﴿And among the People of the Book are those who believe in God and what has been revealed to you and what has been revealed to them, humbling themselves before God﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 199], and so on.

Note (tanbīh):

Al-Biqāʿī said: The context indicates that the implied meaning is: "and most of them are not characterized by these attributes." Al-Rāzī said: When He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Among the People of the Book is a upright community﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 113], the complete statement would have been: "and among them is a blameworthy community" (ummah madhmūmah). However, He omitted mention of the blameworthy community according to the practice of the Arabs, whereby mention of one of two opposites suffices without mentioning the other opposite. The verification of this is: the two opposites are known together, so mention of one of them is sufficient to convey knowledge of both, and therefore it is fitting to omit the other opposite. Abū Dhuʾayb said:

*Her heart called me to her, and I obey its command, / yet I do not know whether its pursuit is rectitude or error.*

He meant: "or error," and so he suffices with mention of rectitude rather than error. This is the view of al-Farrā' and Ibn al-Anbārī. Al-Zajjāj said: There is no need to posit an implied "blameworthy community," because its mention has already preceded, and because we have noted that knowledge of both opposites is together, so mention of one suffices in place of the other, as one says: "Zayd and ʿAmr are not equal: Zayd is wise, pious, intelligent," which suffices so that it is not said: "and ʿAmr is not like that." Likewise here, since His saying "They are not equal" has preceded, that suffices in place of that implication. — End, summarized.

I say: There is no barrier to the verse that follows being the second part, opposite to the first, for the heading "those who disbelieved" corresponds by its meaning to what precedes it, as is not hidden. And God knows best.

The Interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[116] ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will never avail them anything against Allah. And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will never avail them﴾, i.e., will never repel [anything] from them. ﴿Anything against Allah﴾, i.e., from the punishment of Allah. Although giving charity from wealth extinguishes the anger of the Lord toward the believers, and He forgives them through the death of their children or their seeking forgiveness, ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾ When He, exalted is He, clarified that the wealth of the disbelievers does not avail them anything, and then they might have spent it on good causes, so it may come to mind that they benefit from it, He removed that doubt and gave as an example its vanishing as scattered dust, by His saying, glorified is He:

**On the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:**

[117] ﴿The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life is like the likeness of a wind containing frost, which strikes the crop of a people who have wronged themselves and destroys it. And Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾

﴿The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life﴾ of noble deeds, and in which they bear the burden of expenditure: ﴿is like the likeness of a wind containing frost﴾, i.e., a severe cold, like the *sarsar* (a violent, biting wind): ﴿which strikes the crop of a people who have wronged themselves﴾ through disbelief and sins, so they incurred anger from Allah: ﴿and destroys it﴾. Likewise, the wind of disbelief, when it strikes the crop of the spending of such a people, destroys it. Thus wrongdoing becomes a wind, because it arises from the desires of the soul, possessing extreme coldness, because it is the wrong of disbelief, which is spiritual death, so it destroys (the crop). This is what al-Mahayimi said.

﴿And Allah did not wrong them﴾ by destroying their crop through sending a wind from Him: ﴿but they wronged themselves﴾ by sending the wind of disbelieving wrongdoing upon their otherworldly crop.

**Subtleties (laṭā'if):**

If it is said: the purpose is to liken what they spent, in its loss, to the crop struck by the frost, yet what they spend has been made to be represented by the wind; so what is the correspondence with the purpose? I answer: this is of the *tashbih murakkab* (composite simile), in which the resemblance occurs between what is intended by the two clauses, even if no resemblance occurs between their individual parts. The intended meaning is the comparison of one state with another state. It is also permissible to intend: the likeness of the destruction of what they spend is like the likeness of the destruction by a wind; or: the likeness of what they spend is like the likeness of a wind that destroys, and thus the correspondence is achieved.

(p-946) Nasir al-Din said in *al-Intisaf*: "The closer view is that the original wording, and Allah knows best, was: *The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life is like the likeness of the crop of a people who wronged themselves, which was struck by a wind containing frost and destroyed it.* But this arrangement was altered in the mentioned simile for a noble benefit, namely the advancement of what is more important. For the wind, which is the likeness of punishment, its mention in the context of warning and threat is more important than the mention of the crop. So it was placed first, with attention to its mention, and relying on the fact that sound understandings will extract the correspondence by returning the speech to its origin in the easiest manner. Similar to this, in altering the arrangement for such a benefit, is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A man and two women from among those whom you accept as witnesses, so that if one of the two errs, the other may remind her﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and the rest of the verse. Likewise, [an example from ordinary speech]: 'I have prepared this piece of wood so that, if the wall leans, I may prop it up,' whereas the original would be: 'so that one of them may remind the other if she errs, and so that I may prop the wall with it if it leans.' Examples of this are numerous. And Allah is the Granter of success."

(p-947)

**The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:**

[118] ﴿O you who have believed, do not take as intimates (*bitana*, confidants) those other than your own; they will not spare you [any] ruin. They wish you would suffer. Hatred has already appeared from their mouths, and what their breasts conceal is greater. We have certainly made clear to you the signs, if you should use reason.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, do not take as intimates those other than your own﴾, i.e., companions who are privy to your affairs, from outside your own kind, who are the Muslims.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The *bitana* of a man and his *walija* (close confidant) are his special friend and chosen companion, to whom he discloses his secrets (*shuqur*) out of trust in him. The word is likened to the *bitana* of a garment, just as it is said: "So-and-so is my *shi'ar*" (the inner garment next to the skin). End of quotation. Among the proverbs of the Arabs, on the confiding of a man to his brother what keeps it hidden from others: "I disclosed to him my *shuqur*" (with a *damma* on the *shin*, and it may be pronounced with a *fatha*), meaning: I informed him of my matter and made him aware of what I keep secret from others. In *al-Qamus* and its commentary: the *bitana* is the companion in confidence who is consulted in matters, and the *walija* is the one who is specially admitted and made aware of the inner aspect of affairs. Al-Zajjaj said: the *bitana* are the intimate insiders to whom one opens up and whom one takes into confidence. It is said: "So-and-so is a *bitana* of so-and-so," meaning: an intimate, companionable insider to him.

As for those who are forbidden here, they are either the People of the Book, as narrated by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Ishaq from Ibn Abbas, that they are the Jews. This is because the context of the surah concerns them, and the preceding passage concerns them. There existed between the Ansar and their Jewish neighbours what is well known of former foster-relations and alliances. Or they are the hypocrites, on account of His saying after this: ﴿And when they meet you, they say, "We have believed"; but when they are alone, they bite their fingertips in rage against you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119], and so on. This is the attribute of the hypocrites, like His saying, Exalted is He, in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And when they meet those who have believed, they say, "We have believed"; but when they are alone with their devils, they say, "Indeed, we are with you"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14], and so on. Perhaps some believers may be deceived by the outward statements of the hypocrites (p-948) and think them truthful, so they disclose secrets to them. Or they are all categories of disbelievers, in keeping with the generality of His saying: ﴿from outside your own﴾, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1]. What confirms this is what Ibn Abi Hatim narrated: it was said to Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him: "There is here a boy from the people of al-Hirah, a Christian, who is a memoriser and a scribe; would you not take him as a scribe?" He said: "Then I would have taken an intimate from outside the believers."

Al-Razi said: Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, made this verse a proof for the prohibition of taking a Christian as an intimate.

The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: In this report, together with this verse, there is evidence that the protected people (*ahl al-dhimma*) may not be employed in writing in which there is an exercise of superiority over the Muslims, and a perusal of the inner workings of their affairs which it is feared they may disclose to the enemies from among the people of war.

Al-Suyuti said in *al-Iklil*: Al-Kiya al-Harrasi said: In the verse there is an indication that it is not permissible to seek the assistance of the protected people in any of the affairs of the Muslims. End of quotation.

The basis for this, as al-Qashani said, is that the *bitana* of a man is his chosen and special friend, whom he takes into his inner confidence and who is privy to his secrets. Such a friend cannot exist except when the two are united in purpose and agree in religion and attribute, loving one another for the sake of Allah and not for some worldly aim. As it is said of friends: "One soul in scattered bodies." So if he is from outside the people of faith, then it is more fitting that he be an enemy in secret (*kashih*). Then He explained their hypocrisy and the hatred they conceal (p-949) by His saying: ﴿they will not spare you [any] ruin﴾, i.e., they do not fall short of corrupting you.

Al-Qashani said: Because true, sincere love can exist only between the monotheists, since it is a shadow of unity. It cannot exist in anything else, since they are in a world of opposition. Rather, sometimes general human kinship draws them together, because they share in the species, in benefits and pleasures, and in their need for mutual cooperation in these. Worldly benefits and psychic pleasures are quick to pass away, so love based on them does not endure, unlike the first love, which rests on a matter that does not change at all.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is said: *alā fil-amr, ya'lū*, when one falls short in it. Then it is used transitively to two objects, as in their saying: *lā ālūka nuṣḥan* ("I will not withhold sincere counsel from you") and *lā ālūka jahdan* ("I will not withhold effort from you"), by way of *tadmīn* (implicit meaning). The meaning is: I do not withhold counsel from you and I do not diminish it for you. *Al-khabāl* is corruption. ﴿They wish you would suffer﴾, i.e., your suffering (*ʿanatakum*), with *mā* being a verbal-noun particle (*mā maṣdariyya*). *Al-ʿanat* is severity of harm and hardship, i.e., they wish for what would destroy you. ﴿Hatred has already appeared from their mouths﴾, i.e., the inner hatred has become manifest until it came out of their mouths, because they cannot control themselves, despite their restraint of themselves and their forcing of themselves against it, so that there escapes from their tongues what makes their hatred of the Muslims known. It has been said: the hidden thoughts of souls appear on the surfaces of faces and in slips of the tongue. ﴿And what their breasts conceal is greater﴾ than what has appeared, because its appearance is not from deliberation and choice but a slip. Such is the case of what is little: ﴿We have certainly made clear to you the signs﴾, which indicate the evil of your taking them as intimates, so that you would refrain from them, sincerely adhere to the religion, befriend the believers, and be hostile to the disbelievers. ﴿If you should use reason﴾, i.e., if you are people of intellect; or, if you understand what has been made clear to you, and act upon it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: what is the grammatical position of these clauses? I say: it is permissible that ﴿who do not spare you﴾ be a qualifier of *bitana*. Likewise ﴿hatred has already appeared﴾. As if it were said: an intimate who does not spare you ruin, whose hatred is evident. As for ﴿We have certainly made clear﴾, it is an independent sentence. And better and more eloquent than this is that all of them be resumptive clauses in the manner of giving the reason for the prohibition against taking them as intimates.

Then Allah, exalted is He, made clear their error in their allegiance, in that they extend it to those who harbour hatred, by His saying:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[119] ﴿Here you are, loving them, yet they do not love you, while you believe in the whole Scripture. When they meet you, they say, "We believe"; but when they are alone, they bite their fingertips at you in rage. Say: "Die in your rage. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is in the breasts."﴾

﴿Here you are, loving them, yet they do not love you﴾ meaning: you associate with them and disclose your secrets to them, while they do not do the same with you. As for His saying, ﴿while you believe in the whole Scripture﴾, the waw (wa) is for the circumstantial clause (hal), and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial element from the pronoun of the object in (they do not love you). The meaning is: they do not love you, while the circumstance is that you believe in their Scripture, so you do not deny any part of it. There is nothing in you that would necessitate their hatred of you. So why do you love them, when they disbelieve in your entire Scripture?

The waw is not taken as a conjunction (coordinating) with (they do not love you) or (you love them), as Abu Hayyan preferred, because that would be in the context of censure, and belief in the Scripture is not like that, for it is pure correctness. Even if it is excused by saying that the meaning is: they combine love for the disbelievers with belief, and these two do not come together, due to its remoteness, the circumstantial clause confirms the error, so consider this. Al-Khafaji related it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: In it is severe rebuke, that they are more steadfast in their falsehood than you are in your truth. A similar verse is: ﴿If you suffer, they suffer as you suffer, but you hope from Allah for what they do not hope for﴾ [al-Nisa': 104]. ﴿When they meet you, they say, "We believe"﴾, out of hypocrisy and deception. ﴿But when they are alone, they bite their fingertips at you in rage﴾ meaning: because of it, in regret and grief, since they find no way to satisfy their vengeance. Biting the fingertips is the habit of the remorseful and powerless, and of one who is enraged when his grief at the loss of his desired object is great. Since this action was frequent in the angry, it became a metonymy (kinaya) for (p-951) anger, so that it is said of an angry man that he bites his hand in rage, even if there is no actual biting. ﴿Say: "Die in your rage"﴾ is a supplication against them, that their rage increase until they perish from it. What is meant by the increase of rage is the increase of what enrages them of the strength of Islam and the honour of its people, and what they have of humiliation, disgrace and destruction in that. Thus in al-Kashshaf. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾, so He knows what is in their breasts of hatred and rancour. It may be that this is part of what is said (al-maqul), meaning: say to them, "Indeed, Allah knows what is more hidden than what you conceal of biting the fingertips in rage." It may also be outside of it, meaning: say that to them, do not be surprised at my being informed of your secrets, for I know what is more hidden than their inner thoughts. It was also said: this is a command to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to be content of soul, strong in hope, and joyful at the promise of Allah, the Exalted, that they will perish of rage through the honouring of Islam and their humiliation by it, without there being any actual speech. As if it was said: speak to yourself with this. Thus Abu al-Su'ud related it.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 120:

Then God, exalted is He, made clear the extent of their enmity through His saying:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[120] ﴿If good befalls you, it grieves them; and if evil befalls you, they rejoice at it. But if you are patient and mindful of God, their scheming will not harm you at all. Indeed, God encompasses what they do.﴾

﴿If good befalls you﴾ means your victory over the enemy, your gaining of spoils, the abundance of your livelihood, and the spread of people into your religion, �ា﴿it grieves them﴾. ﴿And if evil befalls you﴾ means an enemy striking some of you, or disunity among you, or drought or calamity, ﹅﴿they rejoice at it﴾ while not knowing the wisdom God has in that.

A subtle point (lata'if):

The original sense of "massa" (to touch) is with the hand, and then every thing that reaches a thing is called a "massa." The expression with it is used for the good, and with "isaba" (to strike) for the evil, for variety of style. He has made them equal elsewhere, as in His saying: ﴿If good befalls you [in]tt(p-952) it grieves them, and if a misfortune befalls you﴾ [al-Tawba: 50], and His saying: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾ [al-Nisa': 79], and He said: ﴿When evil touches him, he is distressed﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 20], ﴿and when good touches him, he withholds﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 21].

Nasir al-Din (Ibn al-Munayyir) said in al-Intisaf: It may be said that "massa" is less firmly established than "isaba," and it is as if it were its lowest degree. So the meaning of the speech, and God knows best, is: if a good thing strikes you even slightly, it grieves them, and they envy you for it. But if the striking takes firm hold of you and the matter reaches the point where the one who gloats would pity you, they do not pity you nor do they cease their envy, and not even in this state; rather they rejoice and are delighted. And God knows best.

This is among the secrets of the eloquence of the Revelation. The expression indicates their excess in both joy and sorrow. If the least of our good grieves them, then the greater is more so; and if they rejoice at the greatest of calamities, at what would move the gloater to pity, then their friendship is not hoped for at all. How then can you take them as intimates?

Al-Biqa'i said: Since this matter is vexing, enraging and painful, He remedied them by pointing to victory on condition of piety and patience, so He said: ﴿But if you are patient and mindful of God﴾, that is: be patient with what God tests you with of hardships, trials and calamities, remain firm in obedience, and reject seeking help from them in your affairs and seeking refuge in their protection. ﴿Their scheming will not harm you at all﴾, because the one who relies upon God, patient with His trial, seeking help from Him and not from another, is victorious in his aim, prevails over his opponent, and is protected by the good care of his Lord. And the one who seeks help from another is forsaken, left to himself, and deprived of the support of his Lord. Al-Qashani conveyed this.

(p-953) It was also said: The purpose of negating harm is not being concerned with it, because one who trains himself in mindfulness and patience becomes little affected and bold against the opponent. And "al-kayd" (scheming) is seeking to bring another into something disliked. ﴿Indeed, God encompasses what they do﴾. It is read with the yā' of the third person, meaning that He knows what they do of scheming in their hostility toward you, and so He will punish them for it. And with the tā' of address, meaning: what you do of patience and mindfulness, and so He will reward you with what you deserve.

An important note:

Al-Razi said: Applying the word "al-muhit" (the encompassing) to God is metaphorical, because "muhit bi'l-shay'" is one who surrounds a thing from all its sides, and that is among the attributes of bodies. But since He, exalted is He, knows all things and is able over all possibilities, it is permissible in the metaphorical usage of the language that He encompasses them. From this is His saying: ﴿And God is encompassing them from behind﴾ [al-Buruj: 20]. End.

I say: What he mentioned is a Jahmiyya (a theological sect) doubt, founded on analogizing the attribute of the Eternal to temporal things and taking its specific properties for Him, and this is analogy with a difference. The revealed matters are received from the customary usage of the Speaker in address, not from newly invented convention. So no one has the right to make the words that came in the Qur'an fixed for meanings, and then wish to explain God's intended meaning by those meanings. The completion of this discussion has been given earlier in the explanation of "al-Rahman al-Rahim" in the basmala at the beginning of the Glorious Revelation. Refer back to it.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[121] ﴿And [remember] when you set out in the morning from your family to settle the believers in their positions for the battle, and Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

﴿When you set out﴾ means you went forth. ﴿From your family﴾ means ﴿you settled﴾, that is, you placed, ﴿the believers in positions﴾, meaning places and stations in which they would stand, ﴿for the battle﴾. ﴿And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ The majority of scholars and the scholars of the military campaigns (ʿulamaʾ al-maghazi) held that these verses were revealed concerning the Battle of Uhud. The purpose of bringing up this Uhud episode alongside the Badr episode [p. 954] is to confirm what has preceded. What came before it concerned being harmed by good and gladdened by calamity, and Allah's custom regarding them in matters of victory, support, and the repelling of the enemy's harm: if they are patient and God-fearing, and [His] change if they change. That is, remind them of what confirms this from your past circumstances, when they were not patient at Uhud, so they were struck, and your calamity gladdened the enemies, and when they were patient and followed, so they were given victory, and their victory distressed the enemy. Directing the address to him (ﷺ) stirs others toward examining things closely and following evidence, without any stopping at what is familiar. This is what is derived from the tafsir of al-Biqaʿi.

This verse is the opening of the narrative, and sixty verses were revealed concerning it. In this surah, some of the wisdoms and praiseworthy aims of this battle are pointed out, as will be mentioned. It took place in Shawwal of the third year (AH), by the consensus of the majority. Its cause was that when Allah, exalted is He, caused the nobles of Quraysh to be killed at Badr, and they suffered a calamity the like of which they had not suffered before, and Abu Sufyan ibn Harb became their leader because their great men had perished, they came to the outskirts of Medina in the Battle of al-Sawiq, and he did not attain what he wanted. He began to incite against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims, and to gather the hosts, nearly three thousand from Quraysh, their allies, and the Ahabish. They brought their women so that they would not flee, so that they would defend them. Then he advanced with them toward Medina, and they camped near Mount Uhud. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) consulted his companions: should he go out to them, or remain in Medina? His own view was that they should not go out from Medina, and that they should fortify themselves within it. If they entered it, the Muslims would fight them at the mouths of the alleys, and the women from the rooftops. ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy agreed with this opinion, and it was indeed the opinion [of the majority]. But a group of the excellent companions, among those who had missed going out on the Day of Badr, hastened and urged him to go out, and insisted upon this. So he rose and entered his house, put on his armor, and came out to them, while the resolve of those insistent ones had weakened. They said: "We have compelled the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to go out." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, if you prefer to remain in Medina, then do so." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It is not befitting for a Prophet, when he has put on his armor, to take it off until Allah judges between him and his enemy."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out [p. 955] with a thousand of his companions, and he appointed Ibn Umm Maktum to lead the prayer for the remaining Muslims in Medina. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had seen a dream while in Medina: he saw that there was a notch in his sword, that cows were being slaughtered, and that he had put his hand into a strong coat of mail. He interpreted the notch in his sword as a man of his household who would be struck; he interpreted the cows as a group of his companions who would be killed; and he interpreted the coat of mail as Medina. He went out on Friday, and when he reached al-Shawt, between Medina and Uhud, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy withdrew from him with a third of the people, angry because his opinion about remaining had been opposed. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, the father of Jabir, followed them, rebuking them, urging them to return, and saying: "Come, fight in the way of Allah, or defend." They said: "If we knew that you would fight, we would not return." So he turned back from them and cursed them. A group of the Ansar asked the Prophet (ﷺ) to seek help from their Jewish allies, but he refused. He took the lava field of Banu Harithah and passed between the orchards, with Abu Khaythamah of Banu Harithah guiding him, until he alighted at the mountain pass of Uhud, leaning against the mountain. He forbade the people from fighting until he commanded them. When it was morning, the day of Saturday, he arrayed himself for battle with seven hundred men, among them fifty horsemen and fifty archers. He appointed ʿAbd Allah ibn Jubayr over the archers, and commanded him and his companions to keep to their positions and not to leave them, even if they saw the birds snatching the army. They were behind the army. He commanded them to shoot the polytheists with arrows so that they would not come upon the Muslims from behind. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wore two coats of mail that day. He gave the banner to Musʿab ibn ʿUmayr, and he placed al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam over one of the two wings, and al-Mundhir ibn ʿAmr over the other. He reviewed the young men that day, and turned back those he considered too young for fighting. Among them were ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, Usamah ibn Zayd, Usayd ibn Zahir, al-Bara ibn ʿAzib, Zayd ibn Arqam, Zayd ibn Thabit, ʿArabah ibn Aws, and ʿAmr ibn Hizam. He permitted those he saw as capable. Among them were Samurah ibn Jundub and Rafiʿ ibn Khadij, and both were fifteen years old. It was said: he permitted those he permitted because they had reached the age of fifteen, and turned back those he turned back because they were under the age of puberty. A group said: he permitted those he permitted for their ability, and turned back those he turned back for their inability, and puberty or its absence had no effect on that. They said: in some wordings of the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar: "When he saw me as capable, he permitted me."

[p. 956] Quraysh arrayed themselves for battle, and they were three thousand, among them two hundred horsemen. They placed Khalid ibn al-Walid over their right wing, and ʿIkrimah ibn Abi Jahl over their left. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave his sword to Abu Dujanah (Simak ibn Kharashah). He was brave and a champion, who swaggered in war. The first of the polytheists to come forward was Abu ʿAmir the Corrupt, whose name was ʿAbd ibn ʿAmr ibn Sayfi. He was called "the Monk" because of his asceticism and devotion in the pre-Islamic period, but the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named him "the Corrupt." He had been the chief of the Aws in the pre-Islamic period. When Islam came, it grieved him, and he openly declared enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He left Medina and went to Quraysh, inciting them against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and urging them to fight him, promising them that his people would obey him and join him when they saw him. So he was the first of the Muslims' opponents whom they met; he called out to his people and made himself known to them. They said: "May Allah not grant you comfort, O Corrupt!" He fought the Muslims fiercely. On that day Hamzah, Talhah, Shaybah, Abu Dujanah, and al-Nadr ibn Anas acquitted themselves with great valor. A group of the Ansar were struck while advancing, not retreating, and the fighting intensified. At the start of the day, the advantage was with the Muslims over the unbelievers, so the enemies of Allah were routed and turned their backs, until they reached their women. When the archers saw their rout, they abandoned their position which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had ordered them to guard, and they said: "O people! The spoils! The spoils!" Their commander reminded them of the covenant of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but they did not listen. They thought the polytheists would not return, so they went in pursuit of the spoils and left the post empty. Only about ten of them obeyed their commander. The polytheists then rallied, killed those of the archers who remained, and came upon the Companions from behind while they were plundering. They surrounded them, and those whom Allah honored with martyrdom were martyred. The enemy reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Musʿab ibn ʿUmayr, the bearer of the banner, fought in front of him until he was killed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was wounded in his face, and his lower right incisor was broken by a stone, and the helmet on his head was smashed. It is said that the one who did this was ʿUtbah ibn Abi Waqqas, and ʿAmr ibn Qamiʾah al-Laythi. Hanzalah al-Ghasil charged at Abu Sufyan to kill him, but Shaddad ibn al-Aswad al-Laythi intercepted him, from [the tribe of] Shuʿub, and killed him. He had been in a state of major impurity (junub), so the Prophet (ﷺ) informed [the people] that the angels had washed him.

[p. 957] The stones showered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) until he fell into some pits there. ʿAli took him by the hand, and Talhah embraced him until he stood up. Malik ibn Sinan al-Khudri, the father of Abu Saʿid, sucked the blood from his wound. Two rings of the helmet's chain-mail became lodged in his face (ﷺ), and Abu ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrah pulled them out. His two front teeth were knocked out, and he became one whose front teeth were missing. The polytheists then attacked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). A group of Muslims stood firm before him and were all killed; the last of them was ʿAmmar ibn Yazid ibn al-Sakan. Then Talhah fought until the polytheists were driven back. Abu Dujanah was shielding the Prophet (ﷺ) with his back, and arrows struck him, but he did not move. The eye of Qatadah ibn al-Nuʿman was struck, and it fell onto his cheek, and [the Prophet] (ﷺ) returned it to its place with his hand, and it healed; it became his best eye. Al-Nadr ibn Anas came upon a group of the Companions who were bewildered and said: "The Messenger of Allah has been killed." He said: "What will you do with life after him? Rise and die as he died." Then he faced the people and fought until he was killed, and seventy wounds were found on him. ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf was wounded that day with twenty wounds, some of them in his leg, so he limped from them. Hamzah, the uncle of the Prophet (ﷺ), was killed. Shaytan called out: "Indeed Muhammad has been killed," because ʿAmr ibn Qamiʾah had killed Musʿab ibn ʿUmayr, thinking he was the Prophet (ﷺ). The Muslims weakened at the cry of Shaytan. Then Kaʿb ibn Malik, the poet, from Banu Salamah, recognized the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He called out at the top of his voice, announcing good news to the people, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was saying to him: "Be silent!" The Muslims gathered around him and rose with him toward the mountain pass. Ubayy ibn Khalaf caught up with him in the pass, and the Prophet (ﷺ) took a spear from al-Harith ibn al-Simmah and thrust it into his neck. Ubayy turned back fleeing. The polytheists said to him: "There is nothing wrong with you." He said: "By Allah! If he had spat on me, he would have killed me," for the Prophet (ﷺ) had threatened him with death. The enemy of Allah died at Sarif on their way back to Mecca. Then ʿAli brought water to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he washed his face and rose. He stood on a rock of the mountain. The time for prayer came, and he led them in prayer while sitting. Allah forgave the Muslims who had fled, and there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those of you who turned back on the day the two hosts met﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:155], and the verse.

[p. 958] About seventy were martyred, most of them from the Ansar. Twenty-two of the polytheists were killed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions returned to Medina. It is said that he said to ʿAli: "The polytheists will not inflict upon us the like of this until Allah grants us victory."

This is a summary of this narrative. The people of the biographies (ahl al-siyar) have related it at greater length than this, and what has been mentioned is sufficient. As for what it contains of rulings, jurisprudence, wisdoms, and praiseworthy aims, these have been fully explained by the Imam Ibn al-Qayyim in Zad al-Maʿad, so refer to it.

Note:
Most scholars interpreted "you set out" (ghadawta) according to its original meaning, which is going forth in the morning, that is, early. Then they raised an objection: he (ﷺ) went out to Uhud after the Friday prayer, as the people of the biographies unanimously agree, so how does it correspond?

Some answered that what is meant is the morning of Saturday, and that in its morning was the arraying for positions. However, this is not supported by "from your family," because his family was not with him at that time.

Others said: what is meant is the morning of Friday, that is: remember when you set out from your family on the morning of Friday to your companions in your mosque, consulting them about the matter of the polytheists. Then He said: and He made from "you set out" a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), to inform that beginning on the cause is beginning on its effect. So He said: "you settle the believers," that is, on the morning of the day of Saturday.

It had occurred to me that the closer reading is to take "going out" (ghudūw) in the sense of departing, not restricted to early morning, and this is often used in that way.

Then I saw in Fath al-Bayan what I had inclined to, and I praised God for the agreement. Its text reads: "He expressed the going out by 'ghudūw,' which is going out in the morning, even though he (ﷺ) went out after the Friday prayer, because 'ghadw' and 'rawāḥ' are sometimes used to express going out and entering without regard to their original meaning, just as one says 'aḍḥā' (he entered the forenoon) even when it is not the time of forenoon." End of quotation.

Al-Biqa'i said: Since the return of 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy the hypocrite (from the army), as will come in the explicit mention at the end of the story, is among the evidences that the hypocrites, let alone those who openly declare enmity, are characterized by what God Most High informs us of them of hostility and hatred, together with the fact that he was the cause of the two groups of the Ansar (al-Ansar, the Helpers of Madinah) being struck with the intent of cowardice (al-fashal), it was most fitting for God to follow this story with the prohibition against taking intimate companions of evil (bitanat al-su', i.e., confidants who do not fall short in corruption). For this reason, He, glory be to Him, began it with His saying, in apposition to (idh ghadawta, "when you set out"), as an explanation of what precedes it, that the intimate companions of evil spare them no ruin (la ya'lunahum khabalan).

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[122] ﴿When two parties among you were about to lose heart, though Allah was their ally. And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾

﴿When two parties among you were about to﴾: that is, the Banu Salamah of the Khazraj and the Banu Harithah of the Aws. ﴿Lose heart﴾: that is, become slack, cowardly and weak, owing to the withdrawal of the hypocrites from their support and their alliance. But Allah protected them, and they went on with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿Though Allah was their ally﴾: their supporter and the one who takes charge of their affairs, so He sustained them with success and protection. ﴿And upon Allah﴾ alone, to the exclusion of all else, whether independently or in association: ﴿let the believers rely﴾ in all their affairs, for He is sufficient for them. Tawakkul (reliance) is a form of tafa''ul from wakala amrahu ila fulan (he entrusted his affair to so-and-so), when one relies on him for its sufficiency and does not take charge of it oneself. The verse contains an indication that a person should repel what befalls him of hardship and calamity by relying upon Allah, and should turn away anxiety from himself by that reliance.

Al-Shaykhan narrated from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "It was concerning us that this verse was revealed: ﴿When two parties among you were about to lose heart, though Allah was their ally﴾." He said: "We are the two parties: the Banu Harithah and the Banu Salamah, and we would not wish that it had not been revealed, because of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Though Allah was their ally.﴾"

That is, due to the great joy at what they gained of honour through Allah's praise and His sending down a verse about them clearly affirming the validity of their alliance. And that resolve did not take them out of Allah's alliance.

﴿And Allah had already given you victory at Badr when you were humble. So fear Allah; perhaps you will be grateful.﴾

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[123] ﴿And Allah had already given you victory at Badr when you were humble. So fear Allah; perhaps you will be grateful.﴾

When Exalted Allah mentioned the story of Uhud, He followed it with the mention of the story of Badr. This is because the Muslims on the day of Badr were at the extreme of weakness in number and equipment, while the disbelievers were at the extreme of strength and power. Then Exalted Allah gave the Muslims victory over the disbelievers, and this became among the strongest proofs that the fruit of reliance upon Him, Exalted is He, and of patience and God-consciousness (taqwa) is victory, support and assistance.

Badr is a place between the two sanctuaries (Makkah and Madinah), nearer to Madinah. It is said that it lies twenty-eight farsakhs (a farsakh being a unit of distance) from it. Or it is the name of a well there, dug by a man named Badr.

His saying ﴿perhaps you will be grateful﴾ means: hoping that you will thank Him for what He has bestowed upon you by His help, through your God-consciousness.

The Battle of Badr has been alluded to in several places of the Revelation (al-Tanzil). It took place in the month of Ramadan, in the second year of the Hijra (migration). Its cause was that the Prophet (ﷺ) received word that a caravan of the Quraysh, carrying great wealth, was coming from Syria towards Makkah. With it were thirty or forty men of the Quraysh, their leader being Abu Sufyan, and with him Amr ibn al-As and Makhrama ibn Nawfal.

So the Prophet (ﷺ) called the people to this caravan and ordered whoever had a mount present to set out. He did not gather a large assembly, because he did not expect fighting. He set out hastily with three hundred and some ten men; they had no horses with them except two horses, and they had seventy camels which they took turns riding. News of his departure reached Abu Sufyan, so he hired Damdam ibn Amr al-Ghifari and sent him to the people of Makkah, calling them to rally in defence of their caravan. They mobilised and gathered in full force. The Prophet (ﷺ) set out on the eighth night of Ramadan, appointing Amr ibn Umm Maktum to lead the prayer. He sent back Abu Lubaba from al-Rawha and appointed him over Madinah. He gave the banner to Mus'ab ibn Umayr, and gave Ali a banner, and to a man from the Ansar another banner, said to have been both black. He placed Qays ibn Abi Sa'sa'a over the rear guard. The banner of the Ansar that day was with Sa'd ibn Mu'adh. They took the pass out of Madinah towards Dhu al-Hulayfa, then reached Suhayrat Yamam, then the well of al-Rawha, then turned to the right away from the road towards al-Safra. Before that the Prophet (ﷺ) had sent Basbas ibn Amr and Adi ibn Abi al-Zaghba to Badr to spy out the news of Abu Sufyan and his caravan. Then he veered to the right away from al-Safra and set out through the valley of Daqran. News reached him of the departure of the Quraysh and their troops, so he consulted his companions. The Emigrants (Muhajirun) spoke and spoke well, but he wanted to hear what the Ansar would say, and they understood this. Then Sa'd ibn Mu'adh spoke, and among what he said was: "If you were to lead us into this sea, we would plunge into it with you. So march with us, O Messenger of Allah, in the blessing of Allah." He was delighted by this and said: "March and rejoice, for Allah has promised me one of the two groups."

Then they moved from Daqran to a place near Badr. He sent Ali, al-Zubayr and Sa'd with a group to seek news. They came upon two boys of the Quraysh and brought them, while he (ﷺ) was standing and praying. They said: "We are water-carriers of the Quraysh." They disbelieved them, out of dislike for the news and hoping that they were from the caravan, for the sake of the spoils and the lightness of the burden. So they began beating them, and they kept saying: "We are from the caravan." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) finished his prayer, disapproved of their conduct, and said to the two boys: "Tell me, where are the Quraysh?" They informed him that they were behind the sand-hill, and that they slaughtered ten camels one day and nine the next. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The people are between nine hundred and a thousand."

Basbas and Adi had gone off spying and had found no news, until they came down and made their camels kneel near the water, and drew water in a waterskin of theirs. Majdi ibn Amr of Juhayna was near them. Adi heard a slave-girl from among the girls of the tribe saying to her companion: "The caravan comes tomorrow or the day after, and I will work for them and pay you what is due to you." She came to Majdi ibn Amr and he confirmed her words. Basbas and Adi returned with the news. Then Abu Sufyan came after them, spying for news. He said to Majdi: "Did you perceive anyone?" He said: "Two riders who knelt down, leaning towards this hill, drew water and then rose." Abu Sufyan came to the place where they had knelt and crumbled some of the dung of their mounts. He said: "By Allah, these are fodder of Yathrib (Madinah)!" He returned quickly, having become wary, and turned the caravan aside onto the coastal road, and so escaped. He sent word to the Quraysh that we have escaped with the caravan, so return.

Abu Jahl said: "By Allah, we will not return until we reach the water of Badr, stay there three days, and the Arabs will fear us forever."

Al-Akhnas ibn Shariq returned with all the Banu Zuhra, who were his allies and obeyed by them, and said: "You only went out to protect your wealth, and it has escaped, so return." The Banu Adi had not gone out with the people, so no one from the Quraysh of the clan of Adi or of Zuhra witnessed Badr.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) got ahead of the Quraysh to the water of Badr, and a rain fell on them from their side that held them back, while on the side of the Muslims it fell on the hard sand of the valley, and it aided them in marching. So the Prophet (ﷺ) camped at the nearest water to Madinah among the waters of Badr. Al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir said to him: "Did Allah make you alight at this place, so that we may not move from it, or did you intend war and stratagem?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No, rather it is opinion and war." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is not a suitable station. Rather, let us go to the nearest water to the people, camp there, build a basin over it, fill it, and fill up all the other wells, so that we have denied them the water." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) approved of this.

Then they built a shelter (arish) on a hill overlooking the battlefield, where the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would stay until victory came to him from his Lord. He walked, showing them the places where the people would fall, one by one.

When the Quraysh camped on their side, they sent Umayr ibn Wahb al-Jumahi to estimate the number of the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He estimated them, returned, and informed them of the news. Hakim ibn Hizam and Utba ibn Rabi'a wanted to turn the Quraysh back so that there would be no war, but Abu Jahl refused, and the polytheists supported him. The two groups faced each other. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) straightened the rows with his own hand, then returned to the shelter, accompanied only by Abu Bakr, and began to supplicate earnestly, while Abu Bakr spoke to him. In his supplication he said: "O Allah! If this band perishes, You will not be worshipped on the earth. O Allah! Fulfil for me what You have promised me."

Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and a group with him from the Ansar were at the door of the shelter, guarding it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dozed, then awoke and said: "Rejoice, O Abu Bakr! The help of Allah has come." Then he went out urging the people on. He threw a handful of pebbles into the faces of the enemy, saying: "May their faces be disfigured." Then they clashed. Utba, his brother Shayba, and his son al-Walid came out seeking single combat. Ubayda ibn al-Harith, Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, and Ali ibn Abi Talib came out to them. Hamza and Ali killed Shayba and al-Walid, and Utba struck Ubayda, cutting off his leg, so that he died. Hamza and Ali went to Utba and killed him. Awf and Mu'adh, the two sons of Afra, and Abdullah ibn Rawaha from the Ansar had come out against them, but they refused except to fight their own kin. The people charged in a surge, and the polytheists were routed. On that day seventy men of them were killed, and seventy were taken captive. Fourteen men of the Muslims were martyred. Then the battle subsided, and he returned to Madinah. He divided the spoils at al-Safra, and entered Madinah eight nights before the end of Ramadan.

The full account is given in the biographies (al-Siyar). Among the most excellent of them in its arrangement and jurisprudential insight is Zad al-Ma'ad (The Provision of the Hereafter, by Ibn al-Qayyim); let one refer to it.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[124] ﴿When you said to the believers, "Is it not enough for you that your Lord should reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?"﴾

﴿When you said to the believers, "Is it not enough for you that your Lord should reinforce you"﴾ for strengthening you, granting you victory, and repelling your enemies; ﴿with three thousand angels sent down﴾ from His heaven to fight His enemies. And His saying:

[p. 964]

**On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:**

[125] ﴿Yes. If you are steadfast and mindful of God, and they come upon you suddenly in this very moment, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels, marked out.﴾

﴿Yes (بَلى)﴾ is either part of what the Prophet ﷺ said to the believers, or the beginning of a address from God, Exalted, confirming the words of His Prophet and adding to what He had promised them, out of generosity and grace. That is: yes, reinforcement with three thousand is sufficient for you, but He will give you more. ﴿If you are steadfast﴾ in fighting them; ﴿and mindful of God﴾, by not fleeing from them; ﴿and they come upon you suddenly in this very moment﴾, that is, at this very hour, so do not be alarmed by their sudden attack; ﴿your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels﴾, arriving at the time of their coming, their descent not being delayed beyond their arrival; ﴿marked out﴾, with the waw vowelled with a kasra, meaning they mark themselves with the implements of war, in the manner of horsemen on the day of battle, so that they may be recognised by them. It is also recited with a fatha on the waw, meaning "marked out" by Him, Exalted is He.

Al-Bukhari related from Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of God ﷺ said on the day of Badr: "This is Jibril, holding the head of his horse, wearing the implements of war."

**Note:**

Regarding the Prophet's ﷺ promise to the believers of reinforcement, in His words ﴿when you said﴾ [Al 'Imran: 124], there are two views.

The first: that it was on the day of Badr, since the context of what precedes it indicates this, namely His words ﴿God had already helped you at Badr﴾ [Al 'Imran: 123]. So ﴿when﴾ (إذ) is an adverbial of time governed by ﴿helped you﴾, meaning: He helped you at the time you said to the believers, when they had shown weakness and implored their Lord. If it is asked: how is this verse, on this view, to be reconciled with His words in Surat al-Anfal concerning the story of Badr: ﴿when you sought help from your Lord and He answered you: "I will reinforce you with a thousand angels, following one another"﴾ [al-Anfal: 9]?

The answer: the specification of the thousand here does not contradict three thousand or more, because of His word "following one another" (مُرْدِفِينَ), meaning that others follow them, and thousands more like them come after them. This is because when they implored, He reinforced them with a thousand, then reinforced them with the full three thousand, then reinforced them with the full five thousand when they were steadfast and mindful of God. This gradual progression and the continuous succession of reinforcement had a more fitting effect and greater strength for strengthening them, and for keeping it hidden, than if it had come only once. It is like the continuous succession of revelation, and its descent again and again. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: God reinforced the Muslims with a thousand, then they became three thousand, then they became five thousand.

What further supports this view is that the context of Badr in al-Anfal, from His words ﴿when God promised you one of the two groups﴾ [al-Anfal: 7] and the verses after it, resembles this context here, as one will perceive who reflects upon it.

[p. 965] The second view: that this promise was on the day of Uhud, since the narrative is in the context of Uhud, and the mention of Badr was inserted as a parenthetical digression within it, to remind them of His favour upon them when He gave them victory at Badr while they were humiliated, and that He is likewise able to give them victory in all other circumstances. Then He returned to the story of Uhud and reported the words of His Messenger to them: ﴿Is it not enough for you that your Lord reinforce you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 124], and so on. Then He promised them that if they were steadfast and mindful of God, He would reinforce them with five thousand. So this is from the words of His Messenger, while the reinforcement at Badr was from the words of God, Exalted is He, and this was with five thousand. The reinforcement at Badr was with a thousand, and this is conditional, whereas that was unconditional. The narrative in this sura is the story of Uhud, fully and at length, while Badr is mentioned in it as a digression; and the narrative in al-Anfal is the story of Badr, fully and at length. So the context here is other than the context in al-Anfal. Ibn al-Qayyim indicated this in Zad al-Ma'ad.

Al-Allama Abu al-Su'ud defended the first view, and showed the weakness of the second with cogent arguments. So let one refer to him.

Al-Khazin related from Ibn Jarir that he said: "The most correct of the views on this matter is to say: God informed about His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that he said to the believers: ﴿Is it not enough for you that your Lord reinforce you with three thousand angels﴾ [Al 'Imran: 124]. So God promised them three thousand angels as reinforcement for them. Then after the three thousand He promised them five thousand, if they were steadfast against their enemies and mindful of God."

There is no indication in the verse that they were reinforced with three thousand, nor with five thousand, nor that they were not reinforced with them. It is possible that God, Mighty and Majestic, reinforced them in the manner reported by those who affirmed that He reinforced them, and it is possible that He did not reinforce them in the manner mentioned by those who denied it. We have no report that is authentic through the channel that establishes that they were reinforced with three thousand, nor with five thousand.

[p. 966] It is not permissible to state an opinion on this matter except on the basis of a report which establishes proof, and there is no such report, so we shall grant the claim of neither of the two parties.

However, the Qur'an does indicate that they were reinforced on the day of Badr with a thousand angels, and that is His words: ﴿when you sought help from your Lord and He answered you: "I will reinforce you with a thousand angels, following one another"﴾ [al-Anfal: 9].

As for the day of Uhud, the indication that they were not reinforced is clearer than the indication that they were. For if they had been reinforced, they would not have been defeated, nor would what befell them have befallen them.

So the correct statement on this matter is to say as God, Exalted is His remembrance, has said.

This is the text of Ibn Jarir, pages 180–181 of the seventh volume, the Ma'arif edition.

If you say: what then do you make of the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, related in the two Sahihs, that he said: "I saw the Messenger of God ﷺ on the day of Uhud, and with him were two men fighting on his behalf, wearing white garments, fighting most fiercely; I had never seen them before or since," meaning Jibril and Mika'il? I say: that was only for the Prophet ﷺ specifically, because he was steadfast and did not flee as his companions fled on the day of Uhud. End.

**Benefit:**

Al-imdad (reinforcement) linguistically means assistance, and what is meant here is assisting the army. Is the assistance of the angels to the army by fighting alongside them? That is supported by the hadith above, and by the hadith of 'A'isha in the two Sahihs, who said: "When the Messenger of God ﷺ [p. 967] returned from the Trench, and laid down his weapons and washed, Jibril came to him and said: 'You have laid down your weapons? By God, we have not laid ours down. Go out to them!' He said: 'Where to?' He said: 'Here,' and pointed to the Banu Qurayza, so the Prophet ﷺ went out to them." Or it is by increasing the numbers of the Muslims and strengthening their hearts, as God, Exalted, said in al-Anfal: ﴿when your Lord revealed to the angels: "I am with you, so strengthen those who believe; I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved"﴾ [al-Anfal: 12]. Or it is by both together, and this is the apparent meaning.

Al-Subki was asked about the wisdom in the angels fighting, although Jibril is able to repel the disbelievers with a feather from his wing. He answered that this was intended so that the virtue would belong to the Prophet and his companions, and so that the angels would serve as reinforcement in the customary way of reinforcing armies, observing the outward form of the means that God, Exalted, has put in place among His servants. And God is the doer of all things. End.

The discussion concerning His saying, exalted is He:

[126] ﴿And Allah made it not but as good tidings for you and that your hearts may be assured thereby. And victory is not except from Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾

﴿And Allah made it not but as good tidings for you﴾ i.e., the reinforcement with the angels was only made so that you would rejoice in it, whereby the strength of your hearts, your courage, your valour and your vigour would increase. ﴿And that your hearts may be assured﴾ i.e., may be at rest, ﴿thereby﴾ i.e., so that they do not despair because of the multitude of your enemy and the fewness of your number. ﴿And victory is not except from Allah﴾ alone, not from the angels nor from others; the apparent causes have no effect of their own. In this is a strengthening of the believers, and a prevention of despair regarding victory when its causes and signs are absent. ﴿The Exalted in Might﴾ i.e., the One who is not overcome in His judgment. ﴿The Wise﴾ who does everything He does in accordance with what His dazzling wisdom requires.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[127] ﴿That He might cut off a part of those who disbelieve, or subdue them so that they turn back frustrated.﴾

﴿That He might cut off a part of those who disbelieve﴾ means: that He might destroy and diminish a group of them by killing and capture, (p-968) as happened on the Day of Badr, when seventy of them were killed and seventy taken captive. The lam (the particle "that"/"in order that") is connected either to His words, ﴿And Allah had already helped you﴾ [Al-'Imran: 123], and what lies between them is a confirmation of its reality and an explanation of how it came about; or it is connected to what the predicate in His words ﴿And victory is not but from Allah﴾ [Al-'Imran: 126] is attached to, of the sense of establishment and firm settlement. ﴿Or subdue them﴾ means: humiliate them and enrage them by defeat, as a strengthening of the believers. ﴿So that they turn back frustrated﴾ means: so that they return with their hopes cut off. The words of His, "...", have been placed between the conjunct and what it is conjoined to in the course of the speech.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 128:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[128] ﴿Thou hast no say in the matter, whether He turns to them in mercy or punishes them; for surely they are wrongdoers.﴾

﴿Thou hast no say in the matter at all﴾ is a parenthetical statement, lest the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) become heedless and see for himself some influence over some of these affairs, and thus veil himself from tawhid (monotheism). That is: you have no part in their affair, in whatever way it may be. You are only a human being commanded to warn. Your duty is only to convey the message; their affair belongs to Allah alone, as al-Qashani stated. In this parenthetical statement there is also a lightening of his grief over their disbelief and his eagerness for their guidance, as He said: ﴿It is not upon you to guide them, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 272]. His words, exalted is He, ﴿or He turns to them in mercy﴾ mean: from the disbelief they are in, so that He guides them to Islam after misguidance. ﴿or punishes them﴾ means: in this world and the Hereafter for their disbelief and their sins. ﴿for surely they are wrongdoers﴾ means: they deserve that because of their persistence in obstinacy.

Al-Bukhari related from Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to supplicate against someone or supplicate for someone, after bowing (qunut); and sometimes when he said "Allah hears whoever praises Him," he would say: "O Allah! Our Lord, and to You is the praise. O Allah! Deliver al-Walid ibn al-Walid, Salamah ibn Hisham, and Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah. O Allah! Tighten Your grip upon Mudar and make it years like the years of Yusuf," saying it aloud. He would also say in some of his prayers, in the Fajr prayer: "O Allah, curse so-and-so and so-and-so," concerning some tribes of the Arabs, until Allah revealed: ﴿Thou hast no say in the matter at all﴾, the verse.

He also traced back what he had reported as a suspended narration from Ibn Umar, that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he raised his head from bowing in the last rak'ah of the Fajr prayer, saying: "O Allah, curse so-and-so, so-and-so and so-and-so," after he had said: "Allah hears whoever praises Him; our Lord, and to You is the praise." So Allah revealed: ﴿Thou hast no say in the matter at all﴾, the verse. Imam Ahmad also related it from Ibn Umar, with the wording: "O Allah, curse so-and-so and so-and-so. O Allah, curse al-Harith ibn Hisham. O Allah, curse Suhail ibn Amr. O Allah, curse Safwan ibn Umayyah." Then this verse was revealed: ﴿Thou hast no say in the matter at all, whether He turns to them in mercy﴾, the verse. And they all repented.

Imam Ahmad said: Hushaim narrated to us, Humayd narrated to us, from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet (ﷺ) had his front tooth broken at the Battle of Uhud, and his forehead was wounded until blood flowed over his face. He said: "How will a people prosper who have done this to their prophet while he calls them to their Lord, the Mighty and Majestic?" So Allah revealed: ﴿Thou hast no say in the matter at all, whether He turns to them in mercy﴾, the verse. Muslim alone related it, and al-Bukhari related it as a suspended narration.

We have already explained in the introduction to the tafsir the reality of the meaning of occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), and that a verse may be cited as evidence in a context because it is among what it encompasses; so the narrator applies the term "revelation" to it in that sense, without intending that this was the cause of its being revealed. The wisdom in his being prevented (ﷺ) from supplicating against them became apparent through their repentance later on. Persistence in supplication is a cause for its being answered, especially from the noblest of His creation. So His wisdom, exalted is He, required that He give them respite until they repented, given His prior knowledge concerning them. In it is also the seeking of entrusting affairs to Allah in grave matters, because of the divine secrets folded within them.

(p-970) A subtle point:

His words, exalted is He, ﴿or He turns to them in mercy﴾ are in the accusative by the implied (an) in the position of a noun conjoined by (aw) to (al-amr) or to (shay'), meaning: you have no say in their affair, or in His turning to them in mercy, or in His punishing them; or: you have no say in their affair, or their being turned to in mercy, or their being punished.

I say: making ﴿or He turns﴾ accusative by coordination with (yakbitahum) is very far-fetched, even though some exegetes preferred it in the aforementioned manner. This is because His words, exalted is He, ﴿Thou hast no say﴾ are a resumptive (independent) statement, as the narrations regarding the occasion of revelation have explicitly stated. And these are the reference in interpretation. And Allah knows best.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[129] ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is a confirmation of what precedes it, namely His saying: ﴿You have no share in the affair﴾ [Al 'Imran: 128]. That is: to Him belongs what is in them, by way of dominion and command. ﴿He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾: He judges among His creation as He wills, there is no one to reverse His judgment, and He is not questioned about what He does. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) that confirms the content of His saying "He forgives whom He wills," with an addition. And in the restriction of this concluding phrase to it, without any indicator, there is a concern with the matter of forgiveness and mercy that is not hidden, as Abu al-Su'ud has noted.

(p-971)

The discussion of His saying, the Exalted:

[130] ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume usury, doubled and redoubled, and fear Allah that you may be successful.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, do not consume usury, doubled and redoubled﴾ This is a prohibition of usury (riba) together with a rebuke for what they used to do in the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance) of multiplying it. A man among them, when his debt reached its due date, would say: "Either you pay my right, or you increase it and I will extend the term." Addressing them by the name (of faith, al-iman) is an indication that it is among the requirements of faith and its affirmation to abandon usury. The earlier discussion in al-Baqarah contained, in the strong emphasis on prohibiting it, what alarms anyone who has even the least measure of piety. And whoever does not abandon it, or something close to it, incurs the guarantee of abandonment (by Allah) in every age: ﴿So if you do not, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 279] ﴿Those are the ones who have purchased the worldly life in exchange for the Hereafter; so the punishment will not be lightened for them, and they will not be helped﴾ [al-Baqarah: 86]. As for His saying ﴿doubled and redoubled﴾, it means repeated increases. It is not meant to restrict the prohibition to it, since its prohibition in every state is known, but rather to take into account their custom, as we have explained. Its position is accusative (naṣb) as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of "usury". It has also been read as (muḍaʿʿafah). ﴿And fear Allah﴾ regarding what you are forbidden from ﴿that you may be successful﴾ by fulfilling your rights and preserving yourselves from your enemies, just as you preserve the rights of things.

Among what reveals the wisdom of placing this verse within the account of the Battle of Uhud is what Abu Dawud related from Abu Hurayrah: that ʿAmr ibn Uqaysh (may Allah be pleased with him) had usury (riba) owed to him in the Jahiliyyah, and he disliked to embrace Islam until he had taken it. So he came on the day of Uhud and said: "Where are my paternal cousins?" They said: "At Uhud." He said: "Where is so-and-so?" They said: "At Uhud." He said: "Where is so-and-so?" They said: "At Uhud." [Page 972] So he put on his coat of mail, mounted his horse, and set off toward them. When the Muslims saw him they said: "Stay away from us, O ʿAmr!" He said: "I have indeed believed." So he fought until he was wounded, and he was carried to his family wounded. Then Saʿd ibn Muʿadh (may Allah be pleased with him) came to him and said to his sister: "Ask him: Is it zeal for your people and anger for them, or anger for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic?" He said: "Rather, anger for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and His Messenger ﷺ." He died, and he entered Paradise, though he had never performed a single prayer to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

al-Dinawari said: Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) used to say: "Tell me about a man who entered Paradise without ever having prayed!" The people would be silent, and Abu Hurayrah would say: "He is the brother of Banu ʿAbd al-Ashhal."

In the narration of Ibn Ishaq: it was mentioned to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said: "Indeed he is among the people of Paradise." This is the summary of what al-Biqaʿi (may Allah have mercy on him) recorded.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[131] ﴿And guard yourselves against the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾

﴿And guard yourselves against the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ by keeping away from following them in usury (ribā) and the like. It is related from Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) that he used to say: "It is the most frightening verse in the Qur'an, in that Allah threatens the believers with the Fire prepared for the disbelievers if they do not guard against Him."

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[132] ﴿And obey Allah and the Messenger that you may be shown mercy﴾

﴿And obey Allah and the Messenger﴾ i.e., in abandoning usury (riba) and the like: ﴿that you may be shown mercy﴾

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[133] ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden whose width is the heavens and the earth, prepared for the God-fearing.﴾

﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden﴾ means: hasten to that which leads to them, namely seeking forgiveness (istighfar), repentance (tawbah), and righteous deeds. (p-973) As for His words ﴿whose width is the heavens and the earth﴾, it means: its width is like theirs, as He said in Surah al-Hadid: ﴿Race to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden whose width is like the width of the heaven and the earth﴾ [al-Hadid: 21]. Regarding "width" there are two views:

The first: it is to be taken in its literal sense. Its specific mention is a reminder of the vastness of its length, since width is ordinarily less than length, as He said, Exalted is He, describing the bedding of Paradise: ﴿its linings are of brocade﴾ [al-Rahman: 54]. That is, consider how much more its outer surface must be. So it is likewise here.

The second: it is a metaphor for expansiveness and spaciousness. Al-Qaffal said: "The intended meaning of width here is not what is opposite to length; rather, it is an expression for vastness, as the Arabs say: 'spacious lands' (bilad 'arida), and it is said: 'this is a broad claim' (da'wa 'arida), meaning vast and great. The principle in this is that whatever has a broad width is not confined, and whatever has a narrow width is thin, so width was made a metaphor for vastness." Al-Zamakhshari said: The intended meaning is describing it with spaciousness and expansiveness, so it is likened to the widest and most extensive of what people know of God's creation. And God knows best.

﴿prepared for the God-fearing﴾

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 134:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[134] ﴿Those who spend in ease and in hardship, and those who suppress anger and pardon people. And Allah loves the doers of good.﴾

﴿Those who spend in ease﴾, i.e., in a state of prosperity and affluence; ﴿and in hardship﴾, i.e., in a state of straitness and difficulty. Spending was mentioned first because it is the hardest thing for the self, so opposing it is a towering virtue (p-974). ﴿And those who suppress anger﴾, i.e., those who hold it back within themselves, restraining from carrying it out while having the power to do so, out of caution against transgressing in it beyond what is due.
