He meant: Muhammad ﷺ did not accept my opinion when I ordered him to remain in Medina and not go out from it. ﴿Say: Indeed the affair, all of it, belongs to God﴾, that is: the planning, all of it, belongs to God, for He, exalted, has planned the affair as it proceeded in His prior decree, so there is no averting it.

The Imam Ibn al-Qayyim, may God sanctify his spirit, said: Their intention in their saying: ﴿Is there anything of the affair for us?﴾ and their saying: ﴿If there had been anything of the affair for us, we would not have been killed here﴾ was not an affirmation of destiny and a return of the whole affair to God. Had that been their intention with the first statement, they would not have been blamed for it, and the reply to them with His saying: ﴿Indeed the affair, all of it, belongs to God﴾ would not have been fitting, nor would the source of this statement have been the thought of the Jahiliyyah. For this reason, many of the exegetes said: their false thought here is the denial of destiny, and their thinking that if the affair were in their hands, and the Messenger of God ﷺ and his Companions followed them and listened to them, then killing would not have struck them, and victory and triumph would have been theirs. So God, mighty and majestic, refuted them in this false thought, which is the thought of the Jahiliyyah, the thought attributed to the people of ignorance, who claim, after the execution of the decree and destiny which could not but be executed, that they were able to repel it, and that if the affair had been in their hands the decree would not have been carried out. So God refuted them with His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed the affair, all of it, belongs to God﴾; so nothing occurs except what His decree and destiny preceded, and what His knowledge and prior Book ran by. What God wills comes to be, necessarily, whether people will it or refuse. And what He does not will does not come to be, whether people will it or not. As for what befell you of defeat and killing, it was by His universal command, which there is no way to repel, whether you had any part in the affair or not; and even if you had been in your houses, and killing had been written for some of you, those for whom killing was written would have gone out from their houses to their resting places without fail, whether they had any part in the affair or not. This is among the clearest refutations of the words of the Qadariyyah, the deniers, who permit that what God does not will may occur, and that He may will what does not occur. End.

﴿They conceal within themselves﴾, that is: they harbor it within themselves, or they say among themselves in secret: ﴿what they do not disclose to you﴾, because it is something God does not approve. Then He explained that after summarizing it, saying: ﴿They say: If there had been anything of the affair for us﴾, that is, of what is heard. ﴿We would not have been killed here﴾, that is: we would not have been defeated, or whoever among us was killed would not have been killed, because we would have remained in Medina and not gone out to the enemy. When God, exalted, informed of what they concealed out of ignorance, supposing that caution averts destiny, He commanded him to reply to them with His saying: ﴿Say: Even if you had been in your houses﴾, that is: even if you had unanimously resolved not to leave your dwellings, you and those destined to be killed: ﴿those for whom killing was written would have come forth﴾, that is, had been decreed in the Preserved Tablet: ﴿to their resting places﴾, that is, those in which God had decreed their killing, and they would not have remained in their homes; for He casts into their hearts the impulse to go out, executing His destiny and His inevitable judgment, which cannot be opposed or averted, according to His saying: ﴿No affliction befalls on earth or in yourselves except that it is in a Book before We bring it into being; indeed that is easy for God﴾ [Al-Hadid: 22]. In this there is exaggeration in refuting their false claim, since it did not merely confirm the killing itself, but specified its place as well. And in the expression "their resting places" there is honor and dignity for them that is not hidden from one of sound taste. ﴿And that God may test what is in your breasts﴾, that is: that He may treat you as one being tested, to bring out what is in your breasts of sincerity and hypocrisy, so that He may make it a proof against you. The believer is not increased by that except in faith and submission, while the hypocrite and the one in whose heart is sickness must have what is in his heart appear upon his limbs and tongue. This is a reason for an implied act before it, coupled with other reasons implied before it, indicating their multiplicity. As if it were said: He did what He did for many benefits and that He might test... etc., or for an act implied after it, meaning: and for the aforementioned testing He did what He did, not out of lack of concern for the affairs of the believers. Making these reasons for "came forth" is rejected by sound taste, for what the context requires is the explanation of the wisdom behind what happened that day of hardship and terror, not the explanation of the wisdom of the obligatory coming forth; so Abu al-Su'ud stated. Then God, exalted, mentioned another wisdom with His saying: ﴿And that He may purify what is in your hearts﴾, that is: He may clear it, cleanse it, and refine it. For the hearts are mixed with what contrary to what was deposited in them of faith, Islam, righteousness and piety through the dominance of natural dispositions, the inclination of souls, the sway of habit, the adornment of Satan, and the seizure of heedlessness. If they were left in constant, enduring well-being, they would not be cleared of this admixture nor purified of it; so the wisdom of the Mighty, the Merciful, required that He decree for them of trials and tribulations what is like a bitter medicine for one who has contracted a disease, which, if his physician does not attend to it by removing and purifying it from his body, fear will be for him of corruption and destruction. So His favor upon them through this breaking and defeat, and the killing of those who were killed among them, equals His favor upon them through His help, support and their victory over their enemy. For Him is complete favor upon them in this and that. So Ibn al-Qayyim stated.

Al-Qashani said: Affliction is a whip of God's whips, by which He drives His servants toward Himself, by purifying them from the attributes of their souls, manifesting what is in them of perfections, and cutting them off from creation toward the Truth. For this reason it is entrusted to the prophets, then the best, then the next best. The Messenger of God ﷺ said, explaining its excellence: "No prophet has been harmed as I have been harmed." As if he said: no prophet has been purified as I have been purified. Indeed, well has the one said:

By God, how excellent are the calamities, for they are the rust of the base and the polisher of the free,

for each of them only shows what is in the place of its readiness.

﴿And God is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾, that is: the consciences accompanying them, a promise and a warning. Then God, exalted, informed about the turning away of those among the sincere believers who turned away on that day, and that it was due to their earning, with His saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 155:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, the Exalted:

[155] ﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met, it was only Satan who caused them to slip, because of some of what they had earned. And Allah has already pardoned them. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.﴾

﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away﴾, meaning: from fighting and from confronting the champions. ﴿On the day the two hosts met﴾, meaning: the host of the Muslims and the host of the polytheists. ﴿It was only Satan who caused them to slip﴾, meaning: he led them into slipping through his deception, despite Allah's promise of victory. ﴿Because of some of what they had earned﴾, meaning: because of the ill effect of some of the sins they had committed, such as abandoning the position (al-markaz) and inclining toward the spoils of war (al-ghanima), despite the prohibition against it. So they were denied divine support and strength of heart. Ibn al-Qayyim said: Their deeds became a host against them, through which their enemy grew stronger. Indeed, deeds are a host for the servant and also a host against him, and the servant necessarily has, at every moment, a raiding detachment (sariyya) from his own self that either defeats him or supports him. He supplies his enemy with his deeds from a direction he thinks he is fighting with them, and he sends to it a detachment that raids him together with his enemy from a direction he thinks he is raiding his enemy. So the servant's deeds drive him by force toward what they require of good and evil. The servant does not perceive this, or he perceives it and feigns blindness. Thus a person's flight from his enemy, while he is able to resist, is only through a host of his own deed, which Satan sent to him and through which he made him slip. Then He, glory be to Him, informed that He had pardoned them by His words: ﴿And Allah has already pardoned them﴾, meaning: through their apology and remorse, because this flight was not out of hypocrisy. And there is no doubt that it was a passing matter, which Allah pardoned, so the courage and steadfastness of faith returned to its place and foundation. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing﴾, meaning: He forgives sin, shows forbearance toward His creation, and overlooks their faults.(p-1014)

﴿O you who have believed, do not be like those who disbelieved and said of their brothers when they traveled through the land or were away at war, "If they had remained with us, they would not have died or been killed," so that Allah may make that a regret in their hearts. And Allah gives life and causes death, and Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, do not be like those who disbelieved﴾: they are the hypocrites, who said, ﴿If we had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 154]. ﴿And said of their brothers when they traveled through the land﴾, meaning they journeyed in it for trade and were struck by drowning or death. ﴿Or were away at war﴾, meaning their brothers, ﴿ghuzzan﴾, the plural of ghazin (one who goes on a military expedition), and were struck by collapse or death. ﴿If they had remained with us﴾, meaning residing, ﴿they would not have died or been killed.﴾

Abu al-Su'ud said: The purpose of the prohibition is not merely to avoid resembling them in uttering this statement, but in believing its content and acting upon its implication.

I say: Rather, the verse conveys both matters: namely, first and foremost, guarding the intended belief, and guarding speech from what leads to misguiding people and undermines the divine station, as the Sunnah has explained, and as I will mention in the following note.

His saying, ﴿so that Allah may make that﴾, meaning the statement, ﴿a regret in their hearts﴾, is connected to (qalu, "they said"), with the lam being the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), similar to its use in ﴿so that it may become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. That is, they said it and believed it, and as a result it became a regret in their hearts. The purpose of the stated cause is to show that no benefit whatsoever results from it. ﴿And Allah gives life and causes death﴾ is a refutation of their false statement, following the explanation of its harm. That is, He alone is the one who affects life and death, without residence or travel having any role in that. For He may give life to the traveler and the warrior even though they plunge into the sources of destruction, and He may cause the resident to die even though he possesses the means of safety.

It is related from Khalid ibn al-Walid, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said at his death: "There is not a span of my body without a blow or a thrust in it, and here I am dying as a camel dies. May the eyes of the cowards never sleep!" ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ is a warning to the believers against resembling those who were mentioned.

Some of the exegetes said: The benefit of the verse is that it is not permissible to imitate the disbelievers. Al-Hakim said: Sometimes that imitation may amount to disbelief. The verse also indicates that the obligation of jihad does not lapse out of fear of being killed.

Note (tanbih):

The verse indicates the obligation to guard speech against words resembling the expressions of the polytheists, words that contradict the Islamic creed, as already mentioned. Imam Ibn al-Qayyim, in Zad al-Ma'ad, devoted a chapter to the Prophet's (ﷺ) guidance on guarding speech and choosing words. He said:

The Prophet (ﷺ) would choose his address carefully and select for his community the finest, most beautiful and gentlest words, and the furthest from the words of the people of harshness, coarseness and obscenity. Until he said: Among that is "the Prophet's (ﷺ) prohibition of the saying of one who, after a matter has passed, says: 'If only I had done such and such.' He said: 'It opens the work of Satan.'" He guided him to what is more beneficial to him than this expression, which is to say: "Allah decreed, and what He willed He did." That is because his saying "If only I had done such and such" will not bring about for him what has escaped him, or prevent him from falling into what he has fallen into; it is a statement that yields no benefit at all. For it does not turn him toward what lies ahead of his affair, nor does it remove his stumble by means of "if only." Within "if only" lies the claim that had the matter been as he assumed in his own mind, it would have been other than what Allah decreed, ordained and willed. For what has occurred of what one wishes were otherwise has occurred only by Allah's decree, qadar (divine predestination) and will. So when he says, "If only I had done such and such, it would have been different from what occurred," this is impossible, since the opposite of what is decreed and determined is impossible. Thus his statement contains falsehood, ignorance and impossibility. And even if it is free from denying divine decree, it is not free from contradicting his own saying: "If only I had done it, I would have repelled (p-1016) what was decreed for me."

If it is said: There is in this no rejection of divine decree and no denial of it, since those means he wishes for are themselves part of the decree. He is saying: "If I had been granted success in this decree, that decree would have been repelled from me," for decree is repelled by decree, just as the decree of illness is repelled by medicine, the decree of sins by repentance, and the decree of an enemy by jihad, and both are from the decree. It is said: This is true, but it benefits only before the disliked decree occurs. When it has occurred, there is no way to repel it. And if there is a way to repel it or lighten it by another decree, then that is more appropriate than his saying, "If only I had done it." Rather, his duty in this situation is to face forward toward the action by which it may be repelled or lightened, and not to wish for what there is no hope of occurring, for that is pure incapacity. Allah blames incapacity, and loves and commands shrewdness (kays). Shrewdness is engaging in the means which Allah has linked to their effects, beneficial to the servant in his livelihood and his hereafter. This opens the work of good and of command. As for incapacity, it opens the work of Satan. For when one is unable to do what benefits him and turns to vain wishes, saying "If it had been such and such" or "If only I had done such and such," he opens the work of Satan, for its gate is incapacity and laziness. This is why the Prophet (ﷺ) sought refuge from both of them. And they are the key to every evil, and from them arise anxiety, grief, miserliness, the burden of debt and the domination of men. All of them originate from incapacity and laziness, and their heading is "if only." Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "For 'if only' opens the work of Satan." The one who wishes is among the most incapable and the most destitute of people, for wishing is the capital of the bankrupt. Incapacity is the key to every evil, and the root of all sins is incapacity, for the servant is unable to obtain the means of acts of obedience, and the means that would turn him away from sins and would come between him and them, so he falls into sins.

Thus this noble hadith gathers, in his (ﷺ) seeking refuge, the roots of evil, its branches, its beginnings, its ends, its sources and its origins. It comprises eight qualities, each two of which are paired. He said: "I seek refuge in You from anxiety and grief," and these two are paired. For a disliked matter that strikes the heart is divided, according to its cause, into two kinds. Its cause is either a past matter, which produces grief, or the expectation of a future matter, which produces anxiety, and both come from incapacity. For what has passed is not repelled by grief, but by contentment, praise, patience, faith in the decree, and the servant's saying: (p-1017) "Allah decreed, and what He willed He did." And what lies ahead is not repelled by anxiety either. Rather, either he has a means of repelling it, and so he should not be incapable of it, or he has no means of repelling it, and so he should not panic over it, but put on its garment, take its equipment, prepare its proper preparation, and shelter in a fortress of tawhid, trust in God, submission before the Lord, surrender to Him, and contentment with Him as Lord in everything. He should not accept Him as Lord only in what he loves and not in what he dislikes. If he is like this, he has not accepted Him as Lord absolutely, and the Lord will not accept him as a servant absolutely. Anxiety and grief benefit the servant not at all; their harm is greater than their benefit. For they weaken resolve, enfeeble the heart, and stand between the servant and striving in what benefits him. They cut off his path of journey, or turn him backward, or hinder and stop him, or veil him from the knowledge which, whenever he sees it, makes him press forward and strive in his journey. They are a heavy burden on the back of the traveler. Indeed, if anxiety and grief prevent him from his desires and wills that harm him in his livelihood and his hereafter, he benefits from them in this respect. This is part of the wisdom of the Mighty, the Wise: that He has set these two soldiers upon the hearts that turn away from Him, that are empty of His love, fear, hope, repentance toward Him, reliance upon Him, intimacy with Him, flight to Him and attachment to Him, so that He may turn them back by the trials He sends upon them of worries, sorrows, griefs and heart-pains, away from many of their sins and their destructive desires. These hearts are in a prison of Hellfire in this world. If good is intended for them, their share of the prison of Hellfire in the hereafter is lessened, and they will remain in this prison until they are freed into the open space of tawhid, turning to God, intimacy with Him, and placing His love in the place where the heart's thoughts and whisperings move, so that the remembrance of Him, His love, His fear, His hope, joy in Him and delight in His remembrance become what dominates the heart and prevails over it. Whoever loses this loses his strength, and there is no stability for him except by it, and no survival for him without it. There is no way to free the heart from these pains, which are the greatest of its diseases and the most corrupting of them, except by this. There is no power or means except by Allah alone, for none brings one to Him except Him, none brings good deeds except Him, none turns away evil deeds except Him, and none guides to Him except Him. When He wills a servant for a matter, He prepares him for it (p-1018): from Him is the bringing into being, from Him is the equipping, and from Him is the aid. When He establishes him in a station, whatever station it may be, He establishes him in it by His praise, and by His wisdom He establishes him in it, and no one else is fitting for it, and no one else is suitable for it. There is no preventer of what Allah gives, and no giver of what He withholds. He does not withhold from His servant a right that belongs to the servant, so that his withholding would be an injustice. Rather, He withholds so that he may seek a way to Him through what He loves, so that He may give him, and so that he may humble himself and abase himself before Him, flatter Him, and give his poverty toward Him its due right, such that he witnesses in every particle of his inner and outer being a complete need of Him, through the successive breaths. This is what is actually the case, even if he does not witness it. Thus He does not withhold from His servant what the servant needs out of stinginess, nor out of any diminishment of His treasuries, nor out of selfishness toward him in what is the servant's right. Rather, He withholds to bring him back to Himself, to honor him by humbling himself before Him, to enrich him through need of Him, to mend him through brokenness before Him, and to make him taste, through the bitterness of withholding, the sweetness of submission and the pleasure of poverty. He clothes him in the robe of servanthood, and by dismissing him He appoints him to the noblest of offices, and He makes him witness His wisdom in His power, His mercy in His might, and His kindness and gentleness in His subduing. His withholding is a gift, His removal is an appointment, His punishment is discipline, His trial is love and a gift, and His giving power over his enemies is a driver that drives him toward Him. In sum, nothing is fitting for the servant except what he has been established in. His wisdom and His praise have established him in the station that suits no one else, and it is not right for him to pass beyond it. End quote.

Then Allah (exalted be He) pointed out that death in the way of Allah is not one of the things that necessitates regret so as to be feared. Rather, it is one of the things that necessitates joy and delight, so He said:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[157] ﴿And if you are killed in the way of Allah or die, forgiveness from Allah and mercy are better than what they accumulate.﴾

﴿And if you are killed in the way of Allah or die﴾, i.e., in it, without fighting: ﴿forgiveness from Allah﴾, i.e., for your sins that will reach you; ﴿and mercy are better than what they accumulate﴾, i.e., the disbelievers, of the benefits of this world and its fleeting pleasures.

(p-1019)

**The interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:**

[158] ﴿And if you die or are killed, to Allah you will be gathered.﴾

﴿And if you die or are killed﴾ in whatever manner, according to the prior decree: ﴿to Allah﴾, that is, to the One who causes you to die, not to anyone else: ﴿you will be gathered﴾, so He will recompense you for your deeds.

**Subtleties:**

**The first:** The grammarian exegetes (nuhat al-mufassirin) went on at length, in His saying, ﴿And they said of their brothers when they journeyed [in the land]...﴾ [3:156], about the grammatical aspects of (إذا) (idhā) here. It may readily occur that the proper particle is (إذ) (idh) and not (إذا), since the verb it governs, (قالوا) (qālū), is in the past tense, whereas (إذا) is an adverb of the future. Some said that (إذا) is used to narrate a past situation, and some said it is for continuity. It was also said that (كفروا) (kafarū) and (قالوا) (qālū) are meant in the future sense, and in each of these views there are disputes and far-fetched interpretations. The truth is that (إذا) may also be used for the past. Al-Majd al-Fayruzabadi said: "(إذا) comes for the past, as in His saying: ﴿And when they saw a trade or amusement, they dispersed to it﴾ [62:11], so there is no difficulty."

Al-Razi transmitted from Qutrub that each of (إذ) (idh) and (إذا) (idhā) may be used in the place of the other. Al-Razi said: "What Qutrub said is a fine statement, because if we permit establishing language by an unknown line of poetry transmitted from an unknown poet, then establishing it by the Mighty Qur'an is all the more permissible. Then he said: I often see the grammarians bewildered in establishing the expressions that occur in the Qur'an. When they cite an unknown line in support of it, they rejoice in it, and I am greatly astonished at them. For if they make the occurrence of that unknown line in agreement with it a proof of its soundness, then making the occurrence of the Qur'an with it a proof of its soundness is more fitting." End of quotation.

**The second:** The passive form with a damma on the mim in His saying, ﴿or died﴾ [3:157], is the original, because the verb from it is (يموت) (yamūtu). It is also read with a kasra, and that is a dialect of the Tayy tribe. It is said (مات يمات) (māta yamātu), like (خاف يخاف) (khāfa yakhāfu). Just as you say (خفت) (khiftu), you say (مت) (mittu).

**The third:** He placed killing before dying in the first case, because it carries more reward and is greater in the sight of Allah. Thus the arrangement of forgiveness and mercy upon it is stronger. He placed dying before killing in the second case, because it is more. The two are equal in the gathering.

(p-1020)

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[159] ﴿So by mercy from Allah, you were gentle with them. And had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you. So pardon them, ask forgiveness for them, consult them in the matter, and when you have decided, rely upon Allah. Indeed, Allah loves those who rely upon Him.﴾

﴿So by mercy from Allah, you were gentle with them﴾, that is, toward those who turned away from you when they returned to you after the defeat, and toward the believers in general, as He said, ﴿to the believers, kind and merciful﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128]. The ما (ma) is either an extra particle for emphasis or indefinite. رَحْمَةٍ (rahmah) is a substitute (badal) from it, clarifying its vagueness. The tanwin is for magnification, meaning: you were not gentle with this extraordinary gentleness, which goes beyond custom, despite what their conduct caused of anger that would normally call for harshness and force, especially with the objection of those who objected to what he had advised. It was only by means of a great mercy. ﴿And had you been harsh﴾, that is, of bad character and rough speech, ﴿hard-hearted﴾, that is, cruel and severe, dealing with them with violence and harshness, ﴿they would have scattered﴾, that is, dispersed, ﴿from around you﴾, so they would not have remained with you, and your call would not have been completed. But Allah made you easy, lenient, open-hearted, soft, gentle, kind, merciful, and compassionate. ﴿So pardon them﴾, that is, for what they neglected of your right, as Allah pardoned them. ﴿And ask forgiveness for them﴾, completing the compassion toward them. ﴿And consult them in the matter﴾, that is, the matter of war and other things, to win their affection, to comfort their hearts, to benefit from their opinions, and to pave the way for the practice of consultation in the community. Al-ʿAllamah al-Razi has offered other aspects regarding the wisdom of His command to him, peace and blessings be upon him, to consult them, among them: that he, ﷺ, although he was the most perfect of people in intellect, the knowledge of creatures is limited, so it is not far-fetched that a person may think of aspects of benefit that did not occur to him. Especially in matters of worldly affairs, for he, ﷺ, said: "You are more knowledgeable of your worldly affairs." Among them: the command to consult them was not because he, ﷺ, needed them, but because when he consulted them, each one of them strove to extract the most appropriate course in that event, so the pure souls would come to agree and concur upon achieving the best of the courses in it, and the agreement of pure souls upon one thing helps in achieving it. This is the secret behind gathering for the prayers, and it is the secret behind the congregational prayer being superior to the prayer of the one praying alone. End of quote.

It is established that he, ﷺ, consulted his Companions on several matters, among them: he consulted them on the day of Badr regarding going out toward the caravan. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, if you were to lead us to the sea's edge, we would plunge into it with you, and if you were to take us to Bark al-Ghimad, we would go with you. We will not say to you what the people of Moses said to Moses: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting right here﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 24]. Rather, we say: go, and we are with you, before you and behind you, and on your right and your left, fighting." He also consulted them about where the camp should be, until al-Mundhir ibn ʿAmr advised advancing ahead of the people. He consulted them at Uhud on whether to remain in Medina or go out to the enemy, and the majority of them advised going out to them, so he went out to them. He consulted them on the day of the Trench regarding making peace with the confederates by giving them a third of Medina's produce that year, but al-Sa'dan, Saʿd ibn Muʿadh and Saʿd ibn ʿUbadah, refused that, so he abandoned it. He consulted them on the day of al-Hudaybiyyah about whether to attack the children of the polytheists, and al-Siddiq said to him: "We have not come to fight anyone, we have only come as pilgrims (ʿumrah)," and he accepted what he said.

He, ﷺ, also said in the story of the slander: "Advise me, O Muslims, concerning people who have slandered my family and accused them. By Allah, I know nothing but good about my family. And they have accused a man, by Allah, of whom I know nothing but good." He consulted ʿAli and Usamah about separating from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her. So he, ﷺ, used to consult them in wars and similar matters. This was cited by al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him.

Al-Khafaji said: The verse contains guidance toward ijtihad (independent reasoning, the exertion of judgment in legal matters) and its permissibility in his presence, ﷺ. Al-Razi said: It indicates that he, ﷺ, was commanded to exercise ijtihad when revelation did not descend upon him, and ijtihad is strengthened by debate and discussion, so for this reason he was commanded to consult. End of quote.

Some exegetes said: The fruit of the verse is the obligation to adhere to noble character, especially for one who calls to Allah, exalted is He, and enjoins good: ﴿Then when you have decided﴾, that is, after consultation, upon a matter about which your soul has become settled, ﴿rely upon Allah﴾ for help in carrying out what you have resolved, not upon the consultation or those consulted. Al-Razi said: The verse indicates that tawakkul (trust in Allah) does not mean that a person neglects himself, as some ignorant people say. Otherwise the command to consult would contradict the command to rely upon Allah. Rather, tawakkul is that a person observes the apparent causes, but does not depend upon them in his heart; he depends upon the protection of the Truth. ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who rely upon Him.﴾

**On the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:**

[160] ﴿If Allah helps you, none can overcome you; and if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him? And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾

﴿If Allah helps you﴾ as He helped you on the Day of Badr; ﴿none can overcome you; and if He forsakes you﴾ as was done on the Day of Uhud; ﴿who is there that can help you after Him?﴾ is a rhetorical interrogation of denial, implying the absence of any helper, in essence and in attribute, and in the manner of emphasis. This is a reminder that the whole matter belongs to Allah, an encouragement to obedience, and an indication of what earns them God Exalted's help and support; and a warning against disobedience and against what makes them deserving of punishment through abandonment. Thus says al-Zamakhshari in (al-Kashshaf). ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾ meaning: let the believers single out their Lord for reliance and committing their affairs to Him, because they know that there is no helper besides Him, and because their faith necessitates and requires that - thus says al-Zamakhshari in (al-Kashshaf).

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[161] ﴿It is not for a prophet to embezzle. And whoever embezzles will bring what he embezzled on the Day of Resurrection. Then every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged.﴾

﴿It is not for a prophet to embezzle﴾ is read with the active voice (*al-bina' lil-ma'lum*), meaning: it is not proper or fitting for any prophet among the prophets to betray (*yakhunu*) in the spoils (*al-maghnam*), given the station of prophethood and the infallibility (*'ismah*) of the prophets from all base qualities, and from the influence of the promptings of the self and of Satan upon them. It is also read with the passive voice (*al-bina' lil-majhul*), meaning: it is not proper that he be attributed with embezzlement (*al-ghulul*) and be accused of betrayal. Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: This verse, ﴿It is not for a prophet to embezzle﴾, was revealed concerning a red woolen cloak (*qatifah hamra'*) that was missing on the day of Badr. Some people said: Perhaps the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took it. So Allah revealed: ﴿It is not for a prophet﴾, the verse. Al-Tirmidhi said: Hasan gharib. Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it from Ibn Abbas, with the wording: The hypocrites accused the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of something that was lost, so Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿It is not for a prophet﴾, the verse. This is a declaration of the exalted station of the Prophet (ﷺ) and a reminder of his infallibility.

Then He alluded to the threat concerning embezzlement with His saying: ﴿And whoever embezzles will bring what he embezzled on the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning: the very thing itself, carried upon his back, so that he is disgraced at the place of gathering (*al-mahshar*), as al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood among us one day and mentioned embezzlement, magnifying it and magnifying its matter, then said: "Let me not find any one of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with a camel upon his neck, making a groaning sound, saying: O Messenger of Allah, help me! I will say: I have no power to help you; I have already conveyed (the message) to you. Let me not find any one of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with a horse upon his neck, neighing, saying: O Messenger of Allah, help me! I will say: I have no power to help you; I have already conveyed (the message) to you. Let me not find any one of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with a sheep upon his neck, bleating, saying: O Messenger of Allah, help me! I will say: I have no power to help you; I have already conveyed (the message) to you. Let me not find any one of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with a soul upon his neck, crying out, saying: O Messenger of Allah, help me! I will say: I have no power to help you; I have already conveyed (the message) to you. Let me not find any one of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with cloths fluttering, saying: O Messenger of Allah, help me! I will say: I have no power to help you; I have already conveyed (the message) to you. Let me not find any one of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with gold upon his neck, saying: O Messenger of Allah, help me! I will say: I have no power to help you; I have already conveyed (the message)." The wording is that of Muslim.

(p-١٠٢٥) Al-Bukhari narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who said: A man called Kirkirah was in charge of the baggage of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he died. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "He is in the Fire." They went to look at him and found a cloak that he had embezzled. And from Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani, that a man among the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) died on the day of Khaybar, and they mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said: "Pray over your companion." The faces of the people changed because of that, so he said: "Your companion embezzled in the way of Allah." We searched his belongings and found beads from the beads of the Jews, not worth two dirhams." Narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i.

Abdullah ibn al-Imam Ahmad narrated from Ubadah ibn al-Samit that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to take a tuft from the side of a camel from the spoils, and say: "I have no more share in it than one of you has. Beware of embezzlement, for embezzlement is a disgrace for its perpetrator on the Day of Resurrection. Return the thread and the needle and whatever is above that. Strive in the way of Allah, the near and the far, in residence and in travel, for jihad is one of the gates of Paradise. Allah, blessed and exalted, saves by it from distress and grief. Establish the limits of Allah, near and far, and do not let the blame of any blamer deter you in (the matter of) Allah." Ibn Majah narrated part of it.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Abdullah ibn Abbas, who said: Umar ibn al-Khattab related to me, saying: "When the day of Khaybar came, a group of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) approached and said: So-and-so is a martyr. So-and-so is a martyr. Until they came upon a man and said: So-and-so is a martyr. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'No! I saw him during the day in a striped garment (*burdah*) which he had embezzled, or a cloak.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O son of al-Khattab! Go and proclaim among the people: Indeed, none will enter Paradise except the believers.'" He said: "So I went out and proclaimed: Beware, none will enter Paradise except the believers." Muslim and al-Tirmidhi also narrated it likewise.

Abu Dawud narrated from Samurah ibn Jundub, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) acquired booty, he would order Bilal to call out among the people, and they would bring their spoils, and he would take the fifth (*khumus*) from it and distribute it. Then a man came after that with a halter of hair and said: O Messenger of Allah, this is from what we took from the booty. He said: 'Did you hear Bilal call three times?' He said: Yes. He said: 'What prevented you from coming?' He made an excuse. He said: 'You will bring it yourself on the Day of Resurrection, and I will not accept it from you.'"

Note of caution: Some exegetes took the bringing of the embezzled thing on the Day of Resurrection to be a metaphor for bringing its sin, using the thing embezzled to stand for the sin it entails, metaphorically. Abu Muslim said: The meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, keeps account of this embezzlement against him, will punish him for it on the Day of Resurrection, and will repay him, because nothing is hidden from Him. Al-Ka'bi (Abu al-Qasim) said: The meaning is that he will become notorious for it, like the notoriety of one who carries that thing. Al-Razi refuted both of them, saying: This interpretation is possible, but the principle to be relied upon in the science of the Qur'an is that the wording must be applied to its literal meaning, unless there is evidence preventing that, and here there is no obstacle to the apparent meaning, so it is necessary to affirm it. End of quotation. Among what supports it is his (ﷺ) saying: "It has a groaning, it has a neighing..." etc., which is apparent in its literal sense, adding to the punishment.

(p-١٠٢٧) ﴿Then every soul will be paid in full what it earned﴾: it will be given the full recompense for what it earned. He generalized the ruling and did not say "then what he earned will be paid in full," so that it would serve as a proof of the intended point and as an emphasis upon it. For when every earner is recompensed for his deed, the embezzler, with the greatness of his crime in this regard, is more deserving (of that recompense). ﴿And they﴾, i.e., the people implied by "every soul," ﴿will not be wronged﴾: the reward of the obedient will not be diminished, nor will the punishment of the disobedient be increased.

Commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted:

[162] ﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah like one who incurs the wrath of Allah, and whose refuge is Hell? And wretched is the destination.﴾

﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah﴾ through obedience; ﴿like one who incurs﴾ returns, i.e., goes back; ﴿with wrath from Allah﴾ because of sins, like the one who defrauds (al-ghall) and whoever is similar to him; ﴿and whose refuge is Hell. And wretched is the destination.﴾

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 163:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[163] ﴿They are of varying degrees in the sight of Allah, and Allah is Seeing of what they do.﴾

﴿They are of varying degrees in the sight of Allah﴾ means: they are distinct levels, varying in rank. It is an eloquent metaphor (tashbih baligh), and the point of comparison is the difference in their states concerning reward and punishment, like degrees (darajat) that differ in height and depth.

Al-Qashani said: That is, each of the people of good pleasure (ridwan) and the people of displeasure (sukht) have degrees that differ, or they vary in the manner of the differing of degrees.

﴿And Allah is Seeing of what they do﴾ means: of their deeds, so He will recompense them according to them.

(p-1028)

The discussion of His saying, the Exalted:

[164] ﴿Certainly did Allah confer favor upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from themselves, reciting to them His verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom, although they were before that in clear error.﴾

﴿Certainly did Allah confer favor﴾ means He bestowed blessing. ﴿Upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from themselves﴾ means from their own kind, an Arab like them, so that they could converse with him, ask him, sit with him, and benefit from him. Since only the people of Islam benefited from this blessing, they were singled out for mention. Otherwise, his sending (peace and blessings be upon him) is a kindness to all the worlds, as the Exalted said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya: 107]. ﴿Reciting to them His verses﴾ means the Qur'an, after they had been people of ignorance, to whom nothing of revelation had come. ﴿And purifying them﴾ means He cleanses them from sins and polytheism through his call. ﴿And teaching them the Book﴾ means the Qur'an. ﴿And wisdom﴾ means the Sunnah (the Prophet's sayings, deeds and approvals). ﴿Although they were before that﴾ means before his sending and purification (peace and blessings be upon him): ﴿in clear error﴾ means evident error, in worshipping idols, eating abominations, the aggression of some of them against others, and other things. Through his sending (peace and blessings be upon him) they were transferred from darkness to light, and they became the most excellent of nations in knowledge, asceticism and worship. Thus the favor of Allah upon them through this became great.

Al-Razi said: In His saying, the Exalted, ﴿from themselves﴾ there is another aspect of favor, namely that it became an honor for the Arabs and a source of pride for them, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and your people, and you will be questioned﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 44]. This is because the pride in Abraham (peace be upon him) was shared among the Jews, the Christians and the Arabs, and the earlier peoples used to take pride in Moses, Jesus, the Torah and the Gospel, whereas the Arabs had nothing equivalent to that. When Allah sent Muhammad and revealed the Qur'an to him, the Arabs' honor became greater than the honor of all other nations. (End of quotation.)

Then He, glorified is He, reiterated to them that what befell them was only because of themselves and due to their own deeds, so He said:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[165] ﴿Why is it that when a calamity struck you, although you had inflicted twice as much (on them), you say, "How is this?" Say, "It is from yourselves." Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.﴾

﴿Why is it that when a calamity struck you, although you had inflicted twice as much (on them), you say, "How is this?"﴾ The hamza is for rebuke (*taqri'*) and affirmation (*taqrir*). The wāw is conjunctive, linking the sentence to what preceded concerning the story of Uhud, or to an elided element such as: "Did you do such-and-such, and you said..." The word "لمّا" (*lammā*) is a temporal adverb whose object is the noun "أصابتكم" (*aṣābatkum*), meaning: "when a calamity struck you," and the calamity was the killing of seventy of you on the Day of Uhud, while you had inflicted double that upon them on the Day of Badr, through the killing of seventy of them and the capture of seventy. The meaning is: "From where is this, when Allah had promised us victory?" ﴿Say, "It is from yourselves."﴾ That is, it is from what your own souls had committed of disobeying the command by abandoning the position (*al-markaz*), for the promise had been conditional upon steadfastness and obedience.

Ibn al-Qayyim said: He, glorified is He, mentioned this very same matter in a more general form in the Meccan surah, saying: ﴿Whatever calamity strikes you is because of what your hands have earned, and He pardons much.﴾ [al-Shura: 30] And He said: ﴿Whatever good reaches you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.﴾ [al-Nisa: 79] Here, the good and the evil are the blessing and the calamity. The blessing is from Allah, which He bestowed upon you as a favour, while the calamity arises only from your own self and your deeds. The first is His bounty, and the second is His justice. The servant moves between His bounty and His justice: His bounty flows over him, His judgment takes effect in him, and His decree concerning him is just. He concluded the first verse with His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent,﴾ after His saying: ﴿Say, "It is from yourselves,"﴾ to inform them of the comprehensiveness of His power together with His justice, and that He is Just and Powerful. In this is the affirmation of divine decree (*qadar*) and of causation (*sabab*). He mentioned the cause and attributed it to their souls, and He mentioned the comprehensiveness of power and attributed it to Himself. The first negates compulsion (*jabr*), and the second negates the view that divine decree is nullified. This resembles His saying: ﴿for whoever wills among you to take a straight path﴾ [al-Takwir: 28] ﴿And you do not will unless Allah wills, Lord of the worlds.﴾ [al-Takwir: 29] In the mention of His power here there is a subtle point, which is that this matter is in His hand and under His power, and that He is the One who, if He willed, would have turned it away from you. So do not seek the removal of its like from anyone else, nor rely upon other than Him. He clarified this meaning and made it fully clear with His saying:

[p. 1030]

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[166] ﴿And whatever befell you on the day the two hosts met, it was by permission of Allah, and so that He might make evident the believers.﴾

﴿And whatever befell you on the day the two hosts met﴾: the two hosts were the Muslims and the polytheists on the Day of Uhud. ﴿By permission of Allah﴾ means: it occurred by His decree and by His allowing the disbelievers (to act). Thus the permission here is the permission of creation and decree (al-idhn al-kawni al-qadari), not the legislative, religious permission (al-idhn al-shar'i al-dini), like His saying about magic: ﴿And they could not harm anyone thereby except by permission of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102]. Then He informed of the wisdom of this decree in His saying: ﴿and so that He might make evident the believers﴾.

(p-1031)

The Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[167] ﴿And that He might make evident those who were hypocrites. It was said to them, "Come, fight in the way of Allah or [at least] repel [the enemy]." They said, "If we had known [there would be] fighting, we would have followed you." They were nearer to disbelief that day than to faith, saying with their mouths what was not in their hearts. And Allah is most knowing of what they conceal.﴾

﴿And that He might make evident those who were hypocrites﴾ That is: that He might make the believers know the hypocrites with knowledge of direct observation and sight, by which one of the two groups is distinguished from the other with a clear distinction. ﴿And it was said to them﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "who were hypocrites" (nāfaqū), included with it within the scope of the relative clause (ṣilah). Or it is an independent statement: ﴿"Come, fight in the way of Allah or repel [the enemy]"﴾, meaning: if you will not fight for the sake of Allah, the Exalted, then fight in defense of yourselves and your wealth. ﴿They said, "If we had known fighting, we would have followed you."﴾ That is: but it is nothing other than casting oneself into destruction. ﴿They﴾ that is, by this statement, ﴿were nearer to disbelief﴾ outwardly, ﴿that day than to faith﴾ outwardly, although there was no faith for them in the inward at all.

Two benefits:

The first: Ibn Kathir said: They used it as evidence that a person may be subject to changing states, so that he is in a state nearer to disbelief and in a state nearer to faith.

The second: al-Wahidi said: This verse is evidence that whoever utters the word of tawhid does not become a disbeliever, and the statement of his takfir is not absolutely applied; because He, the Exalted, did not absolutely apply the description of disbelief to them, although they were disbelievers, due to their outward profession of "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." End of quotation.

﴿saying with their mouths what is not in their hearts﴾ That is: they display the opposite of what they conceal; their hearts do not agree with their tongues regarding faith. His words, ﴿with their mouths﴾, are an emphasis in the manner of: ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38]. ﴿And Allah is most knowing of what they conceal.﴾

The explanation of His words, exalted is He:

[168] ﴿Those who said of their brothers while they themselves sat back, "If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed." Say, "Avert from yourselves death, if you are truthful."﴾

﴿Those who said of their brothers﴾ i.e., concerning their relatives among the slain of Uhud. ﴿while they themselves sat back﴾ i.e., while they had remained behind from them, forsaking them. ﴿"If they had obeyed us"﴾ i.e., in returning. ﴿"they would not have been killed"﴾ just as we were not killed. ﴿Say﴾ as if you claim the ability to repel death. ﴿"Avert﴾ i.e., repel. ﴿from yourselves death"﴾ i.e., for it is nearer to you than to them. ﴿"if you are truthful"﴾ in your claim that caution averts death. The meaning is: your not being killed was because it had not been decreed for you, not because you repelled it by sitting back, while it had been decreed for you; for that is something with no way to it.

Ibn al-Qayyim said: Among the wisdom in God's decree in this incident was His making the hypocrites speak what was in their souls, so that the believers heard it, heard God's refutation of them and His answer to them, and came to know the roots of hypocrisy, what it leads to, and how its bearer is deprived of the happiness of this world and the Hereafter. So the corruption of this world and the Hereafter returns upon him. How many are the wisdoms within this story, far-reaching, and the blessings upon the believers, abundant! And how many are the warnings and frightenings in it, the guidance and admonition, and the explanation of the causes of good and evil and their outcomes and final ends!

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 169:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[169] ﴿And do not think of those who have been killed in the way of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for.﴾

﴿And do not think of those who have been killed in the way of Allah as dead﴾ is a resumed statement, brought to clarify that the killing which they fear and warn people against is not something to be feared; rather, it is among the most noble goals for which the competitors vie. This follows the explanation that caution neither benefits nor avails. That is: do not think of them as dead, their spirits having been rendered inactive. ﴿Rather﴾ they are ﴿alive﴾, above the life of this world, because they are brought near ﴿with their Lord﴾ (p-1033), since they offered their spirits to Him. This does not mean that their spirits remain and return to Him, for the spirits of others share in that; rather, it means that they are ﴿provided for﴾ with the provision of the living, not a figurative provision but a real one. As Ibn 'Abbas related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "When your brothers were struck at Uhud, Allah placed their spirits in the bellies of green birds that go to the rivers of Paradise, eat from its fruits, and take shelter in lamps of gold in the shade of the Throne. When they found the goodness of their drink and food and the excellence of their resting place, they said: 'Would that our brothers knew what Allah has done for us, so that they would not shun jihad or shrink from war.' Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: 'I will convey it on your behalf,' and Allah revealed these verses: ﴿And do not think...﴾." Thus did Imam Ahmad narrate it; Abu Dawud and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak also narrated it. Muslim related from Masruq who said: "We asked 'Abd Allah about this verse: ﴿And do not think of those who have been killed...﴾ etc. He said: 'We have indeed asked about that, and he said: Their spirits are in the bellies of green birds, which have lamps hung from the Throne; they roam in Paradise wherever they wish, then they return to those lamps. Their Lord looked down upon them with a look and said: Do you desire anything? They said: What could we desire, while we roam in Paradise wherever we wish?! He did this to them three times. When they saw that they would not be left alone unless they were asked, they said: O Lord! We wish that our spirits be returned to our bodies until we are killed in Your way once more. When He saw that they had no need, they were left alone.'"

Imam Ahmad narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The martyrs are at a river called Bariq at the gate of Paradise, in which there is a green dome; their provision comes out to them from Paradise morning and evening." Ahmad alone narrated it, and Ibn Jurayj narrated it with a good chain.

Ibn Kathir said: It seems that the martyrs are of several categories: among them are those whose spirits roam in Paradise, and among them (p-1034) are those who remain at this river at the gate of Paradise. It is possible that the endpoint of their journey is this river, where they gather, and their provision is brought to them there in the morning and evening, and Allah knows best. Then he said: We have related in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad a hadith containing good news for every believer, that his spirit will be in Paradise, roaming there also, eating from its fruits, seeing the freshness and joy within it, and witnessing the honour that Allah has prepared for it. It is with a sound, strong, and mighty chain, in which three of the four Imams, the leaders of the followed schools, are united. Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated it from Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, from Malik ibn Anas al-Asbahi, may Allah have mercy on him, from al-Zuhri, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ka'b ibn Malik, from his father, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The soul of the believer is only a bird that feeds on the trees of Paradise until Allah, Blessed and Exalted, returns it to its body on the day He resurrects him." Its statement "ya'laqu" means: it eats. In this hadith, the spirit of the believer is in the form of a bird in Paradise; as for the spirits of the martyrs, as has preceded, they are in the crops of green birds, so they are like stars in comparison with the spirits of believers in general, for they fly by themselves. So we ask Allah, the Generous, the Bestower, to make us die in faith. End of quotation.

Note:

Al-Wahidi said: The most sound view concerning the life of the martyrs is what has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ), that "their spirits are in the bellies of green birds, and they are provided for, eat, and enjoy themselves."

Al-Baydawi said: The verse indicates that the human being is other than the perceptible physical frame; rather, he is a substance perceived by its own essence, which does not perish with the ruin of the body, and whose perception, contemplation, and enjoyment do not depend on it. This is supported by His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿The Fire, they are exposed to it﴾ [Ghafir: 46], and the hadith: "The spirits of the martyrs are in the bellies of birds," etc.

(p-1035) Al-Shihab said: That is, the human being is not merely the body without the immaterial soul; rather, in reality, he is the immaterial soul, and applying the term to the body is due to its strong attachment to it. He is a substance perceived by its own essence, that is, without needing this body, since he is described after his separation from it as enjoying, and the like. End of quotation.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The verse indicates that the spirit of man is a subtle body that does not perish with the ruin of the body, and whose perception, pain, and enjoyment do not depend on it. Whoever holds that human souls are abstract says: the meaning is that the souls of the martyrs take the form of green birds, or are attached to them, and thus they enjoy what has been mentioned. End of quotation.

We have already set forth, in Surat al-Baqarah, in a similar verse, further discussion beyond this. So reflect.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[170] ﴿Rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty, and they receive good tidings concerning those who have not yet joined them from behind them: that there is no fear for them, nor do they grieve.﴾

﴿Rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾ means: in what He has given them of reward, honor, and kindness, a bounty over which one does not grieve at its loss. ﴿And they receive good tidings concerning those﴾, that is, concerning their brothers, the fighters in the way of Allah, who ﴿have not yet joined them﴾, meaning they have not been killed and so joined them, ﴿from behind them﴾. This is related to *yalhaqu* (ﻳَﻠْﺤَﻘُﻮا, "join"). The meaning is that they remained behind after them, while they had already preceded them. Or, ﴿have not yet joined them﴾ means they have not attained their excellence and rank. ﴿That there is no fear for them, nor do they grieve﴾ is a *badal* (substitute) for *alladhina* (the ones), a *badal al-ishtimal* (substitution by inclusion, ﺑَﺪَلُ ٱشْتِمالٍ) that clarifies that their rejoicing is about the condition of their brothers, not about their persons. The meaning is: they rejoice in what has become clear to them of the state of those whom they left behind among the believers, namely that they will be raised on the Day of Resurrection secure, which Allah gave them as good tidings, so they rejoice in it. In this is the state of the martyrs and their rejoicing over those left behind, an incitement to those who remain after them to strive earnestly in struggle and to desire attaining the ranks of the martyrs.

(p-١٠٣٦)

[171] Concerning the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

﴿They rejoice in a blessing from Allah and bounty, and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers.﴾

That is, they are gladdened by what Allah has bestowed upon them, by the increase in honour He has granted them beyond it, and by the full payment of their reward.

Abu al-Su'ud said: It is repeated to show that the rejoicing mentioned is not merely the absence of fear and sorrow, but that it is accompanied by a great blessing, whose worth cannot be measured, namely the reward of their deeds. He then said: By "the believers" is meant either the martyrs, and referring to them as "the believers" serves to announce the exalted rank of faith and that it is the basis of the happiness they attained. Or it means all people of faith, both martyrs and others, the full payment of their rewards for their faith being mentioned and counted among what the martyrs rejoice in, by virtue of the brotherhood in religion. End quote.

Ibn al-Qayyim said: Allah Exalted consoled His Prophet and his allies concerning those among them who were killed in His way with the most excellent and gentle consolation, one most conducive to contentment with what He had decreed for them, by His words: ﴿And do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah as dead﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169] and the verses that follow. He combined for them everlasting life, a station of nearness to Him, the fact that they are with Him, the continuous provision flowing to them, their joy in what He has given them of His bounty, which is beyond contentment, indeed it is the perfection of contentment, and their rejoicing in their brothers, whom, by being gathered with them, their happiness and bliss are completed, and their rejoicing in the blessing and honour renewed for them at every moment. In the course of this trial, He, glorified is He, reminded them of what is greater in favour and blessing for them, a blessing with which they confronted every trial that befell them and every affliction, which all dissolved in the face of this favour and blessing, leaving no trace whatsoever. This is His favour to them in sending a messenger from among themselves, who recites His signs to them, purifies them, teaches them the Book and wisdom, and rescues them from the misguidance they were in before his coming, guiding them to right guidance, from wretchedness to success, from darkness to light, and from ignorance to knowledge. So every affliction and trial that befalls the servant after the attainment of this great news is a very small matter compared with the abundant good. Just as harm from rain afflicts people, compared with the good they gain from it. He informed them that the cause of the calamity is from their own selves, so that they would beware, and that it is by His decree and destiny, so that they would affirm His oneness, rely upon Him, and fear no one but Him. He informed them of the wisdoms He has in it, lest they accuse Him in His decree and destiny, and so that He would make Himself known to them through the various kinds of His attributes and names. He consoled them with what He had given them that is far greater in rank and worth than what they had missed of victory and spoils, and He comforted them concerning their slain with the reward and honour they attained from Him, so that they would vie for it and not grieve over them. So to Him belongs praise as He deserves, and as befits the nobility of His Face, and the majesty of His glory.

Then Ibn al-Qayyim said: When the battle ended, the polytheists turned back. The Muslims thought that they were heading to Medina to seize the offspring and the wealth, and this weighed heavily upon them. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib: "Go out on the trail of the people and see what they are doing and what they intend. If they have led the horses aside and mounted the camels, then they are heading for Mecca; but if they have ridden the horses and driven the camels, then they are heading for Medina. By Him in whose hand my soul is! If they intend it, I will march against them and then engage them there." 'Ali said: So I went out on their trail, watching what they were doing. They led the horses aside, mounted the camels, and set their course for Mecca. When they resolved to return to Mecca, Abu Sufyan appeared over the Muslims and then called out: "Our appointment is the season at Badr." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Say: Yes, we have done so." Abu Sufyan said: "That is the appointment." Then he and his companions departed. When they had gone part of the way, they blamed one another, and some of them said to others: "You have achieved nothing! You struck their strength only, and then left them, while remnants of them remain who are gathering against you. Return, so that we may uproot their root." This reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he proclaimed among the people and called them to set out to meet their enemy, saying: "No one goes out with us except one who witnessed the fighting." 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy said to him: "Let me ride with you." He said: "No." The Muslims responded to him despite the severe wounds and fear they had, saying: "We hear and obey." Jabir ibn 'Abdullah asked his permission and said: "O Messenger of Allah! I love that you do not attend any battle without my being with you, but my father left me in charge of his daughters, so permit me to march with you." He permitted him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims with him marched until they reached Hamra' al-Asad. Ma'bad ibn Abi Ma'bad al-Khuza'i came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and embraced Islam. He ordered him to catch up with Abu Sufyan and dishearten him. So he caught up with him at al-Rawha', without Abu Sufyan knowing of his Islam, and said: "What is behind you, O Ma'bad?" He said: "Muhammad and his companions have burned with rage against you and have come out with a host the like of which they have never mustered before, and those among their companions who stayed behind have regretted it." Abu Sufyan said: "What do you say?" He said: "I do not think you should set out until the first of the army appears from behind this hill." Abu Sufyan said: "By Allah, we have resolved to turn back against them to uproot them." He said: "Do not do that, for I am sincerely advising you." So they turned back on their heels to Mecca." End quote.

And to this refers His words, Exalted is He:

**The explanation of His saying, may He be exalted:**

[172] ﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger after wounds had afflicted them. For those among them who did good and were mindful of Allah is a great reward.﴾

﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger﴾: that is, to the call of Allah and His Messenger to go out in pursuit of Abu Sufyan, to frighten him. ﴿After wounds had afflicted them﴾ at Uhud. ﴿For those among them who did good﴾ by obeying Him. ﴿And were mindful﴾ of opposing Him. ﴿A great reward.﴾

Al-Bukhari narrated from ʿAʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, regarding this verse. She said to ʿUrwa: "O son of my sister! Your two fathers were among them: al-Zubayr and Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both. When the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) suffered what they suffered on the Day of Uhud, and the polytheists turned away from him, he feared that they would return, and said: 'Who will go after them?' Seventy men from among them volunteered, including Abu Bakr and al-Zubayr."

Abu Hisham said: "When Maʿbad turned back Abu Sufyan and those with him, as mentioned earlier, a caravan from ʿAbd al-Qays passed by Abu Sufyan, and he said: 'Where are you heading?' (p-١٠٣٩) They said: 'We are heading to Madina.' He said: 'Why?' They said: 'We want provisions.' He said: 'Will you convey a message from me to Muhammad, which I send you with? I will bring you raisins tomorrow at ʿUkaz if you meet us there.' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'When you meet him, tell him that we have gathered to march against him and his companions, to wipe out what remains of them.' The caravan passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was at Hamra al-Asad, and they informed him of what Abu Sufyan and his companions had said. They said: 'Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.' So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed concerning that:"

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[173] ﴿Those to whom the people said, "Indeed the people have gathered against you, so fear them," but it increased them in faith, and they said, "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs."﴾

﴿Those to whom the people said﴾, i.e., the caravan that met them, ﴿"Indeed the people"﴾, i.e., Abu Sufyan and his companions, ﴿"have gathered against you"﴾, i.e., the armies, in order to uproot you, ﴿"so fear them"﴾, and do not go out to them. ﴿But it increased them﴾, i.e., that statement, ﴿in faith﴾, i.e., in affirmation of Allah and certainty. The meaning is: they did not pay attention to it and were not weakened; rather, their resolve to obey the Messenger (ﷺ) in everything he commands and forbids was strengthened by it. In the verse is evidence that faith varies in increase and decrease, for the increase of certainty through the support of proofs and the abundance of reflection is beyond doubt. ﴿And they said, "Allah is sufficient for us"﴾, i.e., He is sufficient for us in their matter, without any preparation or number on our part. ﴿And He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾, i.e., the one to whom affairs are entrusted and delegated.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[174] ﴿So they returned with favor from Allah and bounty, no harm touched them, and they followed the pleasure of Allah. And Allah is the possessor of great bounty.﴾

﴿So they returned﴾ meaning: they came back from Hamra' al-Asad. ﴿with favor from Allah and bounty﴾ meaning: well-being, complete courage, an increase in faith, and steadfastness in the religion. ﴿no harm touched them﴾ meaning: no killing or wounds afflicted them. ﴿and they followed the pleasure of Allah﴾ meaning: in obeying His Messenger by their going out and their boldness. ﴿And Allah is the possessor of great bounty﴾ in that He bestowed upon them well-being and what was mentioned with it, and protection from everything that would grieve them. In this there is a rebuke to the one who stayed behind and a correction of his opinion, in that he deprived himself of what they gained.

Benefit:

Al-Suyuti said in (al-Iklil): In His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they said: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173], there is a recommendation of this phrase in times of distress and great matters.

Note:

That the verse refers to the expedition of Hamra' al-Asad is what al-Hasan, Qatadah, 'Ikrimah and others said. It is also narrated that it was revealed concerning the expedition of Badr al-Sughra (the Lesser Badr). Ibn Abi Najih said, from Mujahid, concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those to whom the people said﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173], that "Abu Sufyan said, when he turned away from Uhud: 'Our appointment is Badr, where you killed our companions!' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Perhaps!' So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ set out for his appointment until he alighted at Badr, and they met the market there, so they traded. That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they returned with favor from Allah and bounty﴾ [Al 'Imran: 174] - he said: and it was the expedition of Badr al-Sughra" - narrated by Ibn Jarir. He also related from Ibn Jurayj who said: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ set out for the appointment with Abu Sufyan, they began to meet the polytheists and ask them about Quraysh, and they would say: 'They have gathered against you; they intend to deceive them by this, wanting to terrify them.' The believers said: ﴿Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173], until they came to Badr and found its markets well-supplied, with no one contesting them over them."

Al-Bayhaqi related from 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿So they returned with favor from Allah and bounty﴾, that he said: "The favor was that they were safe, and the bounty was that a caravan passed during the days of the season, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ bought it and profited from it, and he distributed the money among his companions."

Ibn al-Qayyim said in (al-Huda): Abu Sufyan said when he turned away from Uhud: "Our appointment between us and you is Badr next year." When Sha'ban came, and it was said: Dhu al-Qa'dah, of the following year, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ set out for his appointment with one thousand five hundred, and the horses were ten mounts, and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib carried his banner, and he appointed 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah as his deputy over Madinah. He arrived at Badr and remained there eight days waiting for the polytheists. Abu Sufyan set out from Makkah with the polytheists, who were two thousand, with fifty horses. When they reached Marr al-Zahran, a stage from Makkah, Abu Sufyan said to them: "This year is a year of drought, and I have decided to return with you," so they turned back, breaking the appointment. So this was named the Badr of the Appointment, and it is also called the Second Badr. - End quote.

Ibn Kathir said: The correct view is that the verse was revealed concerning the expedition of Hamra' al-Asad.

Commentary on the Words of God Most High:

[175] ﴿Indeed, that is only Satan, frightening you of his allies. So do not fear them, but fear Me, if you are believers.﴾

﴿Indeed, that is only Satan﴾, i.e., the saying of Satan: ﴿frightening [you] of his allies﴾, i.e., he frightens you by his saying. "His allies" means the disbelievers. In this case, "his allies" is the second object of "yukhawwif" (frightens), and the first is omitted, meaning: he frightens you of his allies, as it has been read in this manner. It was also said: there is no omission in it, and the meaning is: he frightens those who follow him. As for one who relies upon God, he does not fear him. ﴿So do not fear them﴾, i.e., his allies, ﴿but fear Me﴾ in opposing My command and My Messenger's, ﴿if you are believers﴾, for faith necessitates preferring the fear of God Most High over the fear of anyone else.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[176] ﴿And let not those who hasten to disbelief grieve you. Indeed, they will not harm Allah at all. Allah intends not to give them a share in the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment.﴾

﴿And let not those who hasten to disbelief grieve you﴾ meaning: do not be concerned or troubled by what appears from them of the traces of plotting against Islam and harm to its people. In the seven canonical readings it is also recited as (yuhzinka) with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy. ﴿Indeed, they will not harm Allah at all.﴾ ʿAṭāʾ said: "He means the friends of Allah." Al-Rāzī transmitted this. Abū al-Suʿūd said: it is a reason for the prohibition and a completion of consolation, by affirming the negation of their harm absolutely, i.e., they will never by that harm the friends of Allah in any way. The attaching of the negation of harm to Allah, Exalted is He, is for their honouring and to indicate that harming them is like harming Him, glorified is He, and in this there is further emphasis in consolation.

Al-Mahāyimī said: i.e., they will not harm the friends of Allah, because Allah protects them. If they harmed them, they would have harmed Allah by rendering Him incapable of protecting them, and they cannot render Him incapable of anything. Rather: ﴿Allah intends﴾ to inflict upon them total harm, which is: ﴿to not give them a share in the Hereafter﴾, i.e., a portion of reward in the Hereafter. ﴿And for them is a great punishment.﴾ Some of the exegetes said: the fruit of this verse is that it is not obligatory to be distressed over the disobedience of the disobedient.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[177] ﴿Indeed, those who exchange faith for disbelief will never harm Allah at all, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾

﴿Indeed, those who exchange﴾, that is, who substitute, ﴿faith for disbelief will never harm Allah at all﴾. In this there is a clear hint that the harm is confined to themselves, as if it were said: they only harm themselves. As for making the relative clause refer to the particular people who were hastening (into disbelief), with the meaning that "buying disbelief with faith" is preferring it over faith, either by taking it in place of faith already present in fact, as is the case of apostates, or by taking it in place of the near potential that is present through witnessing its proofs in the Torah, as is the case of the Jews and their hypocrites, then the repetition serves to establish the ruling and confirm it, by stating its cause, through changing the subject's designation. For what is mentioned in the scope of the relative clause, namely the aforementioned exchange, is explicit that its harm falls upon themselves, and that it does not extend to others at all. How could it be otherwise, when it is a sign of total loss and everlasting deprivation, indicating the complete foolishness of their minds and the feebleness of their opinions? How then could there proceed from them what depends on strength of resolve, soundness of judgment, and firmness of planning, namely harming the party of Allah, who are more rare than the uniquely spotted (horse) and more unassailable than the eagle of the sky? And if the relative clause is taken in its generality, with the aforementioned exchange meaning the common genus that includes both of the two meanings mentioned, and with taking disbelief in place of what has taken the place of faith itself, namely the near readiness for it, which is obtained through witnessing the revealed Revelation and considering the proofs set up in the horizons and in the souls, as is the custom of all disbelievers, then the sentence serves to confirm the content of what precedes it, establishing universal rules under which particular rulings fall. This is what Abu al-Su'ud stated. Then he said: His words, exalted is He, ﴿and for them is a painful punishment﴾ is an independent sentence explaining the utmost severity of their punishment, by mentioning the extent of its painfulness after mentioning the extremity of its magnitude. It has been said: since it is the custom that a buyer rejoices in what he has bought and is delighted at obtaining it when the transaction is profitable, and suffers pain when it is a loss, He described their punishment as painful, taking that into account. End of quotation.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[178] ﴿Let not those who disbelieve suppose that Our granting them respite is good for their souls. We grant them respite only that they may increase in sin, and for them is a humiliating punishment.﴾

﴿Let not those who disbelieve suppose that We grant them respite﴾: that is, by prolonging their lifespans, giving them time, leaving them free and to their own affairs for a long age. ﴿is good for their souls﴾: rather, it is the cause of an increase in their punishment, because ﴿We grant them respite only that they may increase in sin﴾ through the abundance of their disobedience, so that they increase in punishment. ﴿And for them﴾: that is, in the Hereafter, ﴿is a humiliating punishment﴾, one that brings disgrace in the lowest levels of the Fire.

Subtleties (lata'if):
