The first: Regarding the word (ma) in His words ﴿innama numli lahum﴾, the first occurrence, there are two possibilities: it may be a verbal (masdariyyah) particle, or a relative pronoun (mawsulah) whose returning pronoun has been omitted. That is, "our granting them respite" or "that which We grant them as respite."

[p. 1044] The second: By the standard of the science of orthography (ilm al-khatt), the (ma) should have been written separately, but it was written joined in the Codex of the Imam (Mushaf al-Imam, the standard codex). It is therefore not to be opposed, and the practice of the Imam in the writing of the codices is to be followed.

The third: The second (ma) in ﴿innama numli﴾ and so on is joined, because it is restrictive (kafah).

The fourth: In His words ﴿humiliating [muhin]﴾ there is a subtle secret, which is that since granting respite includes enjoyment of the good things and adornments of this world, and that calls for arrogance and haughtiness, their punishment is described as humiliation, so that their recompense corresponds to their deeds.

Then, glorified and exalted is He, pointed to some of the wise purposes and praiseworthy ends that were present at the Battle of Uhud, namely that the sincere believer be distinguished from the lying hypocrite. When God, Mighty and Majestic, granted victory to the Muslims over their enemies on the Day of Badr, and their fame spread, some who were not inwardly with them entered Islam outwardly. The wisdom of God, Mighty and Majestic, required that He cause His servants a trial that distinguished the believer from the hypocrite. So the hypocrites raised their heads in this battle, spoke what they had been concealing, their hidden things became manifest, their allusions became explicit, and people divided clearly into disbeliever, believer and hypocrite. The believers came to know that they had an enemy within their own homes, who were with them and did not leave them, so they prepared against them and guarded themselves from them. Thus He, exalted is He, said:

The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 179:

[179] ﴿Allah would not leave the believers in the state you are in until He distinguishes the wicked from the good. Nor would Allah disclose the unseen to you, but Allah chooses from His messengers whomever He wills. So believe in Allah and His messengers. And if you believe and are mindful of Allah, you will have a great reward.﴾

﴿Allah would not leave﴾ means: would not abandon ﴿the believers in the state you are in﴾ of mixing ﴿with the hypocrites (p-1045). Rather, He continues to test you, ﴿until He distinguishes﴾ the hypocrite ﴿from the believer, the wicked from the good﴾. He distinguishes them only through this testing, because ﴿Allah would not disclose to you the unseen﴾, meaning the unseen by which He would distinguish what is in the hearts of creatures of faith and disbelief. ﴿But Allah chooses from His messengers whomever He wills﴾ by informing them of the unseen, as He revealed to the Prophet ﷺ what appeared from them of words and deeds, as He recounted some of it concerning them previously. He thus exposes them before the assembled witnesses and rescues you from their evil neighborhood.

Ibn al-Qayyim said: This is an istidrak (a qualifying addition) to what He negated regarding His creatures' knowledge of the unseen, as He said: ﴿He is the Knower of the unseen, and He does not disclose His unseen to anyone﴾ (al-Jinn: 26), ﴿except whom He has approved of from among messengers﴾ (al-Jinn: 27). Your share and your happiness lie in believing in the unseen which He discloses to His messengers. If you believe in it and are mindful of Allah, you will have the greatest reward and honor, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So believe in Allah and His messengers﴾, those whom He has chosen to be followed in beliefs and deeds. ﴿And if you believe﴾, correcting your beliefs, ﴿and are mindful of Allah﴾, reforming your deeds, ﴿you will have a great reward.﴾ Here are some subtle points:

The first: Describing the believer and the hypocrite as the good and the wicked is a marking of each of them with what befits them, and an indication of the reason for the ruling.

The second: The singular forms al-khabith (the wicked) and al-tayyib (the good) are used although what is meant by each is plural and multiple, especially after mentioning what is meant by one of them, namely "the believers" in plural form. This signals that the basis for separating one of the two groups from the other is their attribute of being characterized by these qualities, not the particular nature of their persons or the multiplicity of their individuals. This is like His saying the Exalted: ﴿That is more suitable that you may not be unjust﴾ (al-Nisa': 3). A parallel is His saying the Exalted: ﴿Every nursing mother will forget what she nursed﴾ (al-Hajj: 2), where He intended to indicate the attribute without addressing whether the one described is rational or otherwise.

The third: Attaching the distinguishing to the wicked, expressed as the hypocrite, although what is immediately understood from the preceding context, that the believers are not left in a mixed state, is attaching it to them and separating them from the hypocrites. This is because the distinction that occurs between the two groups is through acting upon the hypocrites and changing them from one state to a state different from the first, while the believers remain in their original state of faith, even though their increased sincerity becomes apparent, not through acting upon them and changing them from one state to another while the hypocrites remain in their concealment. Also, this gives greater emphasis to the warning, as indicated in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾ (al-Baqarah: 220).

The fourth: The reason the act of not leaving was not attributed to them is that it indicates concern for the one to whom it is attributed, for what is immediately understood from it is that they are not left in an unsuitable condition, as sound taste bears witness.

(p-1047) The fifth: The mention of choosing in His saying: ﴿chooses from His messengers﴾, etc., is to signal that approaching such hidden secrets is attainable only by one whom Allah the Exalted has nominated for a noble station, whose aspirations fall short of it, and whom He has selected above the masses to guide them. The generalization of choosing to all the messengers, peace be upon them, indicates that his ﷺ status in this matter is a firm matter with an established origin, proceeding according to the practice of Allah the Exalted followed among the messengers, peace be upon them.

The sixth: The generalization of the command in His saying the Exalted: ﴿So believe in Allah and His messengers﴾, although the structure of the noble text is directed toward belief in the Prophet ﷺ, to make belief in him obligatory through the demonstrative method, and to indicate that this necessarily entails belief in all of them, because he confirms what is before him of the messengers, and they are witnesses to the validity of his prophethood ﷺ. What is commanded is belief in everything that he ﷺ, peace and blessings be upon him, brought, so it primarily includes affirming what he reported about the states of the hypocrites.

This is what we have drawn from the tafsir of the scholar Abu al-Su'ud, may Allah have mercy on him. He considered it likely that this noble verse is intended to explain the wisdom in Allah the Exalted granting respite to the disbelievers after explaining that they are evil for them. The meaning is: Allah would not leave the sincere ones mixed indefinitely as He left them in that state until now, for a secret that requires it. Rather, He separates the hypocrites from them. For this reason He did so on that day, when He left the disbelievers to themselves, displaying to them the appearance of victory, so He revealed what was in the hearts of those with sickness of the wicked things within them, and they were exposed before the assembled witnesses.

(p-1048)

**On the interpretation of His saying, the Exalted:**

**[180]** ﴿And let not those who withhold what Allah has given them of His bounty think that it is good for them. Rather, it is evil for them. They will have that which they withheld hung around their necks on the Day of Resurrection. And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

﴿And let not those who withhold what Allah has given them of His bounty think that it is good for them﴾: Know that when He, the Exalted, had strongly urged the giving of one's self in jihad in the preceding verses, He began here to urge the giving of wealth in the way of Allah. He clarified the severe threat for whoever withholds it from that giving. He presented what they withheld under the heading "Allah's giving them of His bounty," to emphasize the wrongness of their conduct, since that is among the things that require giving it in His way, as in His saying: ﴿And spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾ [al-Hadid: 7]. ﴿Rather, it is evil for them﴾: to draw down punishment upon them, and to state explicitly that it is evil for them, while its being evil is understood from the negation of its being good, for emphasis in that. The tanwin (nunation) is for magnification. ﴿They will have that which they withheld hung around their necks on the Day of Resurrection﴾: an explanation of the manner in which what they withheld becomes an evil outcome.

Many of the exegetes held that this threat is by way of figurative expression (tamthil), i.e., they will be bound to the burden of what they withheld in the way a collar is bound. Others held that it is to be taken literally, that it is a kind of tangible otherworldly punishment, and they supported this with what al-Bukhari narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever Allah gives wealth but does not pay its zakat, on the Day of Resurrection his wealth will be made into a bald, venomous snake with two black spots over its eyes, which will encircle him on the Day of Resurrection; then it will seize him by his two cheeks, meaning his jaws, and then say: 'I am your wealth, I am your treasure.'" Then he recited this verse: ﴿And let not those who withhold﴾ to its end.

(p-1049) Imam Ahmad and al-Nasa'i narrated from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed, the one who does not pay the zakat of his wealth, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will make his wealth on the Day of Resurrection into a bald, venomous snake with two black spots, which will cling to him and encircle him, saying: 'I am your treasure, I am your treasure.'"

Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "No servant withholds the zakat of his wealth except that there will be made for him a bald venomous snake that follows him; he flees from it while it follows him, and it says: 'I am your treasure.'" Then 'Abdullah recited, as its confirmation in the Book of Allah: ﴿They will have that which they withheld hung around their necks on the Day of Resurrection﴾. al-Tirmidhi said: Hasan sahih.

The Hafiz Abu Ya'la narrated from Thawban, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever leaves behind him a treasure, it will be made for him into a bald venomous snake with two black spots, which will follow him, and he will say: 'Woe to you, who are you?' It will say: 'I am your treasure which you left behind after you.' It will not cease to follow him until it puts its hand into his mouth and bites it off, and then it will follow the rest of his body." Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: Its chain is good and strong, but they (the compilers of the six books) did not record it. It was narrated by al-Tabarani from Jarir ibn 'Abdullah al-Bajali. Ibn Jarir and al-Hafiz Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from the hadith of Bahz ibn Hakim, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "No man comes to his master asking him for some surplus wealth that he has, and he denies him it, except that there will be summoned for him on the Day of Resurrection a snake licking its lips over that surplus which he withheld."

Ibn Jarir narrated it marfu': "No kinsman comes to his kinsman asking him for some bounty that Allah has placed with him, and he is stingy with it toward him, except that there will be brought out for him from Hell a snake licking its lips until it encircles him." He also narrated it mawquf and mursal.

Al-shuja' (as in ghurab and kitab): the snake in general, or the male of it, or a fine type of it, which is the boldest of them. Thus in al-Qamus and its commentary.

Then He, the Exalted, pointed out that, even if they do not spend their wealth in His way, it returns to Him, by His saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾, i.e., what their inhabitants inherit of wealth and other things. So why do they withhold from Him His own property and not spend it in His way? A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾ [al-Hadid: 7]. The inheritance, on this reading, is in its literal sense. Or the meaning is that He will cause the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth to perish, and the possessions of their people, after their perishing, will pass to His pure dominion, just as the property of the one who bequeaths passes to the heir. So what is here takes the course of inheritance, since creatures claim possessions outwardly; but in truth all belongs to Him, and on this reading it is metaphorical.

Al-Zajjaj, may Allah have mercy on him, said: That is, Allah, the Exalted, will cause their inhabitants to perish, and the two will perish along with what is in them, so no one will have any dominion over them. They were addressed in terms of what they know, because they regard what returns to a person as inheritance to be his property. ﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾: that is, He will requite you for withholding and stinginess.

The discussion of the words of Allah, Exalted is He: [181] ﴿Allah has indeed heard the statement of those who said, "Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich." We will record what they have said and their killing of the prophets without right and We will say, "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾

﴿Allah has indeed heard the statement of those who said, "Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich."﴾ Al-Hafiz Ibn Mardawayh and Al-Hafiz Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: When the words of Allah, Exalted is He, were revealed: ﴿Who is it that will loan Allah a goodly loan so He may multiply it for him many times over?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245], the Jews said, "O Muhammad! Your Lord has become poor, so He asks His servants for a loan." So Allah revealed this verse.

(p-1051) Muhammad ibn Ishaq related from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Abu Bakr al-Siddiq entered the house of learning (bayt al-midras) and found many people of the Jews gathered around a man among them called (Finhas), who was one of their scholars and rabbis, and with him was a rabbi called (Ash'ya'). Abu Bakr said to him, 'Woe to you, O Finhas! Fear Allah and embrace Islam, for by Allah you know that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah; he has come to you with the truth from Him, and you find him written with you in the Torah and the Gospel.' Finhas said, 'By Allah, O Abu Bakr, we have no need of Allah because of poverty; rather, He is in need of us. He does not humble Himself to us as we humble ourselves to Him, and we are free of Him. If He were rich, He would not have borrowed from us as your companion claims. He forbids you from usury and gives us, and if He were rich He would not have given us usury.' Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, became angry and struck Finhas's face a severe blow, and said, 'By Him in whose hand my soul is! Were it not for the covenant between us and you, I would strike your neck, O enemy of Allah. So contradict us as much as you can, if you are truthful.' Finhas went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, 'O Muhammad! See what your companion has done to me.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, 'What led you to do what you did, O Abu Bakr?' He said, 'O Messenger of Allah, the enemy of Allah said a monstrous statement. He claims that Allah is poor and that they are rich. When he said that, I became angry for the sake of Allah at what he said, so I struck his face.' Finhas denied that and said, 'I did not say that.' So Allah revealed concerning what Finhas said: ﴿Allah has indeed heard﴾ the verse."

Since such a statement, whether it stems from belief or from mockery of the Qur'an and the Messenger — and the latter is the apparent meaning — proceeds only from a great rebellion (p-1052) due to its being extremely grave and terrible, He alluded to His severe threat with His words: ﴿We will record what they have said﴾, i.e., what they uttered of this great and shameful statement, in the scrolls of the recording angels. ﴿And their killing of the prophets without right﴾. It was arranged together with what precedes it only to signal their previous ugly deeds, and that this is not the first crime they committed, and that one who has dared to kill the prophets should not be considered too far from uttering this statement. ﴿And We will say, "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 182:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[182] ﴿That is for what your hands have put forward, and [because] Allah is not ever unjust to the servants.﴾

﴿That is for what your hands have put forward, and [because] Allah is not ever unjust to the servants.﴾ That is: it will be said to them, as reproach, rebuke, belittlement and humiliation, because of their violation of the sanctity of Allah, the sanctity of His words, and of His prophets who conveyed them.

Subtleties (lata'if):

The first: The plural form is used in the verse although the speaker was one (as has been related), for the satisfaction of the rest with that. Its parallels in the Revelation are many.

The second: The idafah in "ʿadhab al-ḥarīq" (the torment of the burning) is explicative (bayaniyyah), meaning: the torment which is the burning.

The third: Dhawq (tasting) is the perception of tastes; then its usage was extended to the perception of all sensible things and states. It is mentioned here because the torment is consequent upon their saying, which arises from miserliness and greed for wealth. The greatest need of a human being for wealth is for obtaining food, and the greater part of his stinginess with it is from fear of losing it; for this reason mention of eating together with wealth is frequent. (Conveyed by al-Baydawi.)

The fourth: The attribution of the hands to their deeds, because whoever does something puts it forward. The expression "the hands" for the selves is from the perspective that most of their actions are performed by them; so it is of the type of expressing the whole by the part upon which the bulk of the work depends.

The fifth: If it is said: "ẓalläm" (very unjust) is an intensive form of injustice, indicating the abundant; and negating abundant injustice does not necessitate negating little injustice. Thus if it were said "bi-ẓālim" (unjust), it would have been more indicative of negating both little and much injustice! The answer to this comes in several aspects:

One: The form indicates attribution (nisbah), of the type of "bazzāz" (cloth-seller) and "ʿaṭṭār" (perfumer), not intensification. The meaning: He is not attributed with injustice.

The second: that fa''āl has come without intending abundance, as in the saying of Tarafah:

"I am not one who alights in the valleys out of fear, but whenever the people seek help, I give help."

He does not mean here that he sometimes alights in the valleys a little, because his next words repel that: "whenever the people seek help, I give help." This indicates the negation of stinginess in every state, and because the completion of praise is not achieved by intending abundance.

The third: that the intensification is for observing the plurality of the servants, from the saying: "So-and-so is unjust to his slave," and "very unjust to his slaves." So the form is intensive in quantity, not in quality.

The fourth: that when abundant injustice is negated, little injustice is negated necessarily, because one who wrongs does so for benefit from the wrong; so when He abandons abundant injustice despite its greater benefit regarding those who are subject to benefit and harm, He is all the more likely to abandon little injustice that yields little benefit.

The fifth: that the intensification is to emphasize a wondrous meaning. This is because the clause: "and [because] Allah is not ever unjust to the servants" is a concluding parenthetical insertion confirming the content of what precedes it, meaning: and the matter is that He, exalted is He, does not torment His servants without a sin on their part. Expressing this by negating injustice is to show the perfection of His exaltedness above that, by depicting it in the form of what is impossible for Him, glory be to Him, to commit of injustice, just as withholding reward for deeds is expressed as wasting them. The intensive form serves to emphasize this meaning by bringing out the torment without sin in the form of exaggerated injustice.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[183] ﴿Those who said, "Indeed, Allah has taken a covenant with us that we not believe any messenger until he brings us an offering which fire consumes." Say, "There have already come to you messengers before me with clear proofs and with what you speak of. So why did you kill them, if you are truthful?"﴾

﴿الَّذِينَ قالُوا﴾ (alladhina qalu, "those who said") is in the accusative, by the implied "I mean" (أعني), or in the nominative, as a term of censure, by the implied "they are those who said." ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ عَهِدَ إلَيْنا﴾ means "Allah commanded us." ﴿ألا نُؤْمِنَ لِرَسُولٍ حَتّى يَأْتِيَنا بِقُرْبانٍ تَأْكُلُهُ النّارُ﴾ means "that we not believe any messenger until he brings us an offering which fire consumes." ﴿قُلْ﴾ means "Say," as a rebuke to them and a demonstration of their lying. ﴿قَدْ جاءَكم رُسُلٌ مِن قَبْلِي بِالبَيِّناتِ﴾ means "There have already come to you messengers before me with clear proofs," that is, with manifest miracles. ﴿وبِالَّذِي قُلْتُمْ﴾ means "and with exactly what you speak of," namely the prescribing of the offering which fire consumes. ﴿فَلِمَ قَتَلْتُمُوهُمْ﴾ means "So why did you confront them with denial, opposition and obstinacy, and kill them?" ﴿إنْ كُنْتُمْ صادِقِينَ﴾ means "if you are truthful in claiming that you follow the truth and submit to the messengers."

(p. 1055)

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[184] ﴿And if they deny you, [O Muhammad], then messengers before you were denied, who came with clear proofs and written scriptures and the illuminating Book.﴾

﴿And if they deny you﴾, i.e., after the refutation of their stated excuse. ﴿Then messengers before you were denied﴾, i.e., do not grieve, and console yourself; messengers before you were denied, ﴿who came with clear proofs and the scriptures﴾. Zubur is the plural of zabur, i.e., the books revealed from Him, Exalted Is He. ﴿And the illuminating Book﴾, i.e., the clear and manifest one. The zabur and the Kitab are one in origin, and they are mentioned separately only because the two descriptions differ. The zabur contains restraining wisdoms, while the illuminating Book is that which encompasses the entirety of the Shari'ah.

Benefit:

On the offering (qurban) of the People of the Book and its prescription among them.

Know that qurban (with a dammah on the qaf), linguistically, means: that by which one draws near to God, Exalted Is He, as a means to His good pleasure. The author of (Murshid al-Talibin) said: The sacrifices of the Hebrews are very numerous, and what was used for this sacrifice, by God's appointment, were bulls, sheep, goats, doves and turtledoves. The sacrifices were of two general kinds: one was offered to atone for sins, and the other as thanks to God for His mercies and blessings.

He then said: The daily sacrifice was very well known, and it was a lamb without blemish, offered as a burnt offering to God as an atonement for sins, twice a day, morning and evening, throughout the year. The one in the morning was offered for the sins of the people committed during the night, and the one in the evening for their sins committed during the day. Before the sacrifice was performed, all the people confessed their sins over the animal to be slaughtered, at the hand of the serving priest, and by this means the sin was transferred to it through the laying of the people's representatives' hands upon its head; then it was slaughtered and offered as a burnt offering. Meanwhile the congregation prostrated in the courtyard, and the priests burned incense on the golden altars, and they presented the petitions to God on behalf of the people. As for the Sabbath day, the sacrifice was doubled, and two lambs were offered at each time.

(p-1056) He then said: The Day of Atonement was distinguished by the annual sacrifice, which is that after the priest offers a bull as an atonement for the sins of his household, he offers two goats as an atonement for the sins of the people. - End quote.

The manner of slaughtering the offering and burning it has been indicated in several places in the Torah. Among them: the Book of Exodus, chapter twenty-nine. Among them: in the first chapter of the Book of Leviticus, called the Levites, and its text reads: The LORD called Moses and spoke to him from the tent of meeting, saying: Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: If any man of you brings an offering to the LORD from the animals, from the herd or the flock you shall bring your offering. If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, let him offer a male without blemish; he shall offer it at the door of the tent of meeting, that he may be accepted before the LORD. He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it will be accepted for him to make atonement for him. Then he shall kill the bull before the LORD, and Aaron's sons, the priests, shall bring the blood and throw the blood against the sides of the altar that is at the door of the tent of meeting. He shall skin the burnt offering and cut it into its pieces; then the sons of Aaron the priest shall put fire on the altar and lay wood on the fire; then Aaron's sons the priests shall lay the pieces, the head, and the fat in order on the wood that is on the fire on the altar; but its entrails and its legs he shall wash with water. And the priest shall burn all of it on the altar, as a burnt offering, an offering made by fire, of a pleasing aroma to the LORD... etc.

And in the sixth chapter of the Book of Leviticus: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying: Command Aaron and his sons, saying: This is the law of the burnt offering: the burnt offering shall stay on the hearth on the altar all night until the morning, and the fire of the altar shall be kept burning on it. The priest shall put on his linen garment, and he shall put on his linen trousers next to his body; and he shall take up the ashes to which the fire has reduced the burnt offering on the altar and place them beside the altar. Then he shall take off his garments and put on other garments and carry the ashes outside the camp to a clean place. The fire on the altar shall be kept burning on it; it shall not go out. And the priest shall burn wood on it every morning... etc.

Some have said: The rabbis claim that the fire which was in the Temple of Solomon, which the Jews were commanded to preserve without ever letting it go out, originated from the fire that came down from heaven after the offering of Aaron and his sons of the burnt offerings, and that it remained until the days of the destruction of the Temple at the hand of Nebuchadnezzar; however, there is nothing in the Torah that states this explicitly. - End quote.

(p-1057) This fire that came down from heaven, its mention appears in the ninth chapter of the Book of Leviticus, and its summary is: Moses commanded Aaron, peace be upon them both, to offer a sacrifice; so he slaughtered a calf and burned its flesh and skin outside the camp, but its fat, its kidneys, and the appendage of its liver he offered upon the altar; then he offered a male goat, a bull, and a ram in a special manner; then Moses and Aaron entered the tent of meeting, and fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering and the fat that was on the altar; and all the people saw it, shouted, glorified, and prostrated - End quote.

Having known this, His saying, Exalted Is He, ﴿Which the fire will consume﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 183] means: that it is slaughtered in the well-known manner, then a fire descends from heaven and consumes it, and this is a miracle and a sign, as happened in the time of Moses and Aaron with the descent of fire and its consumption of the burnt offering, as we have mentioned. And also in the time of Solomon, for it has come in the ninth chapter of the Second Book of Chronicles: that when Solomon finished the prayer, fire descended from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices, and all the children of Israel were witnessing the descent of the fire. End quote.

And His saying, Exalted Is He:

**The interpretation of His statement, may He be exalted:**

[185] ﴿Every soul shall taste death. And you will only be paid your full rewards on the Day of Resurrection. So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has triumphed. And the life of this world is but the enjoyment of delusion.﴾

﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾ is like His statement: ﴿Everyone upon it will perish. And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor﴾ [al-Rahman: 26–27]. In this verse there is consolation for all people, and a promise and a warning for the believer and the disbeliever alike. ﴿And you will only be paid your full rewards on the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning: you will be given the full recompense of your deeds on the Day of Resurrection, good for good and evil for evil.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "This implies the negation of what is related, that the grave is a garden from the gardens of Paradise, or a pit from the pits of Hell," I say: the word "tawfiyah" (full payment) removes this suspicion, because the meaning is that the full payment and completion of rewards will occur on that day, and what occurs before that is only a part of the rewards. (p. 1058)

Al-Razi said: God, may He be exalted, has shown that the complete reward and full recompense do not reach the responsible person except on the Day of Resurrection, because every benefit that reaches the responsible person in this world is mixed with griefs and worries, and with fear of its ending and cessation. The complete reward and perfect recompense reach the responsible person only on the Day of Resurrection, because there joy occurs without sorrow, security without fear, pleasure without pain, and happiness without fear of its ending. (p. 1059) The same applies to punishment: in this world no pain occurs that is pure and free of any admixture of pleasure, but rather comfort and alleviations are mingled with it. The complete, pure and lasting pain is only that which occurs on the Day of Resurrection. We seek refuge in God from it.

﴿So whoever is drawn away﴾, meaning: is kept far away, ﴿from the Fire﴾, which is the gathering place of calamities and evils, ﴿and admitted to Paradise﴾, which gathers all pleasures and joys, ﴿has triumphed﴾, meaning: has attained the great success, which is winning the desired goal, namely salvation from the wrath of God and from everlasting punishment, and attaining the good pleasure of God and everlasting bliss.

Imam Ahmad related from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wishes to be drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise, let his death come upon him while he believes in God and the Last Day, and let him treat people with what he would like to be treated with." Muslim also related it.

﴿And the life of this world is but﴾, meaning its pleasures, ﴿the enjoyment of delusion﴾. "Mata'" (enjoyment) is what one enjoys and benefits from, and "ghurur" (with a dammah on the ghayn) is the verbal noun of "gharra," meaning he deceived him and made him covet by falsehood. (p. 1060) The life of this world is described thus because its pleasures promise long life and hope of permanence, so they deceive a person and then cast him down.

One of the early generations (al-salaf) said: "The world is a fleeting enjoyment, about to vanish and cease. So take from this enjoyment, and act in it with obedience to God as much as you are able."

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 186:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[186] ﴿You will surely be tested in your possessions and in your persons, and you will surely hear much hurtful talk from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate partners with Allah. But if you are patient and mindful of Allah, indeed that is among the matters requiring resolve.﴾

﴿You will surely be tested﴾ means: you will surely be tried. ﴿In your possessions﴾ by what afflicts them of calamities; ﴿and your persons﴾ by killing, captivity, wounds, and what befalls them of kinds of hardship, fears, and adversities. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits﴾ [al-Baqarah: 155], to the end of the two verses. That is: the believer must be tested in some part of his wealth, or his self, or his child, or his family. And in the hadith: "A person is tested according to the measure of his religion; if his religion is firm, the trial is increased." ﴿And you will surely hear from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate partners with Allah much hurtful talk﴾ (p-1061) by word and deed. ﴿But if you are patient﴾ in the face of that ﴿and mindful of Allah﴾, that is, of opposing His command, exalted is He; ﴿indeed that﴾, that is, patience and God-consciousness (taqwa), ﴿is among the matters requiring resolve﴾, that is, among the firmly willed affairs for which the strivers vie. That is: it is what every person must resolve upon, because of the perfection of excellence and nobility it contains. Or: it is among what Allah, exalted is He, has resolved upon, commanded, and emphasized. Meaning: that is one of the resolutions of Allah, exalted is He; you must be patient and mindful of Allah. In presenting the command to be patient and mindful in the form of a conditional, there is a manifest display of the perfection of Allah's kindness to His servants. This was related by Abu al-Su'ud.

Some of the exegetes said: the fruit of the verse is the obligation of patience, and that jihad does not lapse with the hearing of what causes harm.

The discussion of the Lord's words:

[187] ﴿And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Book: "You shall make it clear to the people and not conceal it." But they cast it behind their backs and sold it for a small price. How wretched is what they buy.﴾

﴿And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Book﴾ — they being the scholars of the Jews and the Christians. ﴿"You shall make it clear to the people"﴾ — i.e., you shall make manifest all of what is in it of rulings and reports, among which is the matter of his prophethood (ﷺ). In His words ﴿"and not conceal it"﴾ there is a prohibition against concealment after the command to clarify, as an emphasis on the obligation of what is commanded. ﴿"But they cast it"﴾ — i.e., the covenant — ﴿"behind their backs"﴾ — i.e., they discarded it and did not heed it. Casting a thing behind the back is a proverb for disdaining it and turning away from it entirely, just as placing it before the eyes is a sign of complete care for it. ﴿"And sold it"﴾ — i.e., they exchanged it for ﴿"a small price"﴾, i.e., something worthless from the trifles of this world. ﴿"How wretched is what they buy"﴾ — by altering the speech of God and casting aside His covenant.

Some of the exegetes said: the fruit of the verse is the obligation to manifest the truth and the prohibition of concealing it, and this includes the clarification of the religion, the rulings, the legal opinions, the testimonies, and other things that must be made manifest. This has already been mentioned, and that what is meant by it is when it does not lead to corruption (mafsadah). Included in concealment is the prevention of books that contain the knowledge of religion, where obtaining knowledge is impossible except from them.

(p-1062) The allamah al-Zamakhshari (may God have mercy on him) said: This verse is sufficient as evidence that it is required of scholars to make the truth clear to the people, and what they know, and not to conceal any of it for a corrupt purpose, such as facilitating matters for the oppressors, comforting their souls, seeking their favor, or obtaining some benefit or the trifles of this world, or out of taqiyyah (dissimulation) regarding what has no evidence or indication, or out of stinginess with knowledge and jealousy lest others be credited with it — end quote.

From Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is asked about knowledge and conceals it will be bridled on the Day of Resurrection with a bridle of fire." — related by al-Tirmidhi. And in Abu Dawud: "Whoever is asked about knowledge and conceals it, God will bridle him with a bridle of fire on the Day of Resurrection." Abu Hurayrah said: Had it not been for what God, Mighty and Majestic, took from the People of the Book, I would not have narrated anything to you. Then he recited: ﴿And when God took...﴾ the verse.

A subtle point:

The allamah Abu al-Su'ud said: In depicting this dealing with the form of a contract of exchange, especially with the use of "purchase" (ishtira'), which indicates desire for what is taken and turning away from the giver, and in expressing the purchased item, which is the essence of the contract and the object of the dealing, by the price, whose nature is to be a means to it, and in making the Book, whose right is that competitors compete for it, accompanied by the "ba'" (bi-) that enters upon instruments and means, is of utmost eloquence and indicates the complete heinousness of their state and the extreme ugliness of it, in preferring the base and worthless over the noble and weighty, and in reversing matters by making the purpose a means and the means a purpose — the grandeur of this matter and the loftiness of its rank are not hidden — end quote.

Then the Exalted indicated that they do not see the ugliness of that, rather they rejoice in it, so He said:(p-1063)

The explanation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[188] ﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have brought, and love to be praised for what they have not done — do not think them safe from the punishment; and for them is a painful punishment.﴾

﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have brought﴾, i.e., in what they did of taking a small price in exchange for changing the words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿and love to be praised for what they have not done﴾, i.e., for fulfilling the covenant without altering or concealing: ﴿do not think them safe from the punishment﴾, i.e., having deliverance: ﴿from the punishment; and for them is a painful punishment﴾ because of their disbelief and their deception.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Humayd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf that Marwan said: "Go, O Rafi' (to his doorkeeper), to Ibn 'Abbas and say: If every one of us rejoiced in what he was given and loved to be praised for what he did not do, we shall all be punished." Ibn 'Abbas said: "What is the matter with you and this? This was revealed only concerning the People of the Book." Then Ibn 'Abbas recited: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture﴾ [Al 'Imran: 187] — up to His saying: ﴿and for them is a painful punishment﴾. And Ibn 'Abbas said: The Prophet ﷺ asked them about something, and they concealed it from him and informed him of other than it. They went out having shown him that they had informed him of what he asked them about, and they sought praise from him for that, and they rejoiced in what they had brought of concealing from him what he had asked them about. This was also narrated by al-Bukhari in his Tafsir, and by Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i in their tafsirs, and by Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Khuzaymah and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak, and by Ibn Mardawayh in similar wording. Al-Bukhari also narrated from 'Alqamah ibn Waqqas that Marwan said to his doorkeeper: "Go, O Rafi', to Ibn 'Abbas" — and he mentioned it. Al-Bukhari narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that: "Some men among the hypocrites, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out to battle and they remained behind from him, rejoiced in their sitting, contrary to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned from the battle, they apologized to him and swore oaths, and loved to be praised for what they had not done, so the verse was revealed: 'Do not think...'" — and Muslim narrated it similarly.

There is no contradiction between the two narrations, because the verse is general in all that has been mentioned. The meaning of the verse being revealed concerning that is that its occurrence came after that, not that one of the two matters was the cause of its revelation, as we have verified more than once.

Note:

This verse, although it is directed at the disbelievers for what has preceded, contains a warning to the believers against what its people were blamed for: persisting in ugly deeds, rejoicing in them, and loving praise for virtues one lacks. Included in this are the show-offs who pretend to have what they were not given, as came in the Two Sahihs from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever claims a false claim in order to increase his wealth thereby, Allah will increase him only in scarcity."

Also in the Two Sahihs: "The one who pretends to be satisfied with what he has not been given is like one who wears two garments of falsehood." Let whoever does what he should not, and rejoices in it, then expects people to describe him with uprightness of conduct, straightness of path, asceticism and devotion to Allah Exalted, beware.

Benefit:

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with the ya' and with a fatha on the ba' in the first, and a damma in the second. The subject of the first is (those who rejoice). As for its two objects, they are omitted, being sufficed by the two objects of ﴿tahsabannahum﴾, because the subject in both is one. So the second subject is an emphasis of the first, and it is good because the speech connected to the first grew long. The fa' is extra, since it is neither for conjunction nor for response, and there are other opinions.

Subtle point:

Opening the warning with their prohibition from the aforementioned supposing is to draw attention to the invalidity of their weak opinions and to cut off their empty hopes, since they used to claim that they would be saved by what they did from the punishment of the Hereafter, just as they were saved by it from worldly accountability, and their rejoicing was based on this. As for the Prophet's ﷺ prohibition, it is an allusion to their aforementioned supposing, not because supposing could arise from him, peace and blessings be upon him — so Abu al-Su'ud stated.

The discussion concerning His saying, exalted is He:

[189] ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is over all things Competent.﴾

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is over all things Competent.﴾ So He is Able to punish them.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 190:

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[190] ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day, are signs for those of understanding.﴾

﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾, that is: in bringing them into being in the state they are in, with their astonishing matters: the one in its elevation and its vastness, and the other in its lowness, its density and its humbleness; and what is in them of great observable signs: of wandering planets and fixed stars, seas, mountains, deserts and trees, plants and crops, fruits and animals, minerals and benefits of varied colors, tastes, smells and properties. ﴿And the alternation of the night and the day﴾, that is: in their succession, and each of them being a successor to the other according to the rising and setting of the sun, or in their varying, with each one increasing as the other decreases and decreasing as the other increases. ﴿Are signs﴾, that is: clear proofs of the Creator, of His great power and His dazzling wisdom. The indefiniteness (of "signs") is for magnification, both in quantity and quality, that is: a great abundance. ﴿For those of understanding﴾, that is: for those possessing minds polished by purification and refinement through constant remembrance of God, as He said:

(p-1067) **The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[191] ﴿Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides, and reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth, saying: "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain. Glory be to You; protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾

﴿Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾ That is, none of their states is free of the remembrance of Allah, which brings about purity of the outward self and affects the purification of the inward self. The intended meaning is the generalizing of remembrance to all times and not being heedless of Him, exalted is He. The mention of these particular states is not to restrict remembrance to them, but because they are the customary states in which a person is generally never free.

﴿And they reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ That is, upon their being brought into existence with these great bodies, and upon the wondrous created things and the marvelous originated things within them, so that this may guide them to the perfect power of the Maker, glorified and exalted is He. Thus they know that they have a Creator who is powerful, who governs, and who is wise, because the greatness of His effects and actions indicates the greatness of their Creator, exalted is He. As it has been said:

*In everything there is a sign of His, indicating that He is One.*

Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated in (Kitab al-Tawakkul wal-I'tibar), from the eminent Sufi Shaykh Abu Sulayman al-Darani, may Allah sanctify his secret, that he said: "I go out from my house, and my sight does not fall upon anything without my seeing in it a blessing of Allah upon me and a lesson for me." The reflection was restricted to creation only because of the prohibition against reflecting upon the Creator, since one cannot reach the essence and attributes of Him.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Salam: "Do not reflect upon Allah, but reflect upon what He has created." It has many corroborating narrations.

Al-Razi said: The proofs of monotheism are confined to two types: the proofs of the horizons (the cosmos) and the proofs of the souls (the self). There is no doubt that the proofs of the horizons are more majestic and greater, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ [Ghafir: 57]. Since the matter is so, it is inevitably commanded in this verse to reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth, because their indication is more wondrous and their evidence is greater. And how could we not say that? If a person looks at a small leaf from the leaves of a tree, he sees in that leaf a single vein extending through its middle, then many veins branch from that vein to both sides, then fine veins branch from them, and the branching continues from every vein into further veins, until they become so fine that the eye cannot see them. At this point he knows that the Creator, in governing that leaf in this form, has profound wisdoms and wondrous secrets, and that Allah, exalted is He, placed within it forces that draw its nourishment from the depths of the earth. Then that nourishment flows through those veins until a portion of that nourishment is distributed to every part of that leaf, by the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing. If a person wished to know the manner of the creation of that leaf, and the manner of governing its bringing into being and the placing within it of the nourishing and growing forces, he would be unable to do so. When he knows that his intellect falls short of comprehending the manner of the creation of that small leaf, then he measures that leaf against the heavens, with what is in them of the sun, moon and stars, and against the earth, with what is in it of seas, mountains, minerals, plants and animals. He knows that this leaf, in comparison to these things, is like nothing. When he knows the deficiency of his intellect in understanding that trivial thing, he knows that he has absolutely no way to become acquainted with the wonders of the wisdom of Allah in the creation of the heavens and the earth. When he knows by this clear proof the deficiency of his intellect and understanding in encompassing this station, nothing remains for him except the acknowledgment that the Creator is more majestic and greater than that a description of describers or the knowledge of the knowers could encompass Him. Rather, he submits that everything He created contains profound wisdoms and great secrets, even if there is no way to know them. To this points His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾, with the intention of (p-1068) the saying, meaning that they reflect while saying that. The word "this" (hadha) contains a kind of magnification: that is, You did not create this wondrous, greatly significant created thing in vain, devoid of wisdom, empty of benefit, but rather arranged with sublime wisdoms and great benefits, among which is that it be an indication of Your knowledge, the obligation of obeying You, and avoiding disobedience to You, and that it be a basis for the livelihoods of the servants and a beacon guiding them to knowledge of the states of the origin and the return.

*A subtle point:*

Abu al-Baqa' said: "Batilan" (in vain) is a *maf'ul min ajlihi* (object of purpose, an accusative indicating the reason). Here, "batil" is an active participle used in the sense of a verbal noun (*masdar*), like "al-'aqibah" and "al-'afiyah." The meaning is: We did not create them in vain. It may also be a *hal* (circumstantial accusative), its estimated sense being: You did not create this devoid of wisdom. It may also be a *na't* (qualifier) of an omitted *masdar*, meaning: a vain creation. End of quote.

His saying: ﴿Glory be to You﴾ means: exalting You above futility, and above creating anything without wisdom. ﴿Protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾. Al-Suyuti said: In it is the recommendation of this remembrance when looking at the sky. Al-Nawawi mentioned it in (al-Adhkar). End of quote. In it is also the teaching of the servants the manner of supplication, which is to begin with praise of Allah, exalted is He, first, as indicated by His saying: ﴿Glory be to You﴾; then after the praise comes the supplication, as indicated by: ﴿Protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾.

From Fadala ibn Ubayd, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard a man supplicating in his prayer without glorifying Allah, exalted is He, and without sending blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "This one has been hasty." Then he called him and said to him, or to someone else: "When one of you prays, let him begin by praising his Lord, glorified is He, and extolling Him, then let him send blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ), then let him supplicate afterward for whatever he wishes." Narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, who said: It is a sound hadith.

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, related about these sincere servants that their tongues are absorbed in the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He, their bodies in obedience to Allah, and their hearts in reflection upon the signs of the greatness of Allah, He mentioned that, along with these acts of obedience, they ask Allah to protect them from the punishment of the Fire. Then they followed that with what indicates the magnitude and severity of that punishment, which is disgrace (khizy), by their saying:

(p-1069)

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[192] ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him, and for the wrongdoers there will be no helpers.﴾

﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾ i.e., You have humiliated him and exposed his disgrace to the people of the gathering (al-mawqif). The secret of this sequence (al-itba') is the great importance of the request (al-su'al), for whoever asks his Lord for a need, when he explains its greatness and its strength, his motivation in that supplication becomes more complete and his sincerity in seeking it becomes more intense, and supplication is not connected to acceptance unless it is accompanied by sincerity. This is also a teaching from Allah, exalted is He, of another art (fann) among the etiquettes of supplication. ﴿And for the wrongdoers there will be no helpers﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) to show the extreme horror of their state, by clarifying the perpetuity of their punishment, through the absence of anyone who would help them and rescue them. Its purpose is to emphasize the appeal (al-istid'a'). The placing of (al-zalimin) in the position of the pronoun of those who are made to enter, is to censure them, and to indicate that their entry into the Fire is due to their wrongdoing (zulm), and their placing things in other than their proper places. The plural (al-ansar) is in view of the plurality of (al-zalimin), i.e., there is no helper from among the helpers for any wrongdoer among the wrongdoers. What is meant by it is one who helps by repelling and overpowering. So there is no indication in the verse of the negation of intercession (shafa'a), and the wrongdoers are, according to what Abu al-Su'ud reported, the disbelievers.

And His words, exalted is He:

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[193] ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, "Believe in your Lord," so we believed. Our Lord, forgive us our sins, remove from us our bad deeds, and cause us to die with the righteous.﴾

﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller﴾ is a recounting of another supplication of theirs. Beginning the supplication with the call (*nidāʾ*) serves to show the utmost humility and supplication. The emphasis (*taʾkīd*, the use of "indeed") signals that the statement issued from them with great eagerness and complete zeal. By "the caller" is meant the Messenger (ﷺ), and the tanwin (indefiniteness) here is for magnification (*tafkhīm*). This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and as one who calls to Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 46]. Describing him (ﷺ) as "the caller" indicates his complete concern with the matter of the call and conveying it to those near and far, because it implies the raising of the voice. ﴿Calling to faith﴾ means for the sake of faith in Allah. If you ask: what is the benefit of combining "the caller" (*al-munādī*) and "calling" (*yunādī*)? I say: the calling is mentioned absolutely, then restricted by "faith," to magnify the status of the caller, for there is no caller greater than one who calls to faith. A similar expression is your saying: "I passed by a guide who guides to Islam." This is because when "caller" is used without qualification, the mind goes to one who calls to war, or to extinguish a conflagration, or to relieve one in distress, or to meet some calamity, or to some benefits. Likewise, "guide" may be applied to one who guides to the road, or guides to sound opinion, and other things. So when you say "calls to faith" and "guides to Islam," you have raised and magnified the status of the caller and the guide. It is said: "He called him to such-and-such" and "to such-and-such" (*daʿāhu li-kadha wa-ila kadha*), and "he summoned him to it and toward it" (*nadabahu lahu wa-ilayhi*), and "he called him to it and toward it" (*nādāhu lahu wa-ilayhi*); similarly "he guided him to the road and toward it" (*hadāhu lil-ṭarīq wa-ilayhi*). This is because the meaning of the endpoint of the goal (*intihāʾ al-ghāya*) and the meaning of exclusivity (*al-ikhtiṣāṣ*) both apply together, as al-Zamakhshari stated.

﴿that believe in your Lord, so we believed﴾: that is, we complied with His command and answered His call. As for "that" (*an*), it is either explanatory (*tafsiriyya*, i.e., "namely," introducing an explanation of the call), meaning "believe," or it is verbal-masdar (*maṣdariyya*, i.e., "that" governing a verb to form a verbal noun), meaning "to believe." ﴿Our Lord﴾ is a repetition for the sake of humble supplication and a display of complete submission. ﴿Forgive us our sins and remove from us our bad deeds﴾: that is, conceal our sins for us and do not disgrace us by them, and remove from us our bad deeds by replacing them with good deeds. ﴿And cause us to die with the righteous﴾: that is, count us among them, so that we will be in their rank on the Day of Resurrection. *Al-Abrar* is the plural of *barr* or *bārr*, meaning one who is abundantly dutiful (*al-birr*, with a kasra), that is, in obedience.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, the Exalted:

[194] ﴿Our Lord, and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers, and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, You do not fail in the promise.﴾

﴿Our Lord, and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾: that is, in return for affirming Your messengers and believing in them. Or, "through the tongues of Your messengers." It refers to the reward. This is a report of another supplication of theirs, joined (ma'tuf) to what came before it. The repetition of the address (al-nida') is for what has passed. ﴿And do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection; indeed, You do not fail in the promise﴾: by this they intended to remind Him of His promise in His saying, ﴿The Day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believed with him﴾ [al-Tahrim: 8], by showing that they are among those who believed with him.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 195:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[195] ﴿So their Lord answered them: "Never will I allow to be lost the work of any worker among you, whether male or female; you are of one another. So those who emigrated, were expelled from their homes, were harmed in My cause, fought, and were killed—I will surely remove from them their misdeeds and admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, as a reward from Allah. And with Allah is the best reward."﴾.

﴿So their Lord answered them that⦆ i.e., that: ﴿I will never allow to be lost the work of any worker among you, whether male or female﴾ is an explanation of (worker) and an emphasis on its generality: ﴿you are of one another﴾, i.e., the male is from the female and the female is from the male; all of you are the children of Adam. This is a parenthetical clause explaining the reason for the sharing of women with men in what Allah promised His worshippers who work. The memorizer Sa'id ibn Mansur related in his Sunan, "from Umm Salamah, that she said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I do not hear that Allah mentions women in regard to emigration with anything,' so Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿So their Lord answered them﴾ the verse—" and the Ansar said: "She was the first woman (zaʿina) to come to us." Al-Tirmidhi related it, and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak, and said: "Sahih according to the condition of al-Bukhari, though they did not record it." Ibn Mardawayh related from Mujahid, from Umm Salamah, who said: "The last verse revealed was: ﴿So their Lord answered them﴾ to its end." And from Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him: whoever is struck by a matter and says five times "Our Lord" (rabbana), Allah will save him from what he fears and give him what he wishes. And he recited the verses.

﴿Those who emigrated﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and it is a detailed explanation of the worker among them, in a manner of magnifying and exalting him. As if it said: "Those who performed these noble deeds, namely emigrating from their homelands, fleeing to Allah with their religion from the abode of trial." ﴿And were expelled from their homes﴾ i.e., those in which they were born and raised. ﴿And were harmed in My cause﴾ i.e., for His sake and because of Him, meaning the path of belief in Allah alone, and it encompasses every harm they suffered from the polytheists. ﴿And fought and were killed﴾ i.e., they waged war against the polytheists and were martyred. ﴿I will surely remove from them their misdeeds﴾ is a oath-clause (qasamiyyah), the predicate of the subject which is the relative pronoun, and this is an explicit promise of what those who supplicated asked for specifically, after He had promised that in general. ﴿And I will surely admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ i.e., beneath their palaces rivers flow, of kinds of drinks: milk, honey, wine, and water unspoiled, and other things that no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and that have not occurred to the heart of any human. ﴿As a reward from Allah﴾ is in the place of the emphasizing infinitive (masdar) for what precedes it, since the removal of misdeeds and admission into Paradise are in the sense of recompense. He attributed it to Himself, exalted is He, to show that it is great, for the great and generous give only abundantly and copiously, as it has been said:

Should He punish, it would be a penalty; and should He give, it would be abundant, and He does not care.

﴿And with Allah is the best reward﴾ i.e., the best recompense for whoever does righteous deeds.

Then Allah (Exalted) made clear the ugliness of what the disbelievers were given of the portions of this worldly life, and He uncovered the meanness of its worth and the evil of its outcome, immediately after explaining the goodness of the reward given to the believers, by His saying:

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[196] ﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve through the land deceive you.﴾

﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve through the land deceive you.﴾ That is: their going about in it for trade and gain. That is, do not look at the abundance of provision and the attainment of what is immediate that they are upon.

[Verse 197] The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿A brief enjoyment; then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place.﴾

﴿A brief enjoyment﴾ means: it is a brief enjoyment, because its duration is short, and because it is a fleeting provision and a passing blessing. Thus it has no worth compared with what Allah has prepared for the believers.

In Sahih Muslim, it is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "By Allah, the world compared to the Hereafter is nothing but like one of you dipping his finger into the sea; let him see what it returns with."

﴿Then their refuge is Hell﴾ means: their destination, to which they resort. ﴿And wretched is the resting place﴾ means: it is the bed (firash) on which they lie.

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[198] ﴿But those who fear their Lord will have gardens beneath which rivers flow, remaining therein forever, as a provision from Allah. And what is with Allah is better for the righteous.﴾

﴿But those who fear their Lord will have gardens beneath which rivers flow, remaining therein forever, as a provision from Allah﴾ is an explanation of the perfection of the good state of the believers. It comes after an explanation and a repetition of it, following an affirmation, with the addition of their eternal abiding in the gardens, so that their joy is complete, their exultation increases, and the evil state of the disbelievers is thereby made fuller. Nuzul (with two dammas, or a damma followed by a sukun) means the dwelling place, and what is prepared for the guest to stay in: ﴿And what is with Allah is better for the righteous﴾, that is, better than the meager, fleeting enjoyments in which the wicked revel. Describing them as "the righteous" serves to indicate that the attributes enumerated are among the deeds of piety, just as they belong to the category of taqwa (God-consciousness).

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated, and the wording is al-Bukhari's, on the authority of Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and found him in an upper room, lying on a mat with nothing between him and it, with a leather pillow under his head stuffed with palm fibre, and at his feet a bundle of tanning leaves, and at his head some hanging hides. I saw the mark of the mat on his side, and I wept. He said: 'What makes you weep?' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, Chosroes and Caesar are in what they are in, and you are the Messenger of Allah!' He said: 'Are you not pleased that they should have this world, and we should have the Hereafter?'"

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abd al-Razzaq narrated on the authority of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that he said: "No soul, whether righteous or wicked, but death is better for it. If it is righteous, Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And what is with Allah is better for the righteous﴾." And he recited: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve suppose that Our giving them respite is good for their souls. We only give them respite that they may increase in sin, and for them is a humiliating punishment﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 178].

Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with him, that he used to say: "There is no believer but that death is better for him, and there is no disbeliever but that death is better for him. And whoever does not believe me, Allah says: ﴿And what is with Allah is better for the righteous﴾, and He says: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve suppose that We give them respite﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 178], the verse." And Razin narrated something similar on the authority of Ibn Abbas.

The discourse on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[199] ﴿And indeed, among the People of the Book are those who believe in God, and in what has been sent down to you, and in what was sent down to them, humbling themselves before God. They do not exchange the signs of God for a small price. Those will have their reward with their Lord. Indeed, God is swift in reckoning.﴾

﴿And indeed, among the People of the Book are those who believe in God, and in what has been sent down to you, and in what was sent down to them, humbling themselves before God. They do not exchange the signs of God for a small price. Those will have their reward with their Lord. Indeed, God is swift in reckoning.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (jumlah musta'nafah) brought to clarify that the People of the Book are not all like those whose failings were recounted: breaking the covenant, distorting the Book, and other things. Rather, among them is a group who believe in God with true belief, and who believe in what was sent down to the Prophet ﷺ along with what they already believe of the earlier scriptures. They are "khashi'in" to God, that is, obedient to Him, submissive and humbled before Him. "They do not exchange the signs of God for a small price," that is, they do not conceal what they possess of the good tidings of Muhammad ﷺ. These are the choicest and elite of the People of the Book, whether they were Jews or Christians. God, exalted is He, has said in Surat al-Qasas: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it﴾ [al-Qasas: 52] ﴿And when it is recited to them, they say: "We believed in it; indeed it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed we were Muslims before it"﴾ [al-Qasas: 53] ﴿Those will be given their reward twice, for what they endured patiently﴾ [al-Qasas: 54], and so on. God, exalted is He, has also said: ﴿And among the people of Musa is a community who guide by the truth and by it do justice﴾ [al-A'raf: 159]. And God, exalted is He, has said: ﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Book is an upright community who recite the signs of God in the night hours while they prostrate﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 113]. These attributes are found among the Jews, but rarely, as was found in 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and those like him among the Jewish rabbis who believed, and they did not reach ten persons. As for the Christians, many of them are guided and submit to the truth, as God, exalted is He, has said: ﴿You will find the most intense of people in enmity toward the believers to be the Jews and those who associate others with God; and you will find the nearest of them in affection to the believers those who say, "We are Christians." That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 82]. ﴿And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they have recognized. They say: "Our Lord, we have believed, so register us among the witnesses"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 83]. ﴿And why should we not believe in God and in what has come to us of the truth, while we hope that our Lord will admit us along with the righteous people?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 84]. ﴿So God rewarded them for what they said with gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein; and that is the reward of the good-doers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 85].

Thus He said here: ﴿Those will have their reward with their Lord﴾.

It is established in the hadith that Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, when he recited Surat Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad (Maryam) in the presence of the Negus, king of Abyssinia, and with him were the patriarchs and priests, wept, and they wept with him until they wet their beards.

It is established in the two Sahihs that when the Negus died, the Prophet ﷺ informed his companions of it and said: "Your brother in Abyssinia has died, so pray over him." He went out to the open ground, arranged them in rows, and prayed over him.

Ibn Abi Hatim and the memorizer Abu Bakr ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "When the Negus died, the Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'Seek forgiveness for your brother.' Some people said: 'He orders us to seek forgiveness for a non-Arab (ilj) who died in the land of Abyssinia?!' So this verse was revealed: ﴿And indeed, among the People of the Book﴾, the verse." Abd ibn Humayd also narrated it as a mursal report. Ibn Jarir narrated it from Jabir, and in it: "The hypocrites said: 'He prays over a non-Arab who died in the land of Abyssinia?!' So it was revealed."

Al-Hakim in his (Mustadrak) narrated from Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "An enemy from their own land attacked the Negus, so the emigrants came to him and said: 'We wish to go out to them until we fight alongside you, and you will see our bravery, and we will repay you for what you did for us.' He said: 'A remedy by the victory of God, mighty and majestic, is better than a remedy by the help of people.'" He said: "And concerning him this was revealed: ﴿And indeed, among the People of the Book﴾, the verse." Then he said: "This is a hadith with a sound chain of transmission, though they (al-Bukhari and Muslim) did not record it."

Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid: "And indeed, among the People of the Book," meaning: the Muslims among the People of the Book.

Abbad ibn Mansur said: I asked al-Hasan al-Basri about the words of God: ﴿And indeed, among the People of the Book﴾, the verse. He said: "They are the People of the Book who were before Muhammad ﷺ, then followed him and recognized Islam, so God gave them the reward of two: for the belief they held before Muhammad ﷺ, and for their following Muhammad ﷺ." Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it.

It is established in the two Sahihs from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Three will be given their reward twice," and he mentioned among them a man from the People of the Book who believed in his prophet and believed in me. (Cited by Ibn Kathir.)

Then, the information at the end of the verse, that He, exalted is He, is ﴿swift in reckoning﴾, is a metonymy for the perfection of His knowledge of the measures of rewards and the degrees of merit, and that He pays each doer what is fitting and in the measure that is fitting. It may also be a metonymy for the nearness of fulfilling what He promised of the reward, since it is one of its necessary consequences. And because it is closer to being an emphasis due to being one of its necessary consequences, it was not joined to it by a conjunction, for this reason. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 3, verse 200:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[200] ﴿O you who have believed, endure and outlast [your enemies] and remain stationed [at the frontier], and fear Allah that you may be successful.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, endure﴾: that is, endure the hardships of acts of obedience and whatever adversities and calamities befall you. ﴿And outlast﴾: that is, surpass the enemies of Allah in endurance under the hardships of jihad. Do not be less patient or steadfast than they are. Al-Musabarah (outlasting) is a form of sabr (patience). It is mentioned after sabr, concerning that which patience must be exercised upon, singling it out for its intensity and difficulty, as stated in al-Kashshaf. ﴿And remain stationed﴾: that is, persist in garrison duty (murabatat al-ghazw) at the enemy's throat, by keeping watch and preparing for war against them, and by tethering horses. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And of steeds of war [i.e., horses kept at the frontier], by which you may terrify the enemy of Allah and your enemy﴾ [al-Anfal: 60]. Ribat (garrison, frontier-station) originally means that each of the two parties ties its horses at its frontier, each prepared against its opponent. Then staying at the frontier itself became called ribat. Sometimes the horses themselves were called ribat, and ribat may figuratively be used for constancy and persistence in a matter, so it is called ribat and murabatah.

Al-Farisi said: "It is a second meaning derived from staying at the frontier, and staying at the frontier is a second meaning derived from tethering horses."

Reports have come encouraging ribat and describing its great reward. Among them is what al-Bukhari related in his Sahih from Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A day of ribat in the way of Allah is better than the world and whatever is in it."

Muslim related from Salman al-Farisi, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "A day and a night of ribat is better than a month of fasting and its night prayers. And if he dies, his deeds that he used to do continue to be credited to him, his provision continues for him, and he is safe from the tempter (al-fattan)."

Imam Ahmad related from Fadalah ibn 'Ubayd who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Every dead person is sealed upon his deed, except one who dies while on ribat in the way of Allah, for his deed continues to grow until the Day of Resurrection, and he is safe from the trial of the grave." Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi related it similarly, and al-Tirmidhi said: hasan sahih. Ibn Hibban also recorded it in his Sahih. Other hadiths remain, which al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir cited in his Tafsir.

Furthermore, among the interpretations of His saying, exalted is He, "ribatu" (remain stationed), is that it may mean awaiting the prayer after the prayer. Muslim and al-Nasa'i related from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of what Allah erases sins by and raises ranks by: performing ablution thoroughly despite hardships, walking much to the mosques, and awaiting the prayer after the prayer. That is ribat, that is ribat, that is ribat." Thus he (ﷺ) likened those mentioned good deeds to ribat.

Al-Hakim in his Mustadrak and al-Hafiz Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman who said: One day Abu Hurayrah approached me and said: "Do you know, nephew, concerning what this verse was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, endure and outlast and remain stationed﴾?" I said: "No." He said: "Indeed, there was no military campaign in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) in which they stationed themselves. Rather, it was revealed concerning a people who maintain the mosques, perform the prayer at its appointed times, and then remember Allah in them. So upon them was revealed: ﴿Endure﴾, that is, upon the five prayers; ﴿and outlast﴾ your souls and your desires; ﴿and remain stationed﴾ in your mosques."

﴿And fear Allah﴾ regarding what is incumbent upon you: ﴿that you may be successful﴾, that is, that you may attain what is a cause for envy. The word "la'alla" (that perhaps) here indicates uncertainty of outcome, so that they do not rely upon hopes.

Conclusion

Concerning what has been reported regarding the final verses of this surah, and regarding the merit of this surah in its entirety. Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: It is established that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite these ten verses from the end of Al 'Imran when he rose at night for his tahajjud prayer."

Al-Bukhari related "from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, who said: I spent the night at the house of my maternal aunt Maymunah, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) talked with his family for a while, then slept. When it was the last third of the night, he sat up, looked at the sky and said: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, are signs for those of understanding﴾ [Al 'Imran: 190]. Then he stood, performed ablution, cleansed his teeth with the siwak, and prayed eleven rak'ahs. Then Bilal called the adhan, and he prayed two rak'ahs, then went out and led the people in the dawn prayer." Muslim related it similarly, and al-Bukhari related it through another route with the wording: "Until, when half the night had passed, or a little before or a little after, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) awoke from his sleep and began wiping the sleep from his face with his hand, then recited the last ten verses of Surah Al 'Imran." The hadith. The group (of compilers) also recorded it through various routes.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, who said: "My uncle al-'Abbas ordered me to spend the night with the household of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to observe his prayer. He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led the people in the final 'isha prayer, and when no one remained in the mosque except me, he got up and passed by me and said: Who is this? Abdullah? I said: Yes. He said: What is it? I said: Al-'Abbas ordered me to spend the night with you tonight. He said: Truly, the truth, the truth. When he entered, he said: Spread out, Abdullah! So he brought a cushion of coarse wool. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) slept upon it until I heard his snoring. Then he sat up straight on his bed, raised his head to the sky and said: 'Glory be to the King, the Holy' three times. Then he recited these verses from the end of Surah Al 'Imran until he finished them."

Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i also related a hadith to this effect from 'Ali ibn 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, from his father.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out one night after part of the night had passed, looked at the sky and recited this verse: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 190] to the end of the surah. Then he said: 'O Allah, place in my heart light, in my hearing light, in my sight light, on my right light, on my left light, before me light, behind me light, above me light, beneath me light, and make for me a great light on the Day of Resurrection.'" This supplication is established in some sound routes from the narration of Kurayb from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him.

Ibn Mardawayh and 'Abd ibn Humayd related a hadith from 'A'ishah in which the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "What prevents me from weeping, when Allah has revealed to me on this night: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 190] to His saying: ﴿Protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾ [Al 'Imran: 191]? Then he said: Woe to one who recites these verses and does not reflect upon them."

Among what has been reported regarding the merit of this surah is what Muslim and al-Tirmidhi related from the hadith of al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an: "The Qur'an will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and its people who acted by it, preceded by Surah al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck three parables for them both, which I have not forgotten since: "It is as if they were two clouds, or two dark shades, with a shaft of light between them (i.e., radiance and light), or as if they were two flocks of birds in ranks, pleading on behalf of their companion."

And Allah, glorified is He, is the Granter of success.

The commentary of this surah was completed on the morning of Friday, 11 Dhu al-Qa'dah al-Haram, in the year 1318, in the sanctuary of the Sananiyyah Mosque, at the qiblah window of the upper right portico, by the hand of its poor servant Muhammad Jamal al-Din al-Qasimi al-Dimashqi. May Allah forgive him, his parents, and the believers.

Amin.
